answer: Three PM objects chain together. pm-control-entry arms supervision: set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> tca-supervision true (companion flag data-supervision; direction ingress, egress, all or na, default all; location all, na, near-end or far-end, default all; show also lists supported-parameters, max 100 elements). pm-threshold carries the limit for the one port instance: add/set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> high-threshold <value> [low-threshold <value>]; values are uint64, int64 or decimal64, or na / not-supported, default na. pm-threshold-profile does the same per resource-type, for example set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200, and its show adds default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value. New resources inherit TCA arming from pm-profile-entry default-tca-supervision.

Four objects. set ntp ntp-enabled true (default true) and ntp-auth-enabled true (default false); assignment-method is manual, dhcp or both, default both. add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <value> key-value <value> [is-trusted <value>]: key-id 1..65534, key-type sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 or md5, key-value a string of 8..40 characters, is-trusted default false, for example add ntp-key-2 is-trusted true key-type sha-1 key-value Infinera. add ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <key-id> binds the key to the server (IPv4, IPv6 or DNS name; origin manual or dhcp, default manual; admin-state lock, unlock or maintenance, default unlock; auth-key-id default not-applicable). Verify with show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>: auth-status ok, yes, bad or none (default none), reach where 377 means all recent probes were answered, plus stratum, offset, delay, jitter, poll and condition (sys.peer, reject, candidate). show clock time-source should read ntp, and show ntp ntp-active-server names the server in use.

protection-switch moves traffic within a protection group; manual-switchover moves the controller card. protection-switch [-f] operation-type=<force|lockout|manual|release> switch-target=<value> protection-group=<value>, operational mode only; switch-target is not needed for the release and lockout operations. Example: protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection. The persistent equivalent is the protection-group attribute pg-request, with values clear, manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout and exercise (bidirectional SNCP only). manual-switchover [-f] resource=<AID> switches the active controller, for example manual-switchover card-1-3, and prompts: Controller will switchover and connection to the management interface will be lost. Do you want to continue? Confirm to proceed. Check the outcome with show controller-card redundancy-status (active, standby, not-in-service).

set-time is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled, so an enabled NTP is why the manual set is rejected. Check show clock: time-source reads ntp or manual (default manual), alongside current-time, universal-time, timezone, DST-active and last-time-jump, which reports the last jump as time1 to time2 and ignores jumps of less than 10 seconds. show ntp gives ntp-enabled (default true), ntp-auth-enabled and ntp-active-server; show ntp-server-status-<ip-address> gives stratum, offset, reach (377 means all recent probes answered), auth-status and condition. If manual time really is wanted, set ntp ntp-enabled false first, then set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z, ISO 8601 with Z for UTC or +/-hh:mm for another zone. Timezone is separate: set clock timezone <name>, default Universal-Time-Coordinated. The time command prints the current time in the system configured timezone, not the one used in set-time.

show ne gives identity: ne-id, ne-name (default 1830 GX), ne-type (G30, G40), node-type (ILA, OADM, XPDR), ne-vendor, ne-site, ne-location, clli, node-controller-chassis-name (default 1), contact, plus recover-mode and equipment-discovery-ready. status, or status system, is the one-shot dashboard: NE name, id and type, active and inactive SW labels, uptime, management IP, alarm counts per severity, and chassis, card and tom counts. status equipment (optionally filtered by chassis id), show equipment and show slot list what is fitted, with supported-type, installed-type and current-equipment per slot. The cost is in restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]: with no resource-id it restarts the active controller card, and type defaults to warm. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting; warm reboots only the processor and is non service affecting; shutdown gracefully powers the card down. Connectivity returns within five minutes, and the command prompts for confirmation unless -f is given.

Slot 2 holds a card, addressed card-<name> with chassis-name and slot-name as creation keys, for example add card-1-4 required-type CHM1R chassis-name 1 slot-name 2. Nested directly beneath card are comm-eth, inventory, port, property, sub-component, tom and usb. Beneath port sit current-fw, serdes and supported-tom-power. The pluggable itself is tom-<card-name>-<port-name>, for example add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD; creating a TOM auto-creates the tributary port termination point, and deleting the TOM deletes it again. Read the pluggable FRU data with show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>, for example show inventory-1-3-1: hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class (uint8 1..8, third-party subtypes only), actual-max-power-draw and fw-status.

The model is show supported-card-<card-type>, for example show supported-card-CHM1R: node-type-compatibility (all, ILA, OADM), supported-subtype, default-card-mode and supported-card-mode, card-width (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), card-height in RUs, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support (default general-c-band), max-power-draw in W, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support (no, yes-with-auto-sensing-baud-rate, yes-with-fixed-baud-rate; default no), default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config (default false), supported-bands (default standardC-band) and supported-features. The matching per-port, per-slot and per-pluggable capability tables are supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name>, supported-slot, supported-tom and tom-type. What the fitted card is actually doing is show card-<name>: required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, category, chassis-name, slot-name, subslot-name, power-profile, max-power-draw, last-reboot-reason, last-reboot-time, parent-card, subcard-list, admin-state, oper-state and avail-state. show capabilities-<name> reports a fitted card's capabilities.

The stack is built bottom up and each layer is a stated pre-condition. The interface-<if-name> must exist first. Then add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <dotted-quad> [version ospfv2|ospfv3, default ospfv2] [router-id-mode manual|use-loopback, default use-loopback]; with use-loopback an IPv4 LO-MGMT address must already be configured. The OSPF instance must be created before add ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> (ospf-area-type normal). Instance and area must both be present before add ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>: enable defaults true, hello-interval 10 s (1..32767), router-dead-interval 40 s (4..65535), retransmission-interval 5 s, transmit-delay 1 s, ospf-cost 10 (1..65535), priority 1 (0..255), ospf-if-routing auto. Progress is in show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<area-id>/<if-name>/<router-id>: state down, init, 2-way, exstart, exchange, loading or full, with role drother, dr, bdr or ptp. The neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface goes down. clear ospf <instance> removes and restarts an instance asynchronously.

Per controller use show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>, where location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> and swload-state is active, inactive or installable, for example show software-load-1-5/active. It reports swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status, swload-information, swload-activation-type (direct, warmstart, coldstart), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label, swload-delta-label and swload-pkg-type. Individual pieces are show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> with state (installed, not-installed, installation-failed, unknown; default unknown), version and description, for example show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg; one level down is show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<component>/<subcomponent>. Bundled firmware is show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> fw-version, and versions of the same firmware can differ per equipment-type. Compare against show current-fw for what the hardware is running.

Start with lldp-admin-status on the facility: set ethernet-<name> lldp-admin-status <tx-only|rx-only|tx-and-rx|disabled>, default disabled, with lldp-ingress-mode and lldp-egress-mode (disabled, snoop, drop, snoop-and-drop). DCN and AUX ports use set comm-eth-<name> lldp-admin-status, with lldp-transmit-interval 1..16383 s, default 30. show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port> is what we send: chassis-id (the chassis serial number), port-id (the port AID), port-description, system-name (the NE name), system-description. show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/ingress is what came back, with last-update, age and ttl; the egress direction is not supported. show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/ingress separates sending from receiving: total-frames-out proves transmission, total-frames-in reception, and total-discarded-frames, error-frames, total-discarded-tlvs, total-unrecognized-tlvs and total-ageouts explain losses. Counters freeze while lldp-admin-status is disabled. Globally, show lldp hold-on-timer, default 900 seconds.

show slot lists every holder as slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> with AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment; an empty installed-type with current-equipment shown as --- means nothing is fitted. Per position FRU detail is show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> (also the <card-name>.<slot-name> and <card-name>-<port-name> forms): hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date and fw-status (not-applicable, current, not-current, unavailable; default not-applicable). Firmware level is show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name>, giving fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status per component, for example current-fw-1-1/CORE_BOOT at 0x20 against an expected 0x28, reported not-current. Hardware detected but not yet accepted by the Node Controller in a multi-chassis setup shows under show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>.

show manifest lists the downloaded manifest files; show manifest-<manifest-file> gives manifest-signature, downloaded-on and information, for example show manifest-G40_BASIC-R6.1.0-F-2023.01.04_15_40-x-sim-u-1940.manifest. Contents come from the two sub-forms: show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> gives state, version and description, where state is installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown) and answers whether each piece got installed; show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> fw-version gives the bundled firmware. show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> signature covers the image files that came with it, and show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type> gives the packaged FRU information for one equipment type. After installation the same per-package state is visible as show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>, show sw-subcomponent, and show packaged-fw for the firmware.

Two profile objects hold them. Alarm severity comes from alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location>, for example set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor, or set alarm-severity-entry-tom/EQPTCOMFAIL severity major. severity is critical, event, major, minor, not-reported or warning; direction is na, ingress or egress; location is na, near-end or far-end; show adds service-affecting (indeterminate, sa, nsa, sa-nsa). set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value> edits the same entries through the profile, and both objects are system managed and cannot be deleted. PM defaults come from set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision <true|false> default-tca-supervision <true|false>, which is exactly what newly created resources of that type get. Above it, set pm-profile global-data-supervision <auto-enabled|manual>, default manual, meaning the flag is controlled per pm-profile-entry or directly per pm-control-entry.

ipsec-spd-entry makes the decision. add ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> priority <uint8> [action <protect|bypass|discard>]: action defaults to protect, priority gives precedence between SPD entries, mode is tunnel or transport (default tunnel), ipsec-protocol is ESP, esn defaults true, anti-replay-window is 32..1024 with default 64 and applies when action is protect, dynamic-ts defaults disabled. Example: add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect. Hanging beneath the SPD entry are ipsec-sa-proposal, ipsec-sa-re-key and ipsec-traffic-selector; beneath a traffic selector hang local-subnet, remote-subnet, local-ports and remote-ports. The selector itself carries next-layer-protocol, any (value 0), opaque (value 255) or a number 0-255, default any. Above the SPD entry sit ikev2-peer and ikev2-local-instance, and security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> associates the SPD entries with a secure entity.

trusted-certificate is the CA you trust: the X509v3 CA root and intermediate certificate trusted by the system, and the thing the others point at through their trust-chain leafref. local-certificate is this node's own identity: the X.509v3 end-entity certificate representing one of the node's secure application identities; only it exposes used-by (the secure-applications, ikev2-peers and so on presently using it), plus self-signed and subject-alternative-names. peer-certificate is the far end: the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application; only it has white-listed, true when it was imported with no associated trust-chain. All three are set/show only, and settable attributes are limited to revocation-mode (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked; default auto), alarm-report-control and label. The fourth name, certificate, is the container command: show certificates, show certificate-revocation and clear certificate for deletion.

Import with import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>], operational mode, PEM format only, for example import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <PEM string> <passphrase>, or with trusted-certificate or peer-certificate as the type. The -i flag also imports intermediate certificates present in a bundle, or those referenced through the AIA extension of a single-certificate file; root certificates must be installed individually. Without a certificate-name the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix, giving names such as trusted-certificate-Nokia-1 and trusted-certificate-Nokia-2. A passphrase applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles. Removal is clear [-f] certificate type=<trusted|local|peer> id=<name>, for example clear certificate trusted id=root, which prompts Are you sure?. The id must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type; bulk options are purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused.

IP traffic is permitted or dropped by ace: add ace-<name>/<sequence-id> [action <drop|accept|reject>] with source-ip-address, destination-ip-address, source and destination lower/upper ports, ttl (1..255, default 255), protocol (default any) and direction (input or output, default input); action defaults to drop. An ACE lives inside acl-<name>, which sets type IPv4 or IPv6 and binds the filter to one interface (1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-B, DCN-2, DCN-2-B); an ACL must be in place before an ACE can be added. Evaluation order is the ace sequence-id, ranging 1-100 for AUX and DCN-B and 1-256 for DCN-A, recommended in multiples of 5 so rules can be inserted later. access-rule and access-rule-list are management access control, not traffic: they permit or deny create, read, update, delete and execute on YANG paths per user-group, the list being processed in order by sequence-id. sw-control-rule has nothing to do with traffic at all; it only sets fail-action (default-action, ignore, system-restart) when a service fails.

Lower sequence-id wins. The access-rule-list is processed in order as given by sequence-id, and within it lower number ids are processed first, so the first rule whose criteria all match applies its action, permit or deny. sequence-id is a uint16 on both access-rule and access-rule-list; if it is not provided it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, meaning the new entry goes to the end of the list, and it can be changed over the lifetime of the list to re-sort entries. On the list, user-group is a leaf-list of user-group names with a maximum of 20 user-groups referenced; the default value * matches all existing user-groups. The system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists. Each rule narrows by module-name (default *), path (default *), attribute (max 10 entries, default *), attribute-value (max 10, only valid with a single attribute) and operation (create, read, update, delete, execute; default *).

The trap community string does not live on snmp-community. The guide states plainly that the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object. Set it there: add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>], or set snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string <value> on an existing target. trap-community-string is a string of 0..32 characters and defaults to infinera, which is what your receiver is most likely rejecting. Other defaults on the target are enabled true, snmp-version v2c (the alternative is v3, where snmpv3-user applies instead), target-port 162 (0..65535) and target-transport udp. snmp-community-<name> only carries community-string (1..32 characters), enabled (default true) and community-string-access, whose only value is read-only; it governs polling access, not traps.

external-fiber-connection is the one filled in for you: the guide states it is set autonomously by TNMS, and although it can be configured manually that is not recommended. It represents the physical link between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or within the same NE in disaggregated configurations, keyed external-fiber-connection-<name> with src-node-id, src-card-name, src-port-name, dst-node-id, dst-card-name, dst-port-name, fiber-connection-type (one-way or two-way, default two-way) and scope (general-purpose or cable-id, default general-purpose; CableID verification skips any connection not scoped cable-id). By contrast fiber-connection is user provisioned and represents a connection between two distinct ports or sub-ports in the same NE, with src-port, dst-port and the same fiber-connection-type. supporting-fiber-connection is read only and simply lists the fiber-connection-list supporting an entity.

Use ipv4-address: add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>, for example add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0 or add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask 255.255.240.0. show adds origin (static, dhcp, auto-config; default static). Addresses beginning with 0, with 127, or with 224 through 255 are disallowed, and only valid netmasks are accepted. The two lookalikes are read only LLDP views of advertised management addresses, and configure nothing: show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> reports the management address received from the remote system on that port and direction (ingress or egress), with if-subtype (unknown, if-index, system-port-number), if-id and address-oid; show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address> is the same information for the local LLDP ports, with no direction key.

The stated pre-condition on ipv4-address is that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. So check show interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method; it is static or dhcp with default static, and it must be static before add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value> is accepted. Correct it with set interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method static, and confirm ipv4-enabled is true (default true). The other refusals come from the address itself: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), 127 (loopback), or 224 through 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental) are disallowed, and only valid netmasks may be configured. To see which interfaces are available, type ? after ipv4-address- for the object completion options, or use show interface, which lists if-name, if-type (ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp, hdlc), supporting-port, backup-port, protection-mode, vrf, admin-state and oper-state.

show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> is the complete picture: it shows the list of system routes from various sources, dynamic protocols and static routes alike, with source-protocol naming the origin (OSPF, BGP, static and so on) and special-next-hop as none, blackhole or unreachable, default none. Routes hang under a RIB, so show rib-<rib-name> gives the RIB with its vrf and address-family (ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast); each routing instance gets one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family and all routes in a RIB share one family. show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> next-hop-address resolves the egress, for example show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN. Hand-typed routes are added with add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> next-hop-address <ip> [distance 1..255, default 1] [advertised true|false, default false] [interface] [origin manual|dhcp, default manual] [special-next-hop blackhole], with ipv6-static-route as the v6 equivalent.

local-ports and remote-ports belong to the management IPsec tunnel; connection-ports is the connectivity one. add local-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>, and remote-ports with the identical key path, define the Layer 4 port ranges of an IPsec traffic selector. start takes all, opaque or a port number; stop defaults to 0 and the value 0 is only accepted when start is all or opaque. Examples: add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53 for a single port, add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all. Both support only add, show and delete. show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> port-name is unrelated to security: it reports the dwdm-line port of the RD or ILAx card realising a degree, so that the OMS of the corresponding dwdm port is created. degree-number is 1..20 and must not exceed max-degrees; index is uint32 1..2 but is always 1 in the 1830 GX because dwdm-line ports are bidirectional.

take-snapshot makes the copy: take-snapshot [db-passphrase=<value>] [db-instance=<value>] [description=<value>], operational mode. db-instance is temp (the default, temporary storage for manual backup and restore), manual (permanent storage for important configurations), or the automatic onehour, oneday, oneweek and rollback; taking an existing instance such as oneweek again overwrites the existing file. description is a string up to 128 characters. It is refused unless the db-passphrase used for snapshot encryption is configured, either globally through set security-policies db-passphrase or supplied on this command; the passphrase needs a minimum of 40 characters, must contain no dictionary words, and may use special characters from the 85-character Z85 set. activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>] puts it back, with the pre-condition that a snapshot must have been taken to activate it and sanity-check-override defaulting to false. show database lists what exists per database-type: active, manual, oneday, onehour, oneweek, rollback, temp, with backup-time and description.

activate is one operational-mode verb with several targets: activate [-f] swimage (activates the currently installable image; a successful activation implies a system restart; db-action auto|empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback, default auto; optional label); activate [-f] database (activates the currently inactive database, also implying a restart; db-instance active|manual|oneday|onehour|oneweek|rollback|temp, restart-type cold|warm default cold, db-passphrase 40..200 chars, sanity-check-override default false; NE name, shelf serial number and software version are checked first); activate activate-file (file-type, clear-type full|keep-networking|initialize-from-script, default full); activate location-led entity=<chassis|card> with led-mode flash|solid (default flash) and timeout 0..120 s (default 0 = no timeout, only one LED test at a time); activate eqpt-fw resource fw-image-name; activate krp; activate otdr and activate otdr-fiber-check; activate loopback <nmc-ID>. The separate database-snapshot command is activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override true|false], db-instance default temp, sanity-check-override default false, pre-condition that a snapshot must already have been taken with take-snapshot.

capabilities is the per-card one: show capabilities-<name>, where name is the card name; it retrieves information about a card's capabilities (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). l0-capabilities is the photonic one: show l0-capabilities takes no parameters and shows the capability details related to the node's Layer 0 functions. oadm-capabilities is the add/drop one: show oadm-capabilities [max-degrees] [max-adgs], where max-degrees is the maximum number of degrees (20; 0 if not supported, degrees exist only on OADM node types and ILA is 0 by convention because it has two fixed directions) and max-adgs is the maximum number of Add/Drop Groups (110; 0 if not supported, ADGs only on OADM node types). Note the maximum degree count is the maximum working degree-number, not necessarily a deployment-supported configuration. For per-card-type capability data rather than a live card, use show supported-card.

For the controller only: show controller-card-<name> [redundancy-status] [redundancy-standby-status] [number-of-switchover-events] [time-of-last-switchover] [additional-details]. redundancy-status is active, standby or not-in-service (default not-in-service); redundancy-standby-status is ready-synchronized, not-ready-synchronizing (default), not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out or card-not-present; number-of-switchover-events (uint32) and time-of-last-switchover are visible only on the active controller; additional-details is a string 0..128. For any card in the shelf use the card base object: add/set/show/delete card-<name>, with required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, chassis-name, slot-name, subslot-name, power-profile, category, last-reboot-reason, last-reboot-time, max-power-draw, admin-state and alarm-report-control. For what a model of card supports use show supported-card-<card-type>: category, card-width, card-height, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, is-field-replaceable, location-led-support, console-port-support (default no), support-serdes-config (default false), supported-bands (default standardC-band), supported-card-mode and default-card-mode.

secure-entity is the optical/L1 line one: add secure-entity-<name> supporting-facility <value> remote-secure-entity <value>, where remote-secure-entity is the remote optical carrier (1830 GX G40), the remote ODU (G30) or the remote OTUFlex (CHM7/CHM7x L1 service encryption). Attributes: enabled true|false default false, alarm-report-control allowed|inhibited default inhibited, re-key-frequency 3600..86400 s default 28800, re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic|continue-traffic default continue-traffic, traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s default 0. macsec-entity is the Ethernet one: add macsec-entity-<name> supporting-facility ethernet-<port>, with enabled default true, link-security-control must-secure|should-secure default must-secure, replay-protection enable|disable, replay-protection-window 0..4294967295 default 0, and read-only negotiated-cipher-suite. Cipher terms: for secure-entity they live in show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> (encryption-algorithm aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length key-length-256, integrity-algorithm none, dh-group ecp-521, number 1); for MACsec they are configured in mka-policy (macsec-cipher-suite, confidentiality-offset).

ase-idler-service is the per-card ASE idler function that fills unused and nmc-failed spectrum: add/delete/set/show ase-idler-service-<name>, function idler, ase-idler-enable enabled|disabled (default disabled), read-only ase-idler-state ase-enabled|ase-partially-enabled|ase-faulted|ase-disabled (default ase-disabled), alarm-report-control allowed|inhibited (default allowed). Example: set ase-idler-service-1-8 ase-idler-enable enabled. ase-idler-source is the ASE pump that produces the idler signal: set/show only (no add/delete), function ase-idler-source, admin-state lock|unlock|maintenance (default unlock), pump-enable enabled|disabled (default disabled), read-only pump-state, and target-output-power -3.00..20.50 dBm default 13. Example: set ase-idler-source-1-3.1-ase pump-enable enabled target-output-power 15.00. sw-service does not belong with them at all: show sw-service-<sv-name> / show sw-services lists the software services and containers running on the node, with equipment, location (host or container), state off|ok|fail, state-details, cpu-usage, memory-usage, uptime, last-start-time and reboot-count.

No, they are not harmless. change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]enabled|disabled toggles Zero Touch Provisioning, and change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot. change-ztp-mode disabled disables ZTP and stops it if it is already in progress; it can be run while ZTP is running. Current setting is read with show ztp. clear [-f] recover-mode clears the recover-mode flag: it confirms the current configuration as is, re-enables communication with the line cards and potentially reconfigures traffic settings, so it may be traffic impacting. It takes no parameters. Both are Operational mode and both prompt for confirmation unless -f is given. By contrast, the carrier-mode commands are read-only: show golden-carrier-mode-<card-type>/<carrier-mode>, show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> and show gcmt just list carrier-mode tuples (capacity, client-mode, baud-rate, application, compatibility-id, status, supported-subtypes).

State: show third-party-app-<app-name> [version] [vendor] [product] [label] [state] [information] [enable]. state is running, stopped or failed (default stopped) and enable is true|false, default false; when enabled the app is started and also started again on system restart, when disabled the app is stopped. Per-location state is show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> [version] [state] [information]. Firmware side: show third-party-fw-<fw-name> [file-status] [path] [version] [crc] [vendor] [part-number] [nsa-upgrade-version] [present-in-eqpt] [applicable-eqpt]; file-status is valid, invalid or missing, and present-in-eqpt/applicable-eqpt are lists of up to 80 resources. Clearing is the app command: clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>, which clears third party apps. To restart rather than clear, use appctl [app-name=]<value> [command=]restart|netls|exec [target=]<system or chassis/card AID, default system> [parameters=] (up to 50 elements, applicable for restart and exec).

Per-session is cli-session-config: set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <10..1000, default 40>, cli-columns <80..4000, default 80>, interactive-mode true|false (default true, set per CLI session and not persistent) and display-timestamp true|false (default false). For more rows on your terminal only, use set cli-session-config-<your-session-id> cli-lines 60. The protocol as a whole is cli: set/show cli enabled (default true; CLI cannot be disabled from within a CLI session), port (1..65535, default 22), script-dir (read-only), default-interactive-mode (default true, affects only newly created sessions) and show-alarm-columns (default default-columns, global effect on all CLI sessions). The two about system configuration are config and extended-config: show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)] displays the system's non-default configuration, fully recursive from the current CLI scope; add/delete/show extended-config-<name> [description] configures non-standard extended config that introduces exceptional behavior globally, and the name must match one known by the system.

The generic attribute assignment is set: set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...]. It changes attributes of existing managed entities, requires at least one attribute-value pair (all from the same entity), supports wildcards (card-*, port-1-4-*, admin* auto-completion), ranges and lists (card-1-[1..4], interface-[DCN,CRAFT]) and filters of the form <attribute>=<value>. It asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances; -v validates and -f forces. The separate operations are set-alarm-state and set-time. set-alarm-state [state=]<value> [[acknowledge-text=]<value>] (all-alarms | [alarm-id-list=]<value>...) changes an alarm's operator state; state is mandatory and the user may select none, ack or close; alarm-id-list takes 1 to 10 alarm ids; acknowledge-text is 0..256 chars. set-time [new-time=]<value> changes the system time, only applicable when time-source is manual (NTP not enabled), using ISO 8601 combined date and time such as 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z or with +/-hh:mm. The one ending in -set is named-value-set: add/set/delete/show named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <1..1024 chars>].

mc is the Media Channel, the spectrum slot on an OMS: add mc-<name> parent-oms <value> lower-frequency <value> upper-frequency <value> (all in MHz); center-frequency and slot-width are calculated by the system, and the referenced supporting-card must be part of a Degree, not an ADG. nmc is the Network Media Channel, the actual carrier inside an MC or directly on an OMS: add nmc-<name> parent-facility <MC or OMS> center-frequency <190650000..196700000 MHz> [width <15000..200000 MHz, default 35000>], plus power and attenuation controls (input-attenuation-target and output-attenuation-target default max, power-actual-rx/tx, ase-insertion-enable default disabled, ase-insertion-soak-timer 0..600 s default 5). Both have auto-delete, default disabled, allowed only on RD66TM sleds with l0-mode-op=hsc-ols. The fillers occupy unused spectrum: mc-f (Media Channel Filler) is show-only with lower-frequency, upper-frequency and slot-width; nmc-f (Network Media Channel Filler) is set/show with admin-state and alarm-report-control plus alloc-lower/upper-frequency, alloc-bandwidth (default 75000 MHz), actual-lower/upper-frequency, actual-bandwidth (default 0), power-actual-rx/tx and monitoring-state (enabled by default).

What runs the scan: activate otdr [entity=]<port> [[otdr-file-prefix=]<value>] triggers an OTDR measurement on the target OTDR port, and activate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<ots-r-id> runs a manual OTDR-based fiber check (up to 3 tests with intermediate and final results; it errors out if a manual scan or automatic Raman fiber check is already running). Where you tune it: otdr-ptp. set otdr-ptp-<name> otdr-range <auto|0..300.0 km, default auto; recommended fiber length plus 10 percent>, otdr-pulse-width <auto|10..20000 ns>, otdr-measurement-speed fast|medium|slow|precision|auto|high-precision (default auto), otdr-ior <auto|1.0..2.0>, otdr-fiber-type (default auto; SMF-ULL must be used for integrated OTDR in RD66TM and D2ILASGM and for HSC-OLS), otdr-resolution <auto|0.4..100.0>, otdr-direction-mode (default counter-prop-in-service), peak-power <auto|5..14.5>, launching-fiber-length 0..50 m default 0. Where the answer comes out: show otdr-ptp otdr-fiber-break-distance (distance of the break in km, not-available if none identified), otdr-last-measurement and otdr-last-measurement-file (the generated .sor file). Live progress is show otdr otdr-state (not-available, idle, measuring, finished, fail), otdr-measurement-time, otdr-measurement-port, otdr-measurement-direction and otdr-ongoing-measurement-profile.

The name server entry comes back because of its origin. dns-server-<address> has an origin attribute with values dhcp (the address was assigned to this system by a DHCP server) and manual (manually configured), default manual; you convert a DHCP-learned entry into a manual one by setting origin to manual, for example set dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin manual. Whether the system holds DHCP-supplied values at all is decided by the global dns object: set dns assignment-method manual|dhcp|both (default both), enabled true|false (default true) and search (DNS search suffix, must contain at least one dot, cleared with an empty string). For the relay, two things must both be configured. Globally: set dhcp-relay mode disabled|ipv4|ipv6 (default disabled) and server-address (at least one IPv4 or IPv6 address must be configured when enabled). Per interface: set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true|false, default false, and this per-interface flag obeys the global dhcp-relay settings. A relay does nothing until the global mode is set away from disabled with a server address and the interface flag is set to true.

The command is clear [-f] system [type=]<value> [[target=]<value>] [[restart-behavior=]<value>] [[action=]<value>], which wipes the system or a specific instance and resets it to factory configuration with a secure wipe. type has three modes. factory-reset resets the system or a particular equipment to factory configuration, stopping target traffic services and removing the respective files and user configurations, which may imply loss of connectivity; it does not take effect for G30 Optical Carrier-Cards (OCC2T, OCC2E) but is supported for the G30 controller card (FRCU), and the shutdown option is not supported on L0 cards. full-wipe cleans the entire system and reinstalls the software on the controller and line cards, removing all files, configurations and software; a base software reinstall from ONIE is then required to recover the system, and it is not supported for G30 line cards (CHM1R, UTM2) or OCC2T/OCC2E. inactive just clears the inactive software partition. target defaults to the entire system or can be a chassis or card AID; restart-behavior is restart (default) or shutdown. The option that leaves logs and PM data behind is clear database: it sets the NE database to default and reboots, but explicitly does not wipe logs, PM data and other non-configuration data (clear-type full, keep-networking or initialize-from-script, default full).

Read show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>. That command lists detected inventory that has not yet been accepted by the Node Controller in a multi-chassis configuration, with hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and detection-timestamp (the last time the Node Controller detected the unprovisioned equipment). If a chassis appears there, it has been seen but not taken in. On the accepted side, show chassis-<name> gives is-node-controller (true/false), chassis-role unknown|main-chassis|sub-chassis (default unknown), expected-serial-number (this is how you inform the Node Controller of a sub-chassis serial number; for the main chassis it is auto-filled), equipment-discovery-ready (false until all equipment was discovered during startup) and alarm-report-ready. To provision it, use add chassis-<name> required-type G31|G32|G34c|G42 expected-serial-number <serial>. show equipment and show inventory cover installed equipment and FRU inventory.

The deciding attribute is amplifier control-mode: auto-max-pw (the automatic mode targeting maximum output power, and the default) or manual. In manual you set gain-target yourself, range 0..40 dB, default 0.0, and read back gain-operating. amp-control-support tells you whether auto is even permitted on that amplifier: auto means manual and auto-max-pw are both supported, manual-only means only manual. gain-range-control follows control-mode automatically (manual control-mode forces gain-range-control manual, auto-max-pw forces auto); with manual gain-range-control you pick gain-range-target standard|low|high. In auto mode you bias the result with gain-adjustment, range -20.00..20.00, default 0, supported only where function is pa or inline. What stops output entirely: amplifier-enable disabled (default disabled), and even when enabled the output power depends on the existence of the OSC signal for node-type ILA, and on OMS related facilities and the existence of an OXcon for node-type OADM. Also forced-shutdown true (shuts down one amplifier on dual-band cards, default false), admin-state lock, and OLOS shutdown after olos-shutdown-soak-timer 0..2000 ms unless olos-shutdown-disable is set true.

Which member is live comes from show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name>: state is active, standby, available or unknown, and role is working or protection; transport-entity identifies the underlying facility. At group level, show protection-group-<name> gives pg-state (no-request, forced-to-working, sf-on-working, wait-to-restore, unavailable and so on, default unavailable), last-switch-trigger, remaining-wtr and switch-failure-reason; show protection lists protection overall. The settings that decide switch behaviour are on protection-group: switching-mode unidirectional (default) or bidirectional; reversion-mode revertive or non-revertive (default non-revertive); hold-off-timer, the trigger soak time before switching, 0..10000 ms in 1 ms steps, default 0; wtr-timer, the clearance soak before reverting, 60..720 s in 1 s steps, default 300, revertive mode only; and the four triggers client-side-olos-trigger, client-side-sd-trigger, network-side-csf-trigger and network-side-sd-trigger, all enabled|disabled with default disabled. Operator action is pg-request (clear, manual-to-working/protection, forced-to-working/protection, protection-lockout, exercise) and pg-control-request freeze|clear-freeze, or the protection-switch command with operation-type force|lockout|manual|release.

Trigger the check with verify [-f] [type-select=]fiber-connection [[target-select=]<port-id>] [allow-switching]. target-select is the port instance-identifier of the CableID-capable card; if omitted, all paths are verified. If the port is involved in multiple CableID paths, all of them are included. allow-switching is boolean, default false: true lets the verification initiate switching on the OPSM so both active and inactive paths are checked, false verifies active paths only. The pre-condition is that the equipment-policies attribute cable-id-control is set to enabled. The command prompts for confirmation unless -f is used, and on acceptance the system raises the CID-verification-in-progress alarm against the NE until all queued requests complete. It is non-blocking and replies that you should use show cable-id-status. Watch progress with show cable-id-status: cable-id-state is idle, running-incl-switching or running-no-switching (default idle), and test-progress is a string such as 1 out of 1 completed (N out of M port-pairs). show cable-id lists the CableID entities, show cable-id-path shows the paths, and terminate cable-id stops all running CableID verification tests.

Where authentication is sent is decided by aaa-server. add aaa-server-<server-name> protocol-supported RADIUS (default) or TACACSPLUS, server-address <IP>, server-priority 1..10 sorting the servers in order of precedence (if omitted, the lowest precedence in use plus 1), transport, server-port default 49, server-port-authentication default 1812, server-port-accounting default 1813, shared-secret (maximum 64 characters, anything longer is denied; displayed as *; default sharedkey), role-supported accounting/authentication/authorization (default all three), enabled true|false default true, source-ip as the source address for RADIUS communications, and common-password used for RADIUS authorization after SSH public key authentication (if blank the username is reused as the password). What happens when it does not answer is governed by timeout, the response timeout for Access-Request messages, 1..90 seconds, default 5, and retry, the number of attempted Access-Request messages to a single server before failing authentication, range 0..5; the total wait time, timeout x (retry + 1), should be less than 5 minutes. TACACS+ counters are visible with show aaa-statistics. The global rule set is authorization mode static-only|static+rules|rules-only, default static+rules.

ssh-authorized-key holds the trusted public key used to authenticate a user logging in to the node, which is what you want for the automation account: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>], where user-name is the local or remote user owning the key (0..32 chars), key-id is a unique name (1..64), public-key is the OpenSSH/PEM encoded string up to 2048 chars, and public-key-algorithm is reported as ecdsa-sha2-nistp256/384/521 or ssh-rsa2048/3072/4096. ssh-known-host holds the remote host's key that the node must trust when it connects out: add ssh-known-host-<id> address <hostname/IPv4/IPv6> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value> [label], with the same algorithms plus ssh-ed25519 (available from R9.0). ssh-host-key is the node's own identity, the global SSHv2 host keys used by both server and client side SSHv2 apps, one per supported algorithm; the system auto-generates one in the default DB and additional keys are added or overwritten via the ssh-keygen RPC. show ssh-host-key-<public-key-algorithm> also returns fingerprint-algorithm md5|sha256 and fingerprint.

The key agreement policy lives in mka-policy: add/set/show/delete mka-policy-<name> with key-server-priority (used by MKA to select the key server), macsec-cipher-suite (cipher suites for Secure Association Key derivation), confidentiality-offset (the number of octets in an Ethernet frame sent as unencrypted plain text) and sak-rekey-interval. sak-rekey-interval is what sets how often the session key rolls over: the Secure Association Key rekey interval in seconds, range 0 or 30..65535, default 30 s. The policy is bound to a port through macsec-mka: set macsec-mka-<name> mka-policy <policy name>, connectivity-association-key and connectivity-association-key-name (both strings 0..64), psk-lifetime and psk-expiration-warning (1..173 days, default 14 days), psk-lifetime-enable enabled|disabled, plus read-only is-key-server (default false) and psk-configured-timestamp. Watch the channels with show sc-tx-<name>/<index> and show sc-rx-<name>/<index>: sci-tx/sci-rx as a 16-character hex string, state in-use or not-in-use, association-number, key-identifier and next-packet-number. Port-level MACsec policy itself is macsec-entity.

NETCONF listens over ssh on port 830 by default (range 1..65535) and is enabled by default (enabled true; NETCONF cannot be disabled from within a NETCONF session). Other netconf attributes: hello-timeout 1..3600 s, default 2; annotate-cli-name default false; static-info-in-notifs, up to 10 YANG identifiers. gNMI over gRPC uses port 50051 by default and grpc enabled is true by default; gnmi-get-encoding-granularity is per-path or per-object, default per-object; the grpc object is system managed and cannot be manually deleted. So neither NETCONF nor gNMI is off out of the box. For completeness, RESTCONF is enabled by default with https-enabled true on https-port 8181, but http-enabled defaults to false on http-port 8080 and RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode; cookie-timeout is 1..300 minutes, default 5. The CLI management protocol itself listens on port 22 by default.

restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>] requires confirmation unless -f is given. If resource-id is omitted the active node controller is restarted; if type is omitted a warm start is done by default. warm reboots the processor of the CHM6, UCM4 and similar and is non service affecting, with connectivity regained within five minutes; on XMM4 a warm reboot is non-service-affecting but visibility is lost for 3 minutes. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting, again with connectivity back within five minutes; a cold reboot of XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost, while a cold reboot of CHM6 or UCM4 is service affecting. shutdown gracefully shuts the card down and it becomes unreachable. No, you cannot assume every card behaves the same: not all cards support all restart types. What can be restarted is card (cold, warm, shutdown), a card sub-component (cold, warm only; list them with show card resources) and tom (cold only). Example: restart card-1-4 DCO cold.

Three things must be in place. First, the global flag: set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates true. Its values are enabled/disabled with default disabled, and application of serdes-templates depends on this flag being true. On enabling, templates are not retro-applied; they apply from that moment onward, and on disabling nothing changes, existing serdes configuration is kept on all TOMs. Second, a template keyed on the TOM part number: add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <1..16 chars>] [card-types-applicable] [ports-applicable], where ports-applicable is all by default or a list of up to 20 port names such as T1, T10. Third, the parameter values: add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> value <value>, for example add serdes-template-entry-T-DQ4CNT-NIN/RxEQ value 3, with names such as RxEQ, TxEQ, RxAmplitude, RxPreCursor, RxPostCursor, TxEQAdaptive (name and value strings 0..256). Templates apply to all line cards that support serdes, so the card's supported-card support-serdes-config must be true. When a TOM with that part-number is plugged in, the template is applied automatically. Manual serdes configuration is still possible and is kept even if it deviates; swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template; and you can force re-application with the apply-template command.

ots is the Optical Transport Section, the fibre span between two nodes: fiber-type-tx/rx (default SSMF), fiber-length-tx/rx auto or 0..500.0 km, span-loss-transmit and span-loss-receive 0..80 dB (99 dB means not configured), span-loss-reference configured|measured (default measured), span-loss-alarm-threshold, external-attenuation-tx/rx 0..30 dB, span-loss-aging-margin-rx 0..10 dB default 1.0, target-power-setting manual|auto|auto-plan (default auto), laser-safety-mode OPLM or APSD, osc-compatibility osc-g30 (default) or osc-7100, osc-less. oms is the Optical Multiplex Section, the multiplexed band carried on the span, on which MCs and NMCs sit: monitoring-mode (intrusive, non-intrusive, not-monitored, ila-with-equalization, integrated-equalization, dge-fixed-attenuation), grid-mode flexible (default) or fixed-50G-96ch/fixed-100G-48ch/fixed-75G-64ch/fixed-75G-64ch-oif/fixed-50G-7100/fixed-150G-40ch, lower-frequency 191300000 and upper-frequency 196150000 MHz, attenuation-control-mode-rx/tx auto|manual, assigned-degree. ops is the Optical Physical Section, a single physical port with a role: tributary, multi-carrier, general-purpose (default), ase-input or active-multi-carrier, plus input-psd-profile -30..-6 dBm/12.5GHz (default -6) and port-expansion no|y-cable. osc is the Optical Supervisory Channel and is the one carrying supervisory traffic: osc-mode OC3 (155 Mbit/s) or 1GE for HSC OLS nodes, l0-comm-interface-type ipv4 or ipv6, osc-control auto (default) or manual, target-output-power -2.5..4.5 dBm, tx-power-adjustment -6..6 dB, voa-attenuation-target-rx 0..30 dB default 10, lof-soak-timer short (default, about 3 ms) or long (adds about 2300 ms).

The behaviour is the Tributary Disable Action on the trib-ptp facility. set trib-ptp-<name> tributary-disable-action <value> defines what the network element does towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed: it either shuts off the laser or inserts a replacement signal. Values are laser-shut-off (the default), none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais and send-nos (1830 GX G30 only). So by default the node turns the client laser off. Delay it with tributary-disable-holdoff-timer, range 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0 where 0 disables the holdoff; it applies when the TDA action is laser turnoff, holding the optical signal as it is until the configured hold-off timer expires, after which the laser is turned off. Related attributes on the same object: near-end-tda enabled|disabled default disabled, tda-degrade-mode enabled|disabled default disabled (BERSD-ODU triggering ALS), and forward-defect-trigger true|false default true, which decides whether a client forward defect such as LF or ODU-AIS received on egress flows through to the line side or instead triggers an egress TDA action. Example: set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off.

The high order ODU is system-created: show odu reports class high-order for the top ODUCn/ODUk, and the HO-ODU appears automatically when the super-channel is created. managed-by defaults to system, and only user-created facilities can be user deleted. trib-ptp is auto-created with the TOM and auto-deleted with it; flexo offers only set/show. You build by hand: add flexo-group-<name> carriers <v> rate <v> modulation-format <v> group-id <1..1048575>; add otu-<name> parent flexo-group-... time-slots <v>; the low order ODUs, add odu-<name> odu-type ODU4i|ODUflexi|ODU4|ODUflex parent-odu <HO-ODU> with time-slots/opucn-time-slots and trib-port-number; and add xcon-<name> source <v> destination <v> (managed-by default user). Pre-condition: the Super-channel must be added before Low Order ODUs can be added. odu-type ODUflex also requires client-signal-type (200GBE, 400GBE, FC4G, FC8G, FC16G, FC32G; default not-applicable).

BER testing is the bert command, Operational mode: bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=egress test-duration=10, plus bert stop|get|delete test-id=. test-signal-type is none|PRBS31|PRBS31NONINV|scrambled-idles (default none); 100GE/400GE use scrambled-idles, ODU4 uses PRBS31. test-duration is minimum 10 seconds, maximum 1000 hours, 0 means indefinite; test-id is generated if omitted but mandatory for bert stop. Standing patterns are injected per facility with test-signal-type on ethernet, stm and odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction>: none, PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9, PRBS31, PRBS31_NONINV (default none), with test-signal-direction ingress|egress|both and test-signal-monitoring true|false (default false). Loopback is set with loopback none|facility|terminal (default none) on ethernet, otu, stm and optical-carrier, with loopback-mode loopback or loopback-and-continue.

Each end needs a provisioned secure-entity plus an authenticated IKEv2 peering. Add secure-entity-<name> with supporting-facility (optical-carrier or odu) and remote-secure-entity pointing at the far-end AID (remote optical-carrier on 1830 GX G40, remote ODU on G30, remote OTUFlex for CHM7/CHM7x), then enabled true (default false). Under it, ikev2-peer-<local-instance>/<peer> must be authenticated: authentication-scheme x.509-certificate (default) or pre-shared-key, with local-certificate and peer-certificate referencing installed certificates. For Datapath Encryption ppk-required must always be true. Both ends must agree on the secure-entity-sa-proposal (aes-gcm-16, key-length-256, integrity none, dh-group ecp-521). Timers: re-key-frequency 3600..86400 s (default 28800), re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic|continue-traffic (default continue-traffic), traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s (default 0).

The telemetry command configures persistent and dynamic telemetry; the object is system-managed and cannot be manually deleted (show telemetry, set telemetry id <string>, 0..4096). What is subscribed: show subscriptions for the list, and show current-subscription-<subscription-name> for the subscriptions configured in the system, giving related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc), encoding (json, bytes, proto, ascii, json-ietf; default json-ietf), transfer-mode (stream, once, poll; default stream) and updates-only (default false). What each one watches: show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>, giving subscription-path (1..520), subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode (target-defined, on-change, sample; default target-defined), sample-interval and heartbeat-interval in ms (default 0), suppress-redundant (default true). Dial-out subscriptions reference a dial-out-server (port default 4334).

The configuration database is encrypted at rest. show db-protection-scheme reports encryption-algorithm xts-aes-256-plain64, integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512 or none, integrity-status passed-on-bootup/failed-on-bootup/disabled, and mode encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity (changed through db-migrate). Before you can take a copy, the db-passphrase that encrypts DB snapshots must be configured, either globally with set security-policies db-passphrase (string 40..200 characters, minimum 40, no dictionary words, Z85 character set) or inline as take-snapshot db-passphrase=***; without it take-snapshot is rejected and automatic snapshots stay disabled. take-snapshot [db-instance=] accepts temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek, rollback, with optional description (0..128). List with show database, then activate-snapshot db-instance <x> db-paraphrase <x>, or upload database to a configured file-server.

Start at show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]: each RIB is keyed by name (1..64), bound to one vrf, and holds a single address-family, ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast; the system provides one default RIB per address family per routing instance. Then show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol] shows the installed route and where it came from; special-next-hop is none (default), blackhole or unreachable, and blackhole/unreachable routes get no next-hop created under them. Check resolution with show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface>, for example show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN. For a static route, show ipv4-static-route-<prefix>/<vrf> gives distance 1..255 (default 1), advertised true/false (default false), origin manual/dhcp and monitoring-state unmonitored/ok/failed. The interface VRF must match the static route vrf. Confirm the instance with show vrf-<name> [type] (mgmt or internal).

Rejection is governed by set security-policies. strict-password-check (true/false, default true) requires minimum length 8 with at least one lower case, one upper case, one number and one symbol, and the user name may not be part of the password; disabled, the only rule is minimum length 1. minimum-password-length is 1..200, default 8. enforce-password-history-check (default true) blocks reuse, with password-history-size 1..200, default 5. These checks apply only to newly defined passwords. Lockout is per user: set user-<user-name> max-invalid-login, consecutive invalid attempts before suspension, 0-255, default 5, and suspension-time in minutes, 0-1440, default 5. show user-<user-name> user-status returns lockout, and failed-logins resets on a successful login. Clear the stuck session with show session to get the session-id in <ip-address>:<port> form, then kill-session <session-id> in Operational mode; it cannot target your own session. max-sessions is 1-20 (default 10), timeout 0-1440 minutes (default 60).

The global container is syslog. remote-logging-switch (true/false, default true) is the single switch that turns off every remote logging destination when set false. Other syslog defaults: source-address localhost, log-file-message-coalescence true, log-relay false, assignment-method both, niap-compliant-logging false, privacy-mode false, alarm-report-control allowed. Local files use add/set log-file-<name>: number-of-files is the maximum retained, uint8 range 1..20, default 10, with the oldest discarded past that count; max-file-size is uint8 1..30 megabytes, default 30; source-facilities default all, sensitive-data none, pattern-match 0..255; default severity is informational and above, and the default system log file cannot be edited or deleted. Remote targets use add log-server-<name>: enabled true, port 514 (1..65535), transport udp (tcp/udp/tls), message-format rfc5424, message-coalescence true. set log-console enabled defaults to false.

What is raised now is the alarm list: show alarms / show alarm-<alarm-id>, filterable by resource, resource-type, AID, alarm-type, perceived-severity, reported-time, service-affecting, alarm-category and operator-state; show current-alarms gives number-of-alarms and last-changed. Manual clearing is clear [-f] alarm [alarm-type=]<value> [resource=...], for example clear alarm DBRESTOREFAIL. Only alarms with no automatic clear criteria qualify: list them with show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true, and this applies only to system-wide alarms not tied to a resource. Acknowledgement is separate: set-alarm-state <state> (none, ack, close) with all-alarms or an alarm-id-list of 1 to 10 ids, plus optional acknowledge-text (0..256). Whether inhibiting reporting drops alarms already up is decided by set alarm-control arc-behavior: leave-alarms (default) keeps them raised, clear-alarms clears them when ARC is set to inhibit.

The Equipment dashboard is the temperature view: status equipment lists chassis, cards per chassis with subtype and toms per card, with temperature sensors, power values, presence, oper-state and alarms (for example chassis-1 temp 25C power 2.1/4400 W, card-1-1 temp 25C, fan speed as a percentage). Its filter is a chassis id only, as in status equipment 5; wildcards are not supported, so it is either all chassis or one. To get down to a single slot use the PM data for that card: show pm card-1-7 returns the real-time temperature (C) parameter with instant, avg, min and max. The physical reflection is the LED objects: show led-<location>/<name> status or show led status, with status values not-available (default), off, yellow, flashing-yellow, green, flashing-green, red, flashing-red, amber, flashing-amber, cycling and cycling-with-off; fault, power and fan1-fault through fan7-fault LEDs exist per FRU.

The line is the OTS facility. show ots-<name> gives span-loss-derived-rx and span-loss-derived-tx, the measured span loss based on OSC including losses external to the fiber (decimal64, 2 fraction digits, 0..99 dB, where 99 dB means OLOS and the value is only relevant when an OSC channel exists), against the configured span-loss-transmit and span-loss-receive (0..80 dB, default 0; 99 dB also means not configured on receive). span-loss-reference selects which is used for automatic target OXcon powers, configured or measured, default measured. span-loss-alarm-threshold is set autonomously by the system, 0..80 dB or 99, default 99, persistent across warm and cold boot, and refreshable with update. span-loss-aging-margin-rx is 0.00..10.00 dB, default 1.0. The amplifier shows the compensation: gain-operating and gain-target 0..40 dB, control-mode auto-max-pw (default) or manual, gain-range-actual standard/low/high, tilt-actual, input-power-mon and output-power-mon (-99.00..99.00 dBm), and control-state converged/fine-tuning/adjusting/stopped. span-loss-control (default enabled) must be enabled when span-loss-reference is measured.

The client enters at trib-ptp-<name>, the tributary client physical termination between the TOM and the protocol layer, carrying service-type (100GBE, 400GBE, OTU4, 4x100GBE, OTU2, OTU2e, 1GBE, 10GBE, OC48, OC192, STM16, STM64) and tributary-disable-action (default laser-shut-off). Above it sits the protocol facility, ethernet-<name> (tx-mapping-mode GMP default, BMP, openZR+, GFP-F, AMP), stm-<name> or a client otu-<name>. That client is mapped into an ODU by add xcon-<name> source ethernet-1-4-T1 destination odu-1-4-T1-1-ODUni-1, whose payload-treatment (transport, switching, transport-without-fec, regen, regen-switching) and network-mapping record the server layer. The line-side low order ODU carries parent-odu to the HO-ODU/ODUCni, framed by otu-<name> with parent flexo-group-1-5-L1-1. The digital-to-optical handover is at the carrier: optical-carrier-<name> on line-ptp-<name> sets frequency (0 or 191275000..196125000 MHz), tx-power, modulation-format and grid-spacing. From there it is layer 0: nmc-<name> with parent-facility an MC or OMS, center-frequency 190650000..196700000 MHz and width 15000..200000 MHz (default 35000), inside mc-<name>.

They are two different knobs. Crossing a counter limit is PM: add or set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> [low-threshold <value>] [high-threshold <value>], where direction is ingress, egress, all or na (default all), location is all, na, near-end or far-end (default all), and the values are uint64/int64/decimal64, na or not-supported (default na). Per resource type the same limits live on pm-threshold-profile, which also exposes default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value. Whether the crossing is reported is tca-supervision (true/false) on pm-control-entry, defaulted for new facilities by default-tca-supervision on pm-profile-entry. How loudly an existing fault is reported is alarm severity: set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <value>, values critical, event, major, minor, not-reported, warning, for example set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor.

Stop the card reporting with alarm-report-control on the card object: set card-<name> alarm-report-control inhibited, values allowed or inhibited (the card page lists Inhibited as the default). The same attribute exists on the facilities the card carries, including amplifier, ethernet, ots, otu, odu, chassis, comm-channel and eth-zr, so inhibit those too if you want the whole slot silent. You can also take the card out of service with set card-<name> admin-state maintenance (values lock, maintenance, unlock; default unlock). What happens to alarms it has already raised is decided system wide by set alarm-control arc-behavior: leave-alarms, the default, leaves current alarms in a raised mode when ARC is set to inhibit, while clear-alarms clears them. Soaking is set alarm-control alarm-soaking-behavior automatic (default) or no-soak. Existing alarms can also be acknowledged with set-alarm-state ack|close all-alarms acknowledge-text=<text>.

A secure-application presents the X509v3 end-entity local certificate named by its active-certificate-id attribute: set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <cert> (string 0..128, and more than one may be listed, for example active-certificate-id certX,certY). show secure-application-<id> in-use reports which certificate is actually active, and status shows enabled or disabled. Before it will come up, the material must be imported with import-certificate: the local-certificate in PEM format, with a passphrase if the private key is encrypted, plus the CA root and intermediate certificates as trusted-certificate so the trust-chain is complete, otherwise status reports untrusted. Root certificates must be installed individually; the -i flag imports intermediates from a PEM bundle. For layer 1 encryption the far end peer-certificate must be imported as well, and mutual TLS additionally needs verify-client-cert required (default disabled).

Use show pm with a pipe to the display filter: show pm <command flag> | display csv, which produces CSV importable to a spreadsheet such as Excel; display xml and display json are also available. Narrow to the 15-minute bins with the pm-filter first, for example show pm pm-15min, or filter by AID, data-type, parameter, resource or resource-type. Useful flags: -t shows the data in a single generic standard table, -i=<chassis-name> limits it to one chassis and may be given only once, -n=<number-of-records> caps records per chassis (default 1000), -s=<skip-records> skips entries so data can be fetched in several requests, -st=<timestamp> and -et=<timestamp> bound the time range (format 2021-02-01T10:00:00+01:00), and -sbin=<number> and -ebin=<number> bound the bins, where bin 0 is the current data and by default all available bins are displayed.

Use show pm-catalog <string>, where the string is the catalog name. For example show pm-catalog parameter-undersized returns pm-parameter-undersized with units packets and type counter. The same information is available per parameter with show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type], for example show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds, and show pm-parameter on its own lists all pm parameters. type is either counter or gauge. units is one of na, dBm, ms, ps, ps/nm, dB, seconds, packets, events, octets, bits, blocks, times, percent, bit-ratio, C, frames, W, V, A, rpm, ps2, mA, words, cw, nm, bytes, errors, MHz. Both commands run in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Turn off real-time collection for that one resource. Either set pm-resource-<resource> real-time-supervision false, where real-time-supervision is true or false with default true, for example set pm-resource-card-1-1 real-time-supervision false; or use set pm-control <entity> data-supervision <true|false>, the real-time data supervision flag for the resource, values true or false with default true, as in set pm-control pm-resource-card-1-1 data-supervision false. show pm-control lists the setting for every resource in the system that supports PM data, and show pm-resource-<resource> returns resource-type, AID, real-time-supervision and real-time-data-last-reset. Both run in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. pm-control-entry holds the PM configuration for one particular resource, for one particular period, direction and location, so the key gives you exactly that scope: set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> tca-supervision true, for example set pm-control-entry-trib-ptp-1-7-T9/pm-15min/ingress/near-end tca-supervision true. period is the PM period (pm-15min, pm-24h), direction is ingress, egress, all or na with default all, and location is all, na, near-end or far-end with default all. The same entry carries data-supervision (true/false) for the collection itself. Read it back with show pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> [supported-parameters] [data-supervision] [tca-supervision], where supported-parameters lists the PM parameters that resource type supports for that direction and location, up to a maximum of 100 elements.

Use show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]. type is the type of PM parameter and is either counter or gauge. units is the unit it reports, one of na, dBm, ms, ps, ps/nm, dB, seconds, packets, events, octets, bits, blocks, times, percent, bit-ratio, C, frames, W, V, A, rpm, ps2, mA, words, cw, nm, bytes, errors or MHz. For example show pm-parameter pm-parameter-undersized returns units packets and type counter, and show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds shows that parameter. show pm-parameter on its own displays the list of pm parameters. The parameter key is an identityref, and the same information is available through show pm-catalog <catalog-name>. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, through the pm-profile object, which holds all resources that support PM data together with their default configuration and is managed by the system so it cannot be manually deleted. Run set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled. The global-data-supervision attribute provides a way to globally enable PM data-supervision without having to toggle it individually: auto-enabled turns the PM data-supervision flag on globally, and manual, the default, leaves the flag controlled via pm-profile-entry or directly per pm-control-entry. show pm-profile displays the current setting. Available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

pm-profile-entry holds the PM configuration per resource type, and that is where new-facility defaults come from: set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision true. default-data-supervision (true/false) decides whether newly created resources of that type have PM data supervision automatically enabled, and default-tca-supervision (true/false) does the same for threshold crossing supervision. direction is ingress, egress, all or na with default all; location is all, na, near-end or far-end with default all; period is the PM period. Read it back with show pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> [default-data-supervision] [default-tca-supervision]. Existing instances stay controlled per resource through pm-control-entry, and set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled enables it globally instead.

Read the real-time-data-last-reset attribute on the pm-resource object for that port: show pm-resource-<resource> real-time-data-last-reset, for example show pm-resource-trib-ptp-1-7-T9 real-time-data-last-reset. It is a date-and-time value giving the date and time of the last real time data reset for the resource, and if the data was never reset it is the date and time of that resource creation. The same show also returns resource-type, AID and real-time-supervision (true/false, default true), and lists the pm-control-entry children such as pm-control-entry-trib-ptp-1-7-T9/pm-15min/ingress/near-end. Real-time data is reset with clear pm real-time, optionally narrowed by resource, resource-type, AID, direction, period or location.

Use the pm-threshold object, which is keyed per resource instance: add pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> high-threshold <value>, then set to change it, show to read it and delete to remove it. For errored seconds the parameter is errored-seconds, the period is the PM period (pm-15min or pm-24h), direction is ingress, egress, all or na with default all, and location is all, na, near-end or far-end with default all. Both low-threshold and high-threshold take a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), or na, or not-supported, and default to na. For the same limit across every resource of a type use set pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>, for example set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200. Reporting of the crossing still depends on tca-supervision on the matching pm-control-entry.

Read them from pm-threshold-profile, which holds the PM configuration per parameter for a resource type: show pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter> [low-threshold] [high-threshold] [default-low-threshold] [default-high-threshold] [min-value] [max-value]. default-low-threshold and default-high-threshold are the system defined default values for that parameter, and min-value and max-value are the minimum and maximum values allowed for it. All are a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), or na, or not-supported. low-threshold and high-threshold are the currently configured values, changed with set pm-threshold-profile-<...>, for example set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200. direction defaults to all and location defaults to all.

Use set clock timezone <value>, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The timezone parameter takes a named zone from the built-in list, for example Beijing-Chongqing-Hong_Kong-Urumqi[GMT+08:00], Eastern Time[US and Canada][GMT-05:00], or Universal-Time-Coordinated; the default is Universal-Time-Coordinated. To see where the time comes from, run show clock time-source: it returns ntp (the NE uses NTP for synchronization) or manual (the NE uses its internal clock). The default value of time-source is manual. show clock also returns current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, uptime-seconds (uint32), DST-active (true/false, default false) and last-time-jump, formatted as <time1> to <time2>, where jumps of less than 10 seconds are ignored. If the DNS server is not properly configured, show clock can take up to 2 minutes to return.

Yes: set ne node-type OADM. node-type can only be set or changed on a 1830 GX G34c chassis, which defaults to ILA; G31 and G32 support OADM only, and G42 defaults to XPDR. G34c has supported OADM since R7.0 (in R6.x it was ILA only). Permitted values are ILA, OADM, XPDR. Preconditions to configure node-type OADM: no OMS monitoring-mode in the system may be ila-with-equalization or not-monitored, that is, no spectrum (or ochm) objects may exist, and no direction-* may exist. Going back to ILA requires: no OMS monitoring-mode on the dwdm-line ports may be intrusive (so no RD or PAx card can exist), and no degree, no oxcon and no nmc may exist. Note also that G34c SLTE mode (l0-mode-op slte) is supported only when node-type is ILA.

show ne-function. It is a show-only command with no parameters, usable in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, and it displays the Network Element generic functions in one list. On a 1830 GX G30 node the output looks like direction-1 through direction-8, then the amplifiers, for example amplifier-raman-1-7, amplifier-1-1-A, amplifier-1-1-B, amplifier-1-3.1-drop, amplifier-1-5-A, amplifier-1-5-B, amplifier-2-1-A, amplifier-2-1-B, amplifier-2-3-A, amplifier-2-3-B, and finally the ne-function entry itself.
