The user is able to define, per card instance, which profile is in effect, and that choice has an impact on the power estimation for the system. To see what a given card type offers, use show supported-power-profile-<card-type>/<name> [profile-description] [power-draw] [default] in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. card-type is the card type and name is the profile name, both strings. profile-description is a description of the profile, string length 0..255. power-draw is the power draw of the associated equipment when not in low-power, of type decimal64. default is true or false and indicates whether that profile is the default one.

The router ID source is controlled by router-id-mode on the bgp-instance. Its values are use-loopback and manual, and the default is use-loopback, meaning the router ID is taken from the loopback IP unless you set it explicitly. When you choose manual you supply the router-id attribute, an IPv6 or IPv4 address; 0.0.0.0/0 is not supported for IPv4 and 0::0.0 is not supported for IPv6. Syntax: add bgp-instance-<instance-id> local-as <value> [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>] [router-id <value>], and both fields can be changed later with set bgp-instance-<instance-id>. instance-id is a string of length 1..255 and local-as is a number in the range 1..4294967295. Example: add bgp-instance-10 local-as 24 router-id-mode use-loopback. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

On bgp-neighbor-<instance-id>/<remote-address> the timers are connect-retry-interval, the interval between attempts to establish a session, 1..65535 seconds with default 120; hold-time, the interval a session is considered active without keepalives or other messages, 3..65535 seconds with default 90 and typically set to 3x the keepalive-interval; and keepalive-interval, 1..21845 seconds with default 30, typically 1/3 of the hold-time. The negotiated value is readable as negotiated-hold-time, 0..65535 seconds, default 0. Authentication is available: secure-session selects the authentication method of the session to the peer with values none or TCP-MD5, default none, and password holds the TCP-MD5 authentication key in ASCII format, string 0..80. All of these can be given on add or changed with set.

The routes to be advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an Interior Gateway Protocol such as OSPF, or by static routes, but not by BGP itself. If the prefix is not present in the IGP tables, you must configure a blackhole static route for it: set the special-next-hop parameter of the static route command to blackhole (special-next-hop takes the value blackhole on both ipv4-static-route and ipv6-static-route). So create the corresponding ipv4-static-route or ipv6-static-route with special-next-hop blackhole alongside your bgp-network entry. The object itself is created with add bgp-network-<instance id>/<remote-address>/<network prefix>, where network-prefix is a decimal 1..64 or 128 and 0.0.0.0/0 and 0::0.0 are not supported as remote-address. A maximum of 100 bgp-network MOs can be configured.

On comm-channel the mtu attribute is the maximum transmission unit size in octets for the physical Ethernet port of the comm channel, and it is available only when the mode is L3. It is a uint16 whose range depends on the platform: 1280..1500 octets on the 1830 GX G30, and 1280..9202 octets on the 1830 GX G40. The default is 1500, and for 1830 GX G40 interface types DCN, AUX, AUX2, OFEC-CC, Craft, CHM6 and UCM4 the default is 1518. mtu can be supplied on add -m comm-channel-<name> or changed with set comm-channel-<name> mtu <value>. Related L3-only attributes are mru, the Maximum-Receive-Unit, 64..1500 octets with default 1500, restart-timer 1..10 seconds default 3, max-failure 2..10 default 5, and peer-address default 0.0.0.0. mode itself takes L1, L2 or L3 and defaults to L3.

LLDP is not running by default. On comm-eth the lldp-admin-status attribute defaults to disabled, meaning the LLDP agent neither transmits nor receives LLDP frames on the port; the other values are tx-only, rx-only and tx-and-rx. It cannot be modified if the mode is L1. Enable it with, for example, set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx. lldp-transmit-interval is 1..16383 seconds, default 30, and lldp-mgmt-addr-if selects the interface IP advertised as management address; it is empty by default, in which case the loopback IP is used if configured, otherwise the DCN/AUX IP. For speed, auto-negotiation defaults to enabled. duplex-mode (default full), rate (1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000 Mbits or maximum, default maximum) and flow-control (default disabled) are only valid when auto-negotiation is disabled; read back operational-duplex-mode, operational-rate and operational-flow-control.

Use the global dhcp-relay object: set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>], and show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address]. mode is the flag indicating the dhcp-relay mode of operation and takes disabled, ipv4 or ipv6, with a default of disabled. server-address holds the DHCP server IP addresses, IPv4 or IPv6; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. Both parameters are usable with show and set, in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Examples: set dhcp-relay mode ipv4, and set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3. Per-interface enabling is done separately with if-dhcp-relay, which obeys these global settings.

Yes. The dns object has an assignment-method attribute that indicates whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values. Its values are manual, dhcp and both, and the default is both, so by default the node accepts DNS servers from DHCP as well as from manual configuration. Syntax: set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>] and show dns [assignment-method] [enabled] [search], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. enabled is the flag indicating whether DNS is enabled, true or false, default true. search is the DNS search suffix name, a string of length 0..64 that must contain at least a single dot; set it to an empty string to clear it. Individual servers carry their own origin attribute (dhcp or manual) under dns-server.

Add one with add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], where address is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the DNS server. Remove one with delete dns-server-<address>, and inspect with show dns-server-<address> [origin]. The origin attribute is the DNS address assignment method and tells you where the entry came from: dhcp indicates a DNS address that was assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the address was manually configured. The default is manual. You can also convert a DHCP-configured DNS entry into a manually configured one by changing this attribute with set dns-server-<address> origin manual. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp.

Use the if-dhcp-relay object, which is keyed by interface: set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled <value>], and read it back with show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]. if-name is the interface object identifier, a string of length 0..255. dhcp-relay-enabled enables the dhcp-relay function on that interface; it takes true or false and defaults to false. It obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global dhcp-relay mode must be set to ipv4 or ipv6 (it defaults to disabled) and a server-address configured for relaying to work. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true.

By default a new interface is statically addressed and protected. On add interface-<if-name> if-type <value>, ipv4-address-assignment-method and ipv6-address-assignment-method each take static or dhcp and both default to static. ipv4-enabled and ipv6-enabled both default to true, so the interface is connected to both stacks and can send and receive IPv4 and IPv6 packets. protection-mode is the user-given protection mode with values unknown, protected and unprotected, and it defaults to protected; the read-only protection-state reports the current state and defaults to unknown. Other defaults: admin-state unlock (lock, unlock, maintenance), alarm-report-control allowed, proxy-arp-enabled false (only applicable to the DCN interface), and if-dhcp-relay false. if-name is a string 0..64 and if-type is one of ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp or hdlc.

Yes, that is what ip-monitoring does. A monitoring instance periodically pings certain destinations and the result takes action on configured static routes. Create it with add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]. action is the action taken when monitoring goes into 'failed' state; it takes none or withdraw and defaults to withdraw. static-route is the list of connected static routes for the instance, maximum 10 elements. next-hop defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address; the instance is not active until the exit interface is configured. probe-interval is 0..60 seconds, default 5; drop-rate is the accepted ping drop rate in 10% steps, range 1..10, default 1; enabled defaults to true. The route reports monitoring-state as unmonitored, ok or failed.

Use add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>, with show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin] and delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>. There is a stated pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. netmask is the subnet given as a netmask and only valid netmasks are allowed. Three address ranges are disallowed: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), addresses beginning with 127 (loopback), and addresses beginning with 224 through 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental). The read-only origin shows the assignment method, static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. To list available interfaces, type ? after ipv4-address-. Examples: add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0' and add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0.

On ipv4-static-route the distance attribute is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255, and it defaults to 1. A discard route is created with special-next-hop, whose value is blackhole (also its listed default). Blackhole static routes are needed because routes advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, not by BGP itself; for prefixes not present in the IGP tables you configure a blackhole static route. Syntax: add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]. advertised defaults to false; set true and the route is advertised in the routing protocol, and for OSPF as an AS external route if OSPF is configured as an ASBR. origin is manual or dhcp, default manual.

It is the same shape but the subnet is given as a prefix length rather than a netmask: add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>, with show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin] and delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed to be configured. Note that an IPv6 /127 subnet is currently supported on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and does not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. if-name is the interface object identifier, string 0..64. The read-only origin gives the assignment method, static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. Type ? after ipv6-address- to list the available interfaces. Examples: add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10 and add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64.

Yes. Static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. Use add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>] and name DCN-B in the interface parameter. The VRF bound to that interface needs to match the vrf given on the static route. Example: add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B. Defaults on the route: distance 1 (range 1..255), advertised false, origin manual (or dhcp), special-next-hop blackhole, label a string 0..256. Access is Operational and Candidate configuration mode.

Use show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. There may be multiple management addresses configured on the remote system identified by a particular index whose information is received on the local system, and each must have a distinct management address type (subtype) and management address (address). lldp-port is the local port connected to this LLDP neighbor, direction is ingress or egress, and address is the string used to contact the management entity, length 0..64. if-subtype is unknown, if-index or system-port-number; if-id is the interface number; address-oid is the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity associated with the advertised management address, string 0..128.

They carry the same attribute set but differ in key and in which side's addresses they show. management-address is keyed show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> and includes a direction key of ingress or egress; it covers the management addresses received on the local system for the remote system on that LLDP port. management-address-local is keyed show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>, with no direction key, and shows the management address information from the local LLDP ports, that is what this node advertises. Both expose if-subtype (unknown, if-index, system-port-number), if-id and address-oid (string 0..128), and both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. For management-address-local the guide notes address-oid is currently an empty string. Example: show management-address-local.

Yes, that is the use-as-source attribute on the networking object. It names the interface to use as the source address and takes a string of length 0..64, with no default stated. Set it with set networking [use-as-source <value>] and read it back with show networking [use-as-source]. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT, and show networking to view the current networking information. use-as-source is the only parameter on this command.

Use show networking-services. It shows the list of network services and takes no parameters at all: the syntax is simply show networking-services, with no keys or optional attribute filters. It runs in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. It is a show-only command; there is no set or add form. For the source-address setting and other networking information, use the separate networking command (show networking / set networking use-as-source).

Because the RIB is the container that fixes the address family. The show syntax is show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]: each entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family, and for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family. So rib-name selects the family context before the prefix and outgoing interface narrow the entry. Parameters: rib-name String length 1..64, pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 -.,]*); destination-prefix an IP prefix; interface the outgoing interface reference (for example DCN); next-hop-address an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Example: show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use clear [-f] ospf [instance=]<value> in Operational Mode. It removes and restarts the ospf-instance whose id you pass as <instance> (string). The operation is asynchronous, so the CLI does not wait for the restart to complete. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation; without it you are prompted. Example: clear ospf 1. The instance itself is created, changed or removed with add/set/show/delete ospf-instance-<instance-id>, and the ospf-instance page points at clear for asynchronous removal of an instance from the configuration.

No. The ospf-area-type attribute has exactly one permitted value, normal, and normal is also the default, so stub and NSSA area types are not configurable here. Areas are managed with add/set/show/delete ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> [ospf-area-type <value>], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. instance-id is uint8 in range 0..255 and ospf-area-id is a dotted-quad. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Example: add ospf-area-1/0.0.0.0.

Use ospf-area-range, which summarizes routes for an OSPF area matching address/mask, and is applicable to Area Border Routers (ABRs) only. Syntax: add|set ospf-area-range-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<prefix> [advertise <value>], plus show and delete on the same AID. advertise takes true or false (advertise or hide) and defaults to true. prefix is an IPv4 or IPv6 prefix, in canonical form, with prefix length up to 32 for IPv4 and up to 128 for IPv6. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode; pre-condition is that the OSPF instance must be created first. Example: add ospf-area-range-1/9.9.9.9/10.220.0.0/16 advertise true. Deleting prompts for confirmation.

Yes. On add ospf-instance-<instance-id> the version attribute takes ospfv2 or ospfv3, with ospfv2 as the default; version appears in add and show but not in set. Full syntax: add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <value> [version <value>] [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>]. The router id is chosen by router-id-mode, which is manual or use-loopback and defaults to use-loopback; with manual you supply router-id as a dotted-quad. Pre-condition: if router-id-mode is use-loopback, the ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. instance-id is uint8 0..255, description is a String of length 0..128, and vrf is show-only. Example: add ospf-instance-2 description xyz router-id-mode use-loopback version ospfv3.

On ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name> the defaults are hello-interval 10 seconds (uint16, 1..32767) and router-dead-interval 40 seconds (uint16, 4..65535). Related defaults: retransmission-interval 5 s (2..3600), transmit-delay 1 s (1..450), ospf-cost 10 (1..65535), priority 1 (0..255, where 0 means not eligible for DR/BDR), enable true, ospf-if-routing auto (active, passive, auto), and read-only ospf-network-type broadcast (or point-to-point). Yes, you can authenticate: ospf-auth-enable is true/false, default false, relevant for ospfv2 or ospfv3; ospf-auth-algorithm is none or HMAC_SHA_256, default HMAC_SHA_256, and ospf-auth-key is an ASCII String of length 0..256, both relevant only for ospfv2. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance and OSPF area must exist first.

Check it with show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id> [state] [role] [address] [priority], Operational Mode. The state values in order are: down (initial, no Hello packets received), init (Hellos received but bidirectional communication not yet established), 2-way (bidirectional communication established, DR/BDR election occurs here), exstart (DR and BDR elected, master-slave relation determined), exchange (neighbors exchange DataBaseDescriptor packets with LSA headers), loading (routers exchange full Link State information based on DBDs) and full (full adjacency achieved). role is drother (Designated Router Other), dr (Designated Router), bdr (Backup Designated Router) or ptp (point-to-point). Note that an OSPF neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface goes down.

Add an OSPFv3 IPsec security association: add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<spi> integrity-algorithm <value> [ipsec-protocol <value>] [ipsec-mode <value>], with matching set, show and delete. spi is a unique uint32 in range 256..4294967295. integrity-algorithm is mandatory on add and accepts AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_384_192, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256, AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_160 and AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96. ipsec-protocol only takes ESP (default ESP) and ipsec-mode only transport (default transport); only transport mode is supported. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Example: add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-1/0.0.0.0/DCN/256 integrity-algorithm AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128.

Use ping [-c=<count>] [-w=<timeout>] [-s=<pktsize>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <ping-dest>, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. -i=<interface> specifies the source interface; by default the interface is selected according to the routing table. -v=<vrf> specifies the VRF; by default the MGMT VRF is used. The interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. -c stops after sending count ECHO_REQUEST packets, -w sets a timeout in seconds after which ping exits regardless of packets sent or received, and -s sets the payload octets exclusive of headers, default 56 plus 8 octets of ICMP header for a total packet size of 64 octets. ping-dest may be an ipv4-address, ipv6-address or domain-name. Example: ping -c=1 -w=10 -s=1024 192.0.2.3.

show protocols gives the single view, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Bare show protocols lists the nine exposed protocols: ssh, cli, serial-console, netconf, restconf, grpc, snmp, http-file-server and data-model-openconfig. Add the name to drill in, for example show protocols ssh. Typical detail: ssh with enabled and port 8022 plus host keys and pre/post-login messages; cli enabled true, port 22, script-dir /storage/scripts; serial-console global-switch enabled, global-timeout 60 minutes; netconf enabled true, port 830, annotate-cli-name false; restconf enabled true, http-enabled false, https-enabled true, http-port 8080, https-port 8181, cookie-timeout 5 minutes, api-root /restconf; grpc enabled true, port 50051; snmp enabled true, port 161, plus snmp-engine-id; http-file-server https-port 8981, http-port 8980, url-base /transfer.

Use show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Each entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key; all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family, and for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family. rib-name is a String of length 1..64, address-family is ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast, and vrf is a leafref to ../../vrf/name showing the VRF the RIB is bound to. Example: show rib-IPv4 displays the RIB identified by the IPv4 key. To see the routes and next hops inside it, use show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> and show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface>.

Use show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol], in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The command shows the list of system routes from various sources, such as dynamic protocols and static route, and the source-protocol attribute is the source protocol for the route entry, for example OSPF, BGP, static. The other displayable attribute is special-next-hop, used for IPv4 and IPv6 static routes, rib:routes and IP Monitoring: none (no special treatment, used for all normal routes, and the default), blackhole (for blackhole routes no next-hop is created under route) and unreachable (likewise no next-hop is created). rib-name is a String of length 1..64 and destination-prefix is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Example: show route.

Yes: show routing, which shows routing information. It takes no parameters at all and is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode; you simply type show routing. For the detail underneath it, use the more specific commands: show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family] for the per-address-family RIBs, show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol] for individual routes and their source protocol, show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address] for next hops, and show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description] for the routing instances.

show supporting-interface-<name>/<interface> shows supporting interface information, that is, the underlying interface that an interface is built on. It is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. There are two parameters: name, the name of the interface, a string; and interface, a reference to the IPv4/IPv6 interface, expressed as the path ../../../../../networking/interface/if-name. Both are used only in show; the command has no set, add or delete form and no other attributes. The analogous command for fiber is show supporting-fiber-connection, which lists fiber connections.

traceroute follows a maximum of 30 hops by default, set with -m=<hopcnt>, a uint8 in range 1..255 (the max time-to-live value probed). The VRF defaults to MGMT: -v=<vrf> specifies the VRF and, if not provided, defaults to MGMT. Full syntax: traceroute [-m=<hopcnt>] [-w=<timeout>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <tr-dest> [pktsize], in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. -w is the timeout in seconds, uint16 range 1..10, default 2. -i selects the source interface, otherwise the interface is selected according to the routing table; -i and -v are mutually exclusive. pktsize is the total probe packet size, default 60 (60 bytes for IPv4). tr-dest may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or domain-name. Example: traceroute -m=10 -w=3 1.2.3.4.

Use show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. name is the VRF name, a String of length 0..32. chassis-name is the associated chassis name for that VRF, so it answers which chassis the instance belongs to. type is mgmt (Management VRF) or internal (Internal VRF). description is a String of length 0..255 describing the VRF and its intended purpose. Example: show vrf-MGMT displays the Management VRF attributes. VRF names also appear as leafrefs from other objects, for instance the vrf attribute on rib and on ospf-instance points at ../../vrf/name.

activate [-f] swimage [label <string>] [db-action <empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback|auto>], Operational Mode. A successful swimage activation implies a system restart. The optional db-action controls the database: auto (default) processes the database with the system default behavior, upgrade-db activates the image while upgrading the current database, empty-db activates the image with an empty database, and rollback rolls back to the previous active software image. If db-action is not provided the system decides automatically. Unless -f is given, you must confirm the activation when prompted; -v forces the validate check again. label names the sw image/manifest file; if not specified the currently installable image is used. Example: activate swimage db-action=empty-db.

No. Only a single location led test can be running at a time, so you cannot flash two cards simultaneously. Start one with activate location-led [entity=]<value> [[timeout=]<value>] [[led-mode=]<value>] in Operational Mode, where entity is a chassis or a card, for example activate location-led card-1-1. led-mode is flash (default, amber light blinking at 1 Hz, used for LED location) or solid (steady amber, used for lamp test, which lights all chassis LEDs amber). Turn it off with terminate location-led <entity>, for example terminate location-led card-1-1; issuing it when no test is active has no effect. Alternatively set timeout, range 0..120 seconds, default 0 meaning no timeout. Note the timeout parameter does not take effect in 1830 GX G30 R5.1, and not all cards support the location LED test.

Use bootstrap ([local-port=]<value> | [neighbor-address=]<value>) [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-password=]<value>, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. It bootstraps a neighbor NE by establishing a TLS connection over the OSC link and provisioning the initial administrator account on that neighbor, for commissioning an OSC peer that has no configured users yet. Select the neighbor either by local-port, the supporting-port of an osc-eth MGMT interface as shown by show interface (for example 1-1-dwdm-line1), or by neighbor-address, the IPv6 link-local address of the OSC peer including zone (pattern 'fe80:.*', length 7..256). With local-port the system maps it to the OCE netdev and resolves the peer address via get_osc_neighbors.sh; if resolution fails the RPC is rejected. new-admin-user is mandatory, length 1..32, and obeys local user naming rules. new-password may be plain text (standard complexity rules apply) or a $<id>$<salt>$<hash> hash, only id 6 (SHA512), salt 2 to 16 chars.

Type cancel-upgrade. That is the whole command; the only flag is -h, which displays help. Syntax is cancel-upgrade [-h] and it cancels any active upgrade in progress. Access mode is Operational mode, and the stated pre-condition is that an upgrade must be in progress for the command to execute successfully. There are no other parameters, no confirmation flag and no target to name.

change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot, so re-enabling it on an in-service node wipes the configuration. Syntax: change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]<value>, in Operational mode, where ztp-mode is enabled or disabled and has no default. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation, so without it you are prompted first. The opposite direction, change-ztp-mode disabled, disables ZTP and will stop ZTP if it is already in progress; the command can be run while ZTP is running, interrupting it. Check the current setting with show ztp.

Use show current-fw-<name>/<fw-name> [fw-version] [expected-fw-version] [fw-status], with AID forms current-fw-<card-name>-<port-name>/<fw-name>, current-fw-<card-name>.<slot-name>/<fw-name> and current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name>. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. Compare fw-version, the current version of the firmware, against expected-fw-version, the expected version; both are Strings of length 0..32. fw-status gives the verdict directly: current means the firmware is up-to-date, not-current means it is not up-to-date against the expected one, and unavailable means the status information is currently unavailable. The default is unavailable. Example: show current-fw-1-3/DCO_1, or plain show current-fw for the whole list.

download [filetype=]<value> accepts crl (a CRL file in PEM format), database (a previously uploaded database), file (any file to the file-system), krp (a key replacement package), local-certificate (PKCS#12 with password-protected private key, or PKCS#7 if pending-import), peer-certificate (X.509v3 in PKCS#12), script (a CLI script from a remote server), swimage (a manifest file and then all files belonging to a SW image), and trusted-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#7 Root or Intermediate CA). The system automatically stores the downloaded file in an appropriate place; there is no need to provide a local location. The exception is filetype=file, where destination may be omitted (default directory, original name), a file-name, a relative path or an absolute path, and you need write access to it; use show transfer to see the default storage directory. A downloaded database is stored as a db-instance=temp database and overwrites any existing temp. Access mode: Operational mode.

Use show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature], available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The signature attribute is the downloaded software image file signature, a String of length 0..1024. manifest-file is the downloaded manifest file and its information and name is the name of the downloaded software image, both Strings of length 0..256. Running show downloaded-image with no AID lists all the downloaded software image files. The command is show-only; there are no set, add or delete forms.

show downloads. It shows a list of downloads and takes no parameters at all. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands for the same area are show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature] for information about downloaded image files including the image signature, show manifest for the downloaded manifest file and its information, and show transfer-status filetype to follow the progress of a download started asynchronously with download -a.

Not any file. The `file` command (Operational mode) performs basic file and directory operations, but file system access is restricted to the current user's access, so not all files/directories are editable. Syntax: `file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value>`. Supported operation values: rename (renames a file or directory), delete (deletes a file), view (listing for a file or directory), sha256sum, md5sum. new-file-path is only used with rename and follows the pattern '[A-Za-z0-9 \-/\.]*'. A `result` attribute reports the file operation result. Examples: `file rename /tmp/a.log /tmp/b.log`, `file view /tmp`, `file delete /tmp/a.log`. To remove system-managed files use `clear [-f] file [filetype=]<value> [target-file=]<value>`, where filetype is swimage, script or krp; `show file <filename>` displays a file's contents.

Both are Operational mode and both are described as performing basic file and directory operations, but `file` (6.108) is the fuller command. `file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value>` supports rename, view, delete, sha256sum and md5sum, plus a `result` attribute, and it carries the related `clear [-f] file [filetype=]<value> [target-file=]<value>` form (filetype swimage, script, krp) and `show file <filename>` to display contents. `file-operation [[operation=]<value>] [new-file-path=]<value> [file-path=]<value>` supports only rename, delete and view, with just the operation, new-file-path (string) and file-path (string) parameters, and no checksum operations and no clear/show forms.

Use `add file-server-<name> server-address <value> protocol <value> [server-port <value>] [user-name <value>] [password <value>] [initial-path <value>] [label <value>]`, editable with `set` and viewable with `show file-server-<name>` or `show file-servers`; `delete file-server-<name>` removes it. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. protocol values are file, ftp, sftp, scp, http and https; ftp and http are applicable only when secure-mode is set to false, and file (local/USB storage) requires initial-path to be provided. Mandatory on add are server-address (IPv4, IPv6 or domain name) and protocol. server-port is optional; if not provided the protocol default is used. Lengths: name 0..64, user-name 0..64, password 0..128, initial-path 0..256, label 0..256 characters. Example: `add file-server-139 server-address '10.220.227.139' protocol 'scp' user-name 'root' password 'Nokia' initial-path '/root'`.

Use `show filetype-<name> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [last-operation]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `name` is the file type for which the transfer happened. `last-completion-status` gives the last transfer status, `last-transfer` is the last transfer start timestamp as a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ (see the set-time command), `last-duration` is the last transfer duration as a time-interval, and `last-operation` is the last transfer operation with values unknown, upload or download. For a per-operation breakdown with progress and byte counts, use `show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation>` instead; transfer status only exists if at least one operation of that kind was done for the specified filetype.

Yes, but HTTP is off by default. Use `set http-file-server [enabled <value>] [http-enabled <value>] [https-enabled <value>] [http-port <value>] [https-port <value>]` and `show http-file-server [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] [url-base]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `enabled` is the master switch for file server access, true/false, default true. `http-enabled` is true/false with default false, so plain HTTP must be turned on explicitly; `https-enabled` is true/false with default true. `http-port` defaults to 8980 and `https-port` defaults to 8981, both plain numbers. `url-base` is show-only, a string of 1..100 characters, default /transfer, and is the base URL used to redirect to the file transfer application.

Use the manifest show commands in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. `show manifest-<manifest-file> [manifest-signature] [downloaded-on] [information]` gives the manifest itself: manifest-signature is a hex-string of length 0..1024, downloaded-on is a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, and information is a string of 0..256. `show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> [state] [version] [description]` gives each package: state is installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown, defaulting to unknown; version is 0..64 characters and description 0..512. `show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` lists the firmware carried per equipment-type. manifest-file is 0..256, equipment-type 0..32, name 1..256, fw-name 0..32. Plain `show manifest` lists the manifests.

No. The packaged-fw commands show the firmware version included in a software-load, and versions for the same firmware can be different per equipment-type. Use `show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` or, without a location, `show packaged-fw-<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]`; plain `show packaged-fw` lists all components' firmware versions in the load. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id>, a string of 0..64 characters. swload-state is active (active software load), inactive or installable. equipment-type is the type of equipment (card, etc) that will use the firmware, 0..32 characters, as are fw-name and fw-version. Example output keys look like packaged-fw-active/CHM6/DCO-OEC and packaged-fw-active/XMM4/IOP.

Yes. `prepare-upgrade [-f] [-i] [-u] [option=]<value> [manifest=]<value> [[db-action=]<value>] [[clear-type=]<value>] [script=]<value> [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-admin-password=]<value>` runs in Operational mode with option=validate to validate the software label/manifest and option=apply to apply it, for example `prepare-upgrade validate <label>` then `prepare-upgrade apply <label>`. Flags: -h help, -i ignore validation failures, -u unattended (auto-activate software after apply), -f force without confirmation. db-action is empty-db, upgrade-db or rollback, default upgrade-db, and is valid for unattended upgrade only. clear-type is full, keep-networking or initialize-from-script, default full, and is only valid for an unattended operation with db-action set to empty-db. new-admin-user (0..64) and new-admin-password are mandatory with keep-networking or initialize-from-script; script (a .cli file, absolute path or a name in /storage/scripts) is mandatory with initialize-from-script.

`clear [-f] recover-mode` clears the recover-mode flag, and this is more than a cosmetic reset. The action clears the current recover-mode state of the NE, confirming the current configuration as is, re-enabling communication with the line cards and potentially reconfiguring the traffic settings. As such it may be traffic impacting. The command runs in Operational mode and has no parameters; the only flag is -f, which forces the command without a confirmation prompt. Usage is either `clear recover-mode` (prompts for confirmation) or `clear -f recover-mode` (no prompt).

Use `show software-load-<swload-state>` for the node, or `show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>` for one card, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. swload-state is active (active software load), inactive, or installable, so `show software-load-active` shows what is running and `show software-load-installable` what is staged; `show software-load-1-5/active` targets chassis 1 slot 5. Attributes are swload-version (0..64), swload-manifest and swload-prepared (true/false), both only of relevance for the installable load, swload-status, swload-activation-type (direct, warmstart, coldstart, only relevant for installable), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label, swload-delta-label and swload-pkg-type. swload-status covers status-unknown plus validate/apply/activate/cancel in-progress, complete, failed and timeout variants. `swversion` gives the same active/inactive/installable summary in one line each.

Use `show software-location-<location-id>`, where location-id is the equipment location as a string of 0..64 characters, in the <chassis-id>-<slot-id> form. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. For example, `show software-location-1-5` retrieves software location information for the card in chassis 1, slot 5. To see a particular load state on that slot, either use `show software-load-1-5/active` (or /inactive, /installable), or go through `show sw-management software-location-<shelf>-<slot> software-load-active`, for example `show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active`, which returns software-load-1-4/active with its sw-component list, swload-version, swload-information, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-delta-label.

Use `show subtype-constraint-<card-type>/<subtype> [min-capacity] [max-capacity] [supported-applications] [unsupported-applications] [description]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. card-type and subtype each represent a group of related PONs for a card type to which the constraints apply and are strings of length 1..20. min-capacity is the minimum capacity supported by the subtype and max-capacity the maximum, both in gbps; a max-capacity of -1 means there is no maximum capacity constraint. supported-applications lists the applications supported by the subtype and unsupported-applications those not supported, both of application type; if either list is empty, that constraint is not applicable. description is the subtype description, a string of 1..255 characters.

Use `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> [state] [version] [description]`, or `show sw-component-<swload-state>/<name>` without a location; plain `show sw-component` lists all SW load components. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The `state` attribute is the package state, with values installed (software package installed), not-installed, installation-failed (software package install failed) and unknown, defaulting to unknown, so installation-failed is what flags a part of the load that did not install. location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> (0..64), swload-state is active, inactive or installable, name is the package name (0..256), version is 0..64 and description 0..512. Example: `show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg`. For finer granularity within a component use `show sw-subcomponent-...`, which carries the same state values.

Use `show sw-container-<container-name> [equipment] [state] [description] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime]`, or plain `show sw-container` for all OS-level containers, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. cpu-usage is the current CPU usage by the container in percentage, range 0...100%, and in a multi-core system it indicates the overall usage relative to all cores; memory-usage is the current memory usage in percentage, range 0...100%. state is off (default state, not launched yet), up (running) or exited. equipment is a leafref to the card AID the container runs on, and uptime is the time since the container started. Example: `show sw-container-frcu31-1-5_pyapi`. For per-service rather than per-container figures, `show sw-services` also reports cpu-usage and memory-usage.

Yes. sw-control-rule adds service-specific custom rules that override the default action upon service failure. Use `add sw-control-rule-<service-name> fail-action <value>`, `set sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action <value>]`, `show sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action]` and `delete sw-control-rule-<service-name>`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. service-name is the name of the service to be monitored, a string of length 0..64. fail-action values are default-action, which performs the policy of restarting the service then rebooting the system if the service is not recovered; ignore, meaning no automatic action is taken on service failure; and system-restart, which performs a warm restart of the system/card software immediately upon service failure. Example: `add sw-control-rule-xmm4-1-1_host_KeyManagement fail-action default-action`.

Yes, `show sw-management`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Syntax: `show sw-management [downloads|software-location-<shelf>-<slot> [software-load-active|software-load-inactive|software-load-installable] |software-load-active|software-load-inactive]`. `show sw-management downloads` shows the download history, listing the downloaded manifest files. `show sw-management software-load-active` shows the active software, including its sw-component and packaged-fw entries plus swload-version, swload-information, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-delta-label; `show sw-management software-load-inactive` does the same for the inactive load. `show sw-management software-location-<shelf>-<slot> software-load-active`, for example `show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active`, narrows it to one shelf and slot.

Use `show sw-service-<sv-name> [equipment] [location] [state] [state-details] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime] [last-start-time] [reboot-count]`, or `show sw-services` for every service and container on the node, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. `reboot-count` is the number of times a service has restarted, a uint16, and is the direct indicator of repeated restarts; pair it with `last-start-time`, the time of the last service start/boot as a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, and `uptime`, the time since the service turned up in days:hours:minutes, since a low uptime with a high reboot-count means it is cycling. `state` is off (not being monitored), ok (ready and functional) or fail (failed to launch/turn-up or unresponsive), with `state-details` giving a brief description. sv-name is unique per service instance and contains card type, shelf and slot, for example `show sw-service-frcu31-1-5_host_DpEncrMgr`.

sw-subcomponent adds one more key level below the package. `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>` is keyed by package name, while `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name> [state] [version] [description]` (or without location-id, `show sw-subcomponent-<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>`) drills into the individual items inside a component, for example `show sw-subcomponent-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg/ztp.deb` versus `show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg`. The attributes are otherwise identical: state with values installed, not-installed, installation-failed and unknown (default unknown), version (0..64) and description (0..512). sw-component-name and sw-subcomponent-name are strings of length 1..256. Both commands are Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Run `swversion`. It retrieves the active, inactive and/or installable versions of the software present on the network element, takes no parameters at all, and is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The output lists the node-level loads and then the per-slot loads with version and label, for example software-load-active R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188, software-load-inactive R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.04.15_14_26-sim-112, software-load-installable R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188, followed by software-load-1-1/active, software-load-1-1/inactive and software-load-1-1/installable. For the full attribute set (status, activation type, manifest, prepared flag) use `show software-load-<swload-state>` instead.

Use `show third-party-fw-<fw-name> [file-status] [path] [version] [crc] [vendor] [part-number] [nsa-upgrade-version] [present-in-eqpt] [applicable-eqpt]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `file-status` is the firmware file status, with values valid, invalid or missing. `crc` is the cyclic redundancy check of the firmware image, used to validate the file when present, a string of 0..64. `path` is the path for the firmware image (0..255). `applicable-eqpt` is the list of resources that this firmware can be applied to, and `present-in-eqpt` the list of resources that already contain this version; each list has max-elements 80. `nsa-upgrade-version` gives the versions from where the upgrade is non service affecting (0..255). vendor, part-number and version are strings of 0..64.

Set it on the transfer object: `set transfer [http-proxy <value>]`, read it back with `show transfer [debug-log-optional-content] [http-proxy]`. Access is Operational and Candidate configuration mode. http-proxy is the proxy server for internally-generated HTTP requests leaving the NE, which includes certificate revocation-related requests, that is CRL downloads and OCSP requests. Note that this proxy is not used for file transfers. The value is a string of length 0..1024 in the format '[http://]<host>[:<port>]', where 'http://' is optional, <host> may be the IPv4 address, IPv6 address or DNS name of the proxy server, and <port> is optional, defaulting to 1080 if omitted. Example: `set transfer http-proxy http://1.2.3.4:1080`.

Use `show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [transfer-type] [session-id] [session-user-name] [filename] [transfer-progress] [bytes-transferred] [total-bytes] [details]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode; plain `show transfer-status` lists all. operation is upload or download. transfer-progress is the transfer completion percentage, 0-100, default 0; bytes-transferred is the bytes transferred so far and total-bytes the total file size, both uint64 defaulting to 0, with total-bytes zero until known at transfer start. details gives the transfer phase: completed, Failed, idle, preparation or transfer, default idle. last-completion-status is a string such as success, fail, in-progress or unknown, where unknown can occur if the system rebooted mid-transfer. transfer-type is sync or async. In synchronous mode a textual progress bar is rendered live in the CLI; for asynchronous transfers (-a) use this command.

Use `show upgrade-status-<resource> [to-swload-version] [status] [start-time] [end-time] [step] [step-start-time] [details]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. Status is reported at NE, chassis and card level: `resource` (0..255) may represent the entire ne, a chassis or a card, and for ne and chassis the results provide aggregated summaries of all cards in that scope, so start at the ne and walk down to find the failing card. `status` values include idle (default), upgrade-in-progress, upgrade-complete, upgrade-partially-failed, upgrade-failed, validate-in-progress/-failed/-complete, apply-in-progress/-failed/-complete, activate-in-progress/-failed/-complete, cancel-in-progress/-complete/-failed and no-communication. `step` (0..128) identifies the current upgrade step and `step-start-time` when it was initiated. `start-time` and `end-time` are the start/end of the current phase, showing 'na' if the entity was idle or finished no phase since startup. `details` (0..255) carries the detail text.

Both use `upload [-a] [-s] [filetype=]<value> ([destination=]<value> | [file-server=]<value> [[path=]<value>]) ...` in Operational mode, but the parameters differ. For logs: `upload debug-log` uploads logs for diagnostic troubleshooting (includes all other logs) and debug-entity is a mandatory parameter, targeting a chassis or card; optional-content adds keyword-selected extra content. Related filetypes are logs, pm-logs (period pm-15min/24h), fdr-log and otdr-result. Example: `upload logs scp://user@138.111.200.1//home/user/`. For certificates, filetypes are local-certificate, peer-certificate and trusted-certificate, and certificate-name must be specified except for trusted-certificate, where omitting a name exports all trusted certificates as a bundle. Only the public part is exported, private keys are not exported, and the output files are in P7 pem format. -a uploads asynchronously (check with `show transfer-status`), -s skips TLS/known-host verification.

Use `show ztp [ztp-mode] [ztp-state] [ztp-details] [ztp-completion-status]`, in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. `ztp-state` is the current state of the ZTP service, progressing through ztp-init (default), dhcp-in-progress, image-download-in-progress, image-install-in-progress, custom-script-execution-in-progress, multi-chassis-setup-in-progress, configuration-apply-in-progress, ztp-completed, plus ztp-state-unknown, ztp-disabled and wait-before-ztp-restart. `ztp-completion-status` summarises node-level completion as not-completed (default) or completed, and `ztp-details` is a string of 0..256 with additional information on the current state. `ztp-mode` is the user-set mode, disabled or enabled, default enabled, set via the change-ztp-mode RPC which is allowed even when NBI is locked; `change-ztp-mode enabled` starts ZTP, reverts the database to factory default and triggers a reboot, `change-ztp-mode disabled` stops ZTP even mid-run.

Use the capabilities command: 'show capabilities-<name>', where <name> is the name of the card (string, no default). It retrieves the capability information for that card. The command is available in both Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The only parameter is 'name'. For broader capability data that is keyed off the card type rather than an installed instance, the companion commands are 'show supported-card-<card-type>' (node-type-compatibility, supported-subtype, supported-card-mode, card-width, max-power-draw, console-port-support, support-serdes-config, supported-features) and 'show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name>' for per-port capability.

'add card-<name> required-type <value> chassis-name <value> slot-name <value>' is the minimum: required-type, chassis-name and slot-name are mandatory. Optional on add: required-subtype, card-mode, subslot-name, power-profile, alias-name, admin-state, alarm-report-control, label. required-type is a String (length 0..32) drawn from the supported list (BLANK, CHM1R, CHM2T, CHM6, CHM7, CHM7X, FAN, FAN-CTRL, IOPANEL, OCC2E, PEM, RD20TM, SPN2, UCM4, UTM2, XMM4 and others). chassis-name is String 1...255, default 1. subslot-name (for example 1-2.3) can only be set at (sub)card creation. admin-state defaults to unlock, alarm-report-control to inhibited. Example: add card-1-7 chassis-name 1 required-type CHM6 slot-name 7 required-subtype C6 power-profile low.

In 1830 GX G40 the chassis ambient temperature has to be set to 40C before a Native ZR TOM will come up. If that parameter is not set, the system raises a port config mismatch alarm and the TOM cannot be provisioned. Set it with 'set chassis-<name> configured-ambient-temperature 40'. The configured-ambient-temperature attribute is a number in Celsius units, has no default, and is used to compute the FRU power consumption; it is available on add, set and show of the chassis object. Verify with 'show chassis-<name> configured-ambient-temperature'. The chassis commands run in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Per card, 'set console-<name> baud-rate <value>' accepts auto-sensing, 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200. The default is 9600 in 1830 GX G30 and 115200 in 1830 GX G40. Yes, it can work it out itself: in auto-sensing mode the system auto-detects the baud rate from 'ENTER' presses on the serial console client side, then locks the detected rate and reports it in actual-baud-rate. Not all cards support auto-sensing. 'show console-<name> auto-sensing-state' shows sensing or locked (default sensing) and is only visible if auto-sensing is enabled for that port. Whether a card type supports it is published as console-port-support (no, yes-with-auto-sensing-baud-rate, yes-with-fixed-baud-rate) on supported-card. Example: set console baud-rate 115200 local-switch force-enable.

Use 'show controller-card-<name> redundancy-status redundancy-standby-status number-of-switchover-events time-of-last-switchover additional-details'. redundancy-status is active, standby or not-in-service (default not-in-service). redundancy-standby-status is the readiness value you want: ready-synchronized means the standby controller is in sync and ready; the other values are not-ready-synchronizing (synchronizing data with the active controller), not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out (protection in lock-out state) and card-not-present; the default is not-ready-synchronizing. number-of-switchover-events (uint32) and time-of-last-switchover are only visible on the active controller card. additional-details is a string (0..128) giving further synchronization status. 'show controller-card' lists all controller cards.

'show equipment' displays installed equipment information; add an option to narrow it, as in 'show equipment card-1-1' for a single card. The available options vary according to the installation. The per-card output lists the child objects (for example controller-card-1-1, console-1-1, port-1-1-AUX-1, port-1-1-AUX-2, port-1-1-CRAFT, port-1-1-DCN, port-1-1-U1) followed by the card attributes: required-type, required-subtype, category, chassis-name, slot-name, max-power-draw, last-reboot-reason, alias-name, AID, admin-state, oper-state, avail-state, alarm-report-control and label. The command is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Both behaviours are equipment-policies attributes. 'set equipment-policies tom-auto-migration enabled|disabled' enables automatic update of the tom subtype based on the present equipment; this update may have direct impact on existing configurations, and it covers subtype migration only, not tom type migration (there is no update between QSFPDD and QSFP28). Degrees are not automatic by default: auto-assigned-degrees is enabled/disabled with default disabled, except that it is enabled if l0-mode-op is hsc-ols. By contrast auto-assigned-directions defaults to enabled, so directions are assigned automatically when a card that supports directions is provisioned. Per-port opt-out for migration is published as allows-auto-migration on supported-port. Check with 'show equipment-policies'.

You have to enable it. 'set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates <value>' is the global switch for serdes-templates; the values are enabled/disabled with default disabled (the CLI value completion shows false and true, for example 'set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates true'). On enabling, templates are not automatically applied to what is already there; they are applied from that moment onward. On disabling there is no impact: the existing serdes configuration is kept on all TOMs, whether it was applied via a template or manually. Application of serdes-templates depends on this flag being true, and re-application can be forced with the apply-template command. Verify with 'show equipment-templates use-serdes-templates'.

Use the fru-info command: 'show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>'. It displays the packaged FRU information associated with a particular equipment-type. manifest-file is a string of length 0..256 and equipment-type is a string of length 0..32; neither has a default. The command is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode and is show-only. For the data read from a physically present unit rather than the packaged information, use 'show inventory-<name>' instead.

Use the inventory command, which shows the inventory data for a present FRU: 'show inventory-<name> serial-number clei'. Addressing forms are inventory-<name>, inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>, inventory-<card-name>.<slot-name> and inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>; for example 'show inventory-1-3-1' for a TOM, or plain 'show inventory' for everything. serial-number is the serial number of the equipment and clei is the Common Language Equipment Identifier, both strings. The same object also carries hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and insertion-date (both YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ or 'NA'), number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class, actual-max-power-draw and fw-status.

'show led-<location>/<name> status', or 'show leds' for the whole list. The object exists even if the FRU is not physically present, and in that case the status reads not-available. The full status value set is: not-available, off, yellow, flashing-yellow, green, flashing-green, red, flashing-red, cycling-with-off (cycling between all supported colors including off), cycling (all supported colors excluding off, used for lamp test), amber and flashing-amber. The default is not-available. location is the AID of the equipment location of the LED, which may be a chassis, card or port AID (string 1..32); name is the LED name within the FRU (string 1..16), for example led-1-1/active, led-1-2/node-critical, led-1-PEM-1/status.

The port-type attribute enumerates: line (line-side coloured CWDM/DWDM transceiver), tributary (standard grey client interfaces), tributary-subport (a tributary split into subports), usb, comm (communication ports), uplink (aggregation ports connecting to an adjunct line function), optical (general optical port, with or without monitoring), otdr (generic OTDR function except external OTDR measurement), ocm (OCM port) and pluggable (the port entity represents the L0 module cage for a QSFP/SFP/SFP+ TOM). In 1830 GX G40 there are three types in practice: comm-eth, USB and trib/line. comm-eth and USB ports are on XMMs only and are found on Slot 1 XMMs; trib/line ports are visible on a CHM6 or CHM7 (slots 4-7) only once a TOM is present and provisioned. Port objects are managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted.

'show resources-<name> internal-cell-switch-total-bandwidth internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth paired-slot-total-bandwidth paired-slot-available-bandwidth'. These four bandwidth attributes apply only to SPN2/SPN2C cards, and the paired-slot pair only to SPN2/SPN2C cards that support Paired Slots. The internal cell-switch total and available bandwidth default to 600.000 Gbit/s if the card has paired slot interconnection capability. The paired-slot total and available bandwidth default to 0 if the card does not have paired slot interconnection capability and to 500.000 Gbit/s if it does. The same object also reports supported-carriers, unassigned-carriers and supported-sub-components. Example output for 'show resources-254-1': internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth 358.750 Gbit/s, paired-slot-available-bandwidth 258.750 Gbit/s.

Read back the status leaf: 'show serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> value status'. status is the state of the advanced parameter as observable on the system once it is configured, with values set (parameter set), unknown (parameter unknown), in-progress (parameter in progress), failed (parameter failed) and not-supported (parameter not supported); the default is unknown. So the parameter has genuinely taken effect only when status reads set. Plain 'show serdes' lists every serdes with its value and status, for example serdes-1-7-T1/RxAmplitude 1 set. The parameter is written with 'add serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> value <value>' and changed with the corresponding set.

A serdes-template is created per tom-part-number (string, length 1..16) and applies to all line cards that support serdes. When a TOM with that part-number is plugged in, the template is applied automatically. You can narrow the port list with ports-applicable: either 'all' (the default, all ports considered) or a list of port names, string length 1..16, maximum 20 elements, for example T1 through T16. The add form also takes card-types-applicable. Application depends on the use-serdes-templates flag being set to true. Manual serdes configuration can still be done and is kept even where it deviates from the template. Swapping a TOM for one with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template if one exists; 'apply-template' forces re-application.

Each individual parameter is its own serdes-template-entry object, composed of a serdes parameter name and its value: 'add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> value <value>'. The entry name is the serdes parameter name (string, length 0..256) and value is the serdes parameter value (string, length 0..256). Edit with 'set serdes-template-entry-<name>/<entry> value <value>', remove with delete, and read with 'show serdes-template-entry-...[value]'. Examples: 'add serdes-template-entry-T-DQ4CNT-NIN/RxEQ value 3' and 'set serdes-template-entry-TR-FC85S-NIN/TxEQ value 2'. Listings show entries such as serdes-template-entry-FTLC9555SEPM-NF/RxAmplitude 2, /RxEQ 1, /TxEQ 2. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, both are on the serial-console object, which holds the global configuration of all serial console ports in the system: 'set serial-console [global-switch <value>] [global-timeout <value>]'. global-switch allows access by serial console, values enabled or disabled, default enabled; note that each console port can override this global behaviour (the per-card console local-switch takes use-global-switch, force-enable or force-disable, default use-global-switch). global-timeout is the serial console inactivity timeout, a number in minutes, default 60, and can be set to zero to disable the inactivity timer. The object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: set serial-console global-switch enabled global-timeout 80.

'show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>' (or 'show slot-<card-name>.<slot-name>' for a subslot) with the attributes [AID] [supported-type] [installed-type] [oper-state] [avail-state] [current-equipment]. current-equipment is the name of the equipment currently required in that slot, for example 1-1, and shows --- when there is none. installed-type is the currently installed type in the equipment holder and is empty when no FRU is present. supported-type is the list of types the holder supports, and if a specific type is provisioned the list contains only that type (for example CHM6,gx:UCM4 versus XMM4). Plain 'show slot' lists every slot in the node. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use 'show sub-component-<card-name>/<sub-component-name> [AID] [description]'; plain 'show sub-component' lists them all. card-name is a string of length 0..64, sub-component-name is a string, AID is the Resource Access Identifier (string 1..64) and description is a user configurable description of the sub-component (string 0..128). Example output: sub-component-1-6/dco-oec with AID 1-6-dco-oec and description 'DCO OEC (Optical Engine Controller) sub-component', and sub-component-1-6/dco-secproc with AID 1-6-dco-secproc. The card's own list of addressable sub-components is also reported as supported-sub-components under 'show resources-<name>', which names the sub-components that can be targeted for operations such as restart. Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Query the card type's capability record: 'show supported-card-<card-type> node-type-compatibility'. node-type-compatibility is the supported NE node-type for a sled card, and is only of relevance for line-cards and carrier-cards. The values are all (compatible with any node-type), ILA (compatible with the ILA, In-Line Amplifier two-directions node type) and OADM (Optical Add/Drop Multiplexer). So a card is usable on an in-line amplifier node if this reads ILA or all. The same command reports supported-subtype, description, default-card-mode, supported-card-mode, card-width, card-height, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support, default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config, supported-bands and supported-features. It works without the card being installed.

'show supported-chassis-<chassis-type> controller-redundancy-supported number-of-front-slots number-of-rear-slots'. controller-redundancy-supported is true or false and states whether that chassis type supports controller redundancy. number-of-front-slots is the count of equipment holder slots in the front plate and number-of-rear-slots the count in the back plate, both uint8. chassis-type is an identityref such as G31, G32, G34c or G42. Example from a 1830 GX G40 node: supported-chassis-G42, description 'G42 3RU chassis', controller-redundancy-supported true, power-control-supported true, depth 600 mm, height 3 RUs, 7 front slots, 12 rear slots, supported-subchassis-type G42. The record also carries supported-subtype, default-subtype, fan-adjustment-on-altitude, dust-filter-replacement, leds and supported-features.

'show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name> port-type configuration-mode allows-auto-migration', for example 'show supported-port-CHM1R/2'. port-type says what the port is for: line, tributary, tributary-subport, usb, comm, uplink, optical, otdr, ocm or pluggable. configuration-mode says who owns it: system-configured means the system automatically configures the card in the slot or the TOM in the port and the user cannot make changes, while user-configured means you can provision or de-provision. allows-auto-migration (true/false, default true) indicates whether TOMs plugged on this port type are auto migrated according to the equipment-policies tom-auto-migration flag. The record also gives direction, faceplate-label, leds (max 10), present (always or in-node-controller-only), default-tom, parent-port and subport-list.

'show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name> requires-blank-when-empty possible-card-types', for example 'show supported-slot-G31/2'. requires-blank-when-empty states whether the slot needs a BLANK filler card when empty, with values not-applicable, optional and required. On a G42, slots 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and the PEM slots read required, while slot 2 and the FAN and FANCTRL slots read not-applicable. possible-card-types is the list of card types allowed in that slot (maximum 15 elements), for example XMM4 for slot 1, IOPANEL for slot 2, CHM6,UCM4 for slots 4-7. The same record gives slot-location (front/rear), slot-vertical-position, slot-horizontal-position, configuration-mode, auto-provision-capable, default-card, reset-power (W at 55C), virtual-slot and leds.

Use 'show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>/<tom-subtype-group> supported-phy-modes default-phy-mode supported-subtype', for example 'show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFPDD/2x100GE-breakout' or 'show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFP28'. It displays the capability information for a supported TOM in the scope of a particular card and port. tom-subtype-group is a string of length 0..32, for example '4x100GE-breakout'. The phy-mode values are 100GE, 200GE, 400GE, 2x100GE, 4x100GE, 100G, 4x10G, 4x10GE, 1GE, 2G5, 10G, 10GE, 2G5E, 40GE, 40G, 4x100G and 200G; supported-phy-mode lists what the TOM supports on that card and default-phy-mode is the one used by default. supported-subtype lists the subtypes allowed for that TOM type on that card/port.

The host-side limit is published per card, port and pluggable form factor: 'show supported-tom-power-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type> supported-power-class supported-max-power-draw'. supported-power-class is the maximum MSA power class the host port supports for that pluggable type, uint8 in range 1..8 (the port may only partially support that class, hence the second leaf). supported-max-power-draw is the maximum power in watts the host port allows for that pluggable type under supported-power-class, a decimal64. tom-type is the pluggable form factor identity matching the TOM required-type, for example CFP2-DCO, QSFP28 or QSFPDD. What the fitted module actually reports is on the inventory object as actual-power-class and actual-max-power-draw, populated only for third-party transceiver subtypes on hosts that enforce power-class rules.

Yes. When you create a TOM with `add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <value>`, the Tributary Port termination point is auto-created with it, and it is automatically deleted when the TOM is deleted. required-type is mandatory on add and takes CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP or SFPPLUS. Optional attributes on add/set: required-subtype (string 0..32), phy-mode, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), alias-name (0..256), admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), label (0..256), enable-serdes (false/true, default false) and power-mode (powered/not-powered, default powered; applicable only to TOMs on the CHM7 card). Example: `add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD`. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show tom-type-<tom-type> [data-rate] [description] [support-third-party-toms] [generic-subtype]`. The support-third-party-toms attribute (values false, true) states whether that TOM type accepts third party TOMs in addition to supported Nokia TOMs. generic-subtype gives the 3rd party subtype string for the TOM, data-rate is the approximate rate as uint16 in Gbps, and description is a human readable string (0..255). tom-type is an identityref naming the TOM type. Run `show tom-type` with no AID to list all supported types. The command is show-only and works in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related: on the TOM itself, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled) is used to override the power class for a 3rd party TOM.

Detected equipment that the Node Controller has not yet accepted in a Multi-Chassis configuration shows under `show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>`. The AID is keyed by the residing chassis serial number (string 0..16) plus the residing slot name (string 0..16); if the equipment is the chassis itself, slot-name is empty. Retrievable attributes are hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number (1..16), clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, see set-time) and detection-timestamp, which is the last time the Node Controller detected the unprovisioned equipment. Available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use `show usb-<card-name>-<port-name> [type] [present] [available-space] [total-space] [usb-path]`. usb-path is the local filesystem path where the USB file-system is mounted and can be used as the target or source for file transfer operations (string 0..32). available-space is the current free space and total-space the total space, both uint16 in MB. All three apply only if type is storage; type is storage or power-supply, where power-supply ports only power external equipment such as passive shelves. present (true/false, default false) indicates whether the USB connector is inserted. Example: `show usb-1-5-U1`, or plain `show usb` to list every USB port in the node with its type and present state. Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Run `activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]` from Operational mode. db-instance names the snapshot to activate and defaults to temp; the paraphrase is a short description of the database being activated, a string of length 40...200. sanity-check-override takes true or false and defaults to false, so the sanity check runs unless you deliberately override it. The stated pre-condition is that a snapshot must already have been taken before it can be activated, using the take-snapshot command. Examples given: `activate-snapshot sanity-check-override` and `activate-snapshot onehour` to activate a snapshot named onehour. Existing snapshots can be listed with `show database`.

Advanced parameter commands can only be executed on the node after `enable-advanced-parameters` on the optical carrier is set to true. Two documented behaviours explain what you are seeing: if no advanced parameter is configured, or the advanced parameter has been deleted, `show advanced-parameter` reports `ERROR: object does not exist`; and if an advanced parameter is configured with an invalid value the configuration is not rejected, but `show advanced-parameter` reports the `failed` status for it. The status attribute values are failed, in-progress, not-supported, set and unknown (default unknown), so check status to confirm the parameter actually took. Syntax: `add|set advanced-parameter-[<card-name>-<port-name>|<optical-carrier-name>]/<advanced-parameter-name> value <value>`, name up to 256 characters.

Force re-application with `apply-template [template-type=]<value> ([[applicable-tom=]<value>[,<value>]*])`. template-type takes serdes-template, which applies all existing serdes-templates to the TOM list given in applicable-tom; the default template-type value is listed as serdes-templage. If applicable-tom is not provided or the list is empty, all system TOMs are considered for template application. Example: `apply-template serdes-template tom-1-7-T1`. Application depends on the global flag: `set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates true` (enabled/disabled, default disabled). Enabling does not retroactively apply templates, they are applied from that moment onward, which is why apply-template is needed for already-installed pluggables. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, use a confirmed commit: `commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>] [-id=<id>]` from Candidate Configuration mode (entered with `configure`). The candidate is committed as usual, but if no confirmation arrives before the timeout elapses the configuration is rolled back to the pre-commit version, so the confirmation acts as a persist trigger. confirm-timeout is given in seconds and the default rollback time is 10 minutes. Confirm with `commit persist`, or abandon with `commit cancel`. For a Persistent Confirmed Commit the commands require the `-id=<id>` parameter, which identifies the commit confirmed, commit persist and confirmed cancel commands. Plain `commit` commits outright, and `commit -m=<message>` attaches a custom message to the commit.
