Use `show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)]`, which displays the system's configuration and skips any configuration left at its default value. The output is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the CLI hierarchy gives the complete system configuration; supply an <entity-id> to limit the scope, or an <entity-type> if all entities of that type are relevant. The guide's tip for a replayable form: a good way to create a CLI script that can restore the system configuration is `show config | display commands`, storing the result for later use (see the display piped command). That saved script can then be fed back in, for example via `configure from-script=<script>` or the clear database initialize-from-script option.

It depends on the target you choose. `configure <target>` takes exclusive or shared, and the default is exclusive: with exclusive, only this session can make changes to the candidate configuration; with shared, multiple sessions can make changes to the candidate configuration. The command runs from Operational mode and switches you into Candidate Configuration mode. You can also control where the candidate starts from: by default it is a copy of the Running Datastore, `from-default` starts from a blank config, removing all non-default configuration, `from-script=<script>` imports configuration from a text file of CLI commands, and `from-commit=<commit-id>` initializes from a past commit-record, which is only available when commit-tracking is enabled. Example: `configure exclusive`.

Use `show current-advanced-parameter-<optical-carrier-name>/<current-advanced-parameter-name> [value]`, which shows the current values of the advanced parameters actually running on the system, as opposed to what `show advanced-parameter` reports as configured. The AID is keyed by the optical carrier name plus the advanced parameter name, both strings, and value is the running value. Run `show current-advanced-parameter` with no AID to see them all, or scope it to one carrier, for example `show current-advanced-parameter-1-4-L2-1/*`. Typical entries returned include BOASetting, CRAvgNCtrl, ClockPreEmphasis, EEPNNLMitigation, FastCDAcqTimeCtrl, NLC, PDLMitigation, PMDEquUpdSpeed, RxCDCompCtrl, RxCDMode, RxCDSlope, RxRollOff, RxVOAMode, TxEqWindowSel, TxHighFreqGain and TxSignalBWControl. Note PMDEquUpdSpeed cannot be added or modified. Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. `clear [-f] database [[clear-type=]<value>] [script=]<value> [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-admin-password=]<value>` sets the NE database to default and reboots the system, but it does not wipe logs, PM data or other non-configuration data; use the `clear system` command when you need a secure wipe or factory default. Three clear-type actions exist: full (default; full wipe, database reset to factory defaults), keep-networking (full wipe but network configurations are kept), and initialize-from-script (full wipe then initialize from a pre-stored .cli script). keep-networking and initialize-from-script both require new-admin-user and new-admin-password and can only be triggered by the SA user. The operation is potentially traffic affecting and may interrupt connectivity; transient alarms after the controller card reboot should be ignored. -f forces without confirmation.

Run `db-migrate [-f] [type=]<value>` from Operational Mode. type defines the protection mode to be configured and takes encryption-with-integrity or encryption; there is no default. To add integrity protection on top of encryption, use encryption-with-integrity, for example `db-migrate -f encryption-with-integrity`. That command enables the integrity check for the system database and will automatically reboot the controller. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Afterwards verify with `show db-protection-scheme`, whose mode attribute reports encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity and is documented as changeable via the db-migrate RPC, with integrity-algorithm moving from none to hmac-sha2-512.

Use `show db-protection-scheme [encryption-algorithm] [integrity-algorithm] [integrity-status] [mode]`. integrity-status reports the status of the integrity check and takes passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup or disabled, so passed-on-bootup is the confirmation you want. integrity-algorithm is hmac-sha2-512 or none, encryption-algorithm is xts-aes-256-plain64 (AES-256 in XTS mode with 64-byte block size), and mode is the current protection scheme, either encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, changeable via the db-migrate RPC. A node with integrity off shows integrity-algorithm none, integrity-status disabled and mode encryption-only. Available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use `diff [-t|-c] candidate`, which compares the candidate datastore against the current system configuration and must be run in Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode. It lists created, deleted and changed objects and shows only configurable attributes; 'new' data is the candidate configuration and 'old' data is the current system configuration. Output forms: default normal diff style, where + marks added objects or new values and - marks deleted objects or old values; -t for a side-by-side table diff; -c to render the differences as CLI commands that reproduce the same configuration; and -d to list the commands being executed. So yes, `diff -c candidate` gives you commands. `diff commit <id> [<id>]` compares a commit-record against the running configuration or another commit-record, and is available when commit-tracking is enabled or a pending Confirmed Commit exists.

Run `discard-changes`. It discards all candidate datastore content and the CLI returns to operational mode. The command takes no parameters and no flags, and its access mode is Candidate Configuration mode, so you must already be in candidate mode to issue it. There is nothing to confirm and nothing partial about it: the whole candidate datastore is dropped in one step, leaving the running configuration untouched. If you instead want to see what you would be throwing away first, run `diff candidate` (or `diff -t candidate` for a side-by-side view) before discarding.

An extended-config is a non-standard configuration that introduces exceptional behavior globally in the system, so treat it with care. Commands are `add extended-config-<name>`, `delete extended-config-<name>` and `show extended-config-<name> [description]`, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. name is a string of length 0..64 and must match a name already known by the system, so you need to know the valid extended-config name in advance; the system supplies no free-form naming. The description attribute (string 0..255) is provided by the system and states the description of the extended-config and its effect in the system, so read it with `show extended-config-<name> description` before adding one.

Query the Golden Advanced Parameters Table with `show golden-advanced-parameter-<card-type>/<name> [description] [type] [supported-values] [direction] [multiplicity] [configuration-impact] [service-impact]`. The service-impact attribute answers the traffic question: service-affecting or non-service-affecting. If it is service-affecting, you must perform an admin lock or maintenance operation, or other relevant operations, before applying the change. configuration-impact identifies the configuration steps needed to apply the change and takes no-change, no-reacquire, reacquire, full-config-pll-change or full-config-no-pll-change. Also returned: supported-values (list of ranges or discrete numbers), direction (transmit, receive, transmit-and-receive), multiplicity (uint8, how many values to enter) and type. All attributes are read-only. Example: `show golden-advanced-parameter-chm7/EEPNNLMitigation`.

Use `lock` (flag -h for help) from Operational Mode. It locks database access to the current session, granting exclusive write access to that CLI session, and is intended for ensuring configuration mastership for a small time. While the database is locked, any other session, CLI or otherwise, that tries to make a configuration receives an error, and a lock will not be possible if another session is already holding the lock. The lock is released either by the `unlock` command or by closing the session that performed the lock, whether explicitly by the user, by an administrator closing the session, or via inactivity time-out. Only the session that performed the lock can trigger the unlock; unlocking a non-locked database, or one locked by another session, fails. After unlock, any session can configure again or take a new lock.

A named-value-set is addressed by two keys, the database entry name and the set name: `named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>`. db-entry-name is the name of the database entry and named-value-set-name is the user assigned name for this named-value-set. What it holds is the value attribute, a value item that is a string of length 1..1024 characters. Full command set, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode: `add named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <value>]`, `set named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <value>]`, `show named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value]` and `delete named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>`.

That depends on the restore-from-chassis-storage setting, shown and set with `show recovery [restore-from-chassis-storage] [restore-status] [backup-status] [last-backup] [next-backup]` and `set recovery [restore-from-chassis-storage <value>]`. Values are disabled (chassis storage is not used for restoration in this NE), auto-restore (SW and DB are stored on chassis storage and restored in recovery mode, then a manual clear recovery-mode is required, letting you validate the restored system before affecting the HW), and auto-in-service (SW and DB are restored in recovery mode and on successful restore the NC automatically leaves recovery mode). The default is auto-in-service, so by default the replacement does pick up the stored SW and DB and come into service on its own. restore-status runs init, image-install-in-progress, db-restore-in-progress, check-completed, failed, disabled, wait-for-upgrade or wait-for-db-restore; backup-status is successful, failed, in-progress or unknown.

Only if the candidate is empty. `rollback commit [<commit-id>]` works both in the Running Datastore (the default) and in the Candidate Datastore, but the rollback operation can be performed on the Candidate Datastore only if it is empty, which is in effect a way to initialize the candidate. So with changes already staged you must discard them first, or roll back against the running datastore. The commit parameter is mandatory; the commit-id is optional and if it is not provided the most recent commit-record is used. The command considers all commit records up to the provided commit-id, obtains the reverse-commands for each record, and replays them in order from latest to oldest, reverting the datastore to the state it was in prior to that commit-record. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

`show commit [<id>|-s=<since>|-n=<number-of-records>]` retrieves commit-record information from the Commit Repository, and it is available only when the commit-tracking policy is enabled, or when a pending Confirmed Commit exists. commit-tracking is disabled by default, so on a node that has never enabled it there are no commit-records to show. Enable it with `set system-policies commit-tracking enabled`; note that disabling the policy again clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. The flags are -n to select an exact number of records, -s to pick a timestamp and show all records created since it, and <id> to select a specific commit-record. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `set system-policies [commit-tracking <value>] [writable-running <value>]` and `show system-policies [commit-tracking] [writable-running]`, both in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. commit-tracking (enabled/disabled, default disabled) enables the commit-repository feature: all configuration changes made via the running or candidate datastores are stored as commit-records that can be visualized, compared and rolled back. Disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. writable-running (enabled/disabled, default disabled) controls the running datastore; disabling it makes configuring via the running datastore impossible, forcing candidate use: CLI allows add/set/delete only in Candidate mode, NETCONF allows edit-config only via the Candidate Datastore, and RESTCONF, gNMI (telemetry still allowed, gNOI still allowed), WebGUI and TL1 become read-only.

The db-passphrase. The system only accepts `take-snapshot` if the db-passphrase used for DB snapshot encryption is configured, either globally as part of security-policies (`set security-policies db-passphrase`) or locally as a parameter of the command, for example `take-snapshot db-passphrase=***`. The passphrase must be a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain any dictionary words, and may use special characters from the 85-character Z85 set; automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. Syntax: `take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]`, Operational Mode. db-instance defaults to temp and takes temp, manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback; type is db-backup (default) or system-backup; description is a string 0...128. Re-taking an existing instance overwrites the existing file. List snapshots with `show database`.

Use the template command. A template is a single entry pairing an object and an attribute with the value to use as that attribute's default: add template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> object <value> attribute <value> value <value> [sequence-id <value>] [label <value>] [condition <value>]. object is the object name (for example odu), attribute the attribute name (for example admin-state), and value is mandatory (for example lock). sequence-id is a number in range 1..65535 that sets processing order, lower ids first. condition is optional and narrows the rule, for example condition card-type=FAN. Use set to edit, show to display, delete template-<group>/<name> to remove. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add template-1/AcmeContact object ne attribute contact value Acme.

No. A template-group is a configuration group holding a list of template entries, created with add template-group-<name> [enabled <value>] [label <value>]. enabled takes true or false, and its default is true only if there is no other template-group enabled, so only one group is enabled at a time. name and label are strings. Inspect with show template-group-<name> [enabled] [label] to see which group is currently enabled, and remove one with delete template-group-<name>. The command runs in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add template-group-1 adds the group and enables it.

Use show templates. This command displays the configuration that defines the data model for system templates. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the level below, show template-group-<name> [enabled] [label] displays an individual template group, and show template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> [sequence-id] [object] [attribute] [value] [label] [condition] displays an individual template entry.

No. Only the session that performed the lock can trigger the unlock. If a session tries to unlock a database that was locked by another session, or a database that is not locked at all, the unlock command fails. The syntax is unlock [-h], where -h displays help, and the access mode is Operational mode. After a successful unlock any session can perform configurations again and can take a new lock. The lock is also released automatically if the session that performed the lock is closed, so the departed operator's lock will clear once their session ends.

Yes. Use validate candidate <candidate> command <string>. It validates any CLI command used to edit a configuration datastore by creating, deleting, merging, or replacing content. candidate is the candidate datastore targeted for validation and command is the command to validate, both strings with no default. If the command is validated, validate replies with OK; otherwise the command fails. Multiple CLI commands can be supplied in one call if they are separated with a semicolon. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: validate 'set ne altitude 600'.

A maximum of 7 rounds of additional-key-exchange can be configured, with additional-key-exchange-id in range 1..7, and each round must use a unique key-exchange algorithm. Syntax: add additional-key-exchange-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>/<additional-key-exchange-id> dh-group <value>. dh-group accepts dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512, ml-kem-768, ml-kem-1024. The rounds must be configured in the same order on both IKE peers; if the configuration does not match, an IKE-CONFIG-MISMATCH alarm is raised. Configuring it is optional, causes the IKE session to go down immediately and renegotiate, and the port level CHILD-SA key exchange is derived from IKE. For PQC safety configure PPK or at least one post-quantum algorithm; ml-kem-1024 is recommended.

Use show data-path-encryption. This command shows the datapath encryption attributes, takes no parameters, and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The related global policy is set with set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <match|ignore>, and on-demand re-keying of a datapath encryption secure entity is done with re-key secure-entity=<value>.

Use the encryption-algorithm command; the algorithm and key length are part of the instance path, so entries are added and deleted rather than set: add encryption-algorithm-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number>/<algorithm>/<key-length>, or without the SPD entry name for the IKE SA form. algorithm accepts null, aes-gcm-8, aes-gcm-12, aes-gcm-16, aes-ctr, aes-cbc, aes-ccm-8, aes-ccm-12, aes-ccm-16, chacha20-poly1305. key-length accepts none, key-length-128, key-length-192, key-length-256, defaulting to none. number is the proposal number for the IKE SA, range 1..max. Example: add encryption-algorithm-ipsec/GX2/1/aes-gcm-8/key-length-192.

On add, integrity-algorithm and dh-group are mandatory and prf is optional: add ike-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number> integrity-algorithm <value> dh-group <value> [prf <value>]. integrity-algorithm accepts none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. dh-group accepts dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512. prf accepts hmac-sha2-256, hmac-sha2-384, hmac-sha2-512, hmac-sha1. number is the proposal number, range 1..max. protocol-id is show-only and is fixed at IKE. Example: add ike-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/1 dh-group dhe-2048 prf hmac-sha2-256 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-384-192.

The top-level ikev2 object carries a single attribute, data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match, set with set ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <value>] and read with show ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match]. It is a global, L1 encryption-specific policy indicating whether the NE must validate that the certificate subject alternate name matches the IKE ID (OPT-IN) or not (OPT-OUT). Permitted values are match and ignore, with no default stated. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match match.

Read host-card-encryption-capability on the ikev2-local-instance: it indicates whether the card on which this IKEv2 local instance is running supports encryption, with values yes, no, unknown and default unknown. It is show-only, via show ikev2-local-instance-<name> [host-card-encryption-capability] [host-card] ...; host-card references the service card running the instance. For the address, local-address-assignment-method is show-only with values auto and manual, defaulting to auto, so the address is picked automatically unless set manually. local-address is a local IPv4 address for the IKEv2 channel with prefix-length 32, default 0.0.0.0, and is settable. Other settable attributes are scope (data-path-encryption, management-ipsec, local-address, local-address-assignment-method), label, admin-state (lock, maintenance, unlock; default unlock) and alarm-report-control (allowed, inhibited; default inhibited). Example: set ikev2-local-instance-1-3 local-address 1.1.180.132.

On ikev2-peer, re-key-frequency is the re-key frequency for the IKE SA with the far-end peer, range 3600..86400 seconds with default 28800, and re-auth-frequency is the re-authentication frequency, range 3600..604800 seconds with default 43200; range and default values may be context-specific. The rule is that re-key-frequency and re-auth-frequency must not be multiples of each other, and they must differ by a few minutes to ensure a significant interval between re-authentication and re-keying. Related attributes: re-key-fail-policy (kill traffic, continue traffic; default continue-traffic) with re-key-traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 seconds default 0, and re-auth-fail-policy with re-auth-traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 seconds default 0.

For the child IPsec SA, dh-group is mandatory on add and integrity-algorithm is optional: add ipsec-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number> dh-group <value> [integrity-algorithm <value>]. dh-group accepts dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448. integrity-algorithm accepts none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. number is the proposal number, range 1..max, and ipsec-spd-entry-name is a string of length 1..32. protocol-id is show-only and fixed at ESP, and esn (Extended Sequence Number support) is show-only with value esn. Example: add ipsec-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/dns/1 dh-group dhe-3072 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512-256.

Yes. The ipsec-sa-re-key command sets time-based and volume-based re-keying for the IPsec child SA: add or set ipsec-sa-re-key-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> [frequency <value>] [bytes <value>] [packets <value>]. frequency is the time-based rekeying frequency, range 3600..86400 seconds, default 14400. bytes rekeys on the amount of bytes transmitted, range 1048576..max, default 1073741824. packets rekeys on the amount of packets transmitted, either disabled or a number in range 1..9223372036854775808, default disabled. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode; delete removes the object.

The action attribute on ipsec-spd-entry indicates the IPsec treatment given to matching IP datagrams, with values protect, bypass and discard, defaulting to protect. Tunneling is the default: mode takes tunnel or transport and defaults to tunnel. Syntax: add ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> priority <value> [description <value>] [action <value>] [ipsec-protocol <value>] [mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [esn <value>] [anti-replay-window <value>] [dynamic-ts <value>]. priority is mandatory (uint8) and gives precedence between entries. ipsec-protocol is ESP. esn defaults to true; anti-replay-window applies when action is protect, range 32..1024 with default 64; dynamic-ts defaults to disabled; alarm-report-control defaults to allowed. Example: add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect.

Create an ipsec-traffic-selector under the SPD entry, then add its address and port ranges as child objects. Syntax: add ipsec-traffic-selector-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name> [next-layer-protocol <value>]. next-layer-protocol is the inner protocol taken from the IPv4 protocol or IPv6 next header field, with values any (value 0), opaque (value 255), or a number in range 0-255, defaulting to any. The selector name is a string of length 1..64 matching pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*). Addresses are then added with local-subnet and remote-subnet (each keyed by prefix) and ports with local-ports and remote-ports (each keyed by start and stop). Example: add ipsec-traffic-selector-ipsec/GX2/Radius/ts1 next-layer-protocol 17.

Because start and stop are part of the instance identifier, not settable attributes: the object is addressed as local-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>, and the command supports only add, show and delete. To change a range, delete the old instance and add the new one. start accepts all, opaque, or a port number. stop is a port-number and defaults to 0; if the stopping port is not set the system assumes 0, and 0 is only accepted if the starting port is set to all or opaque. Examples: add local-ports-ipsec/GX2/tacacs/ts1/all, and add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53 for the single port 53.

Use add local-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>. prefix is the list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, or broadcast for IPv4 only) and is part of the instance path, so the command offers only add, show and delete, no set; to change a subnet, delete it and add the replacement. The local instance name, peer name and traffic selector name are strings of length 1..64 with pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*), and the SPD entry name is a string of length 1..32. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add local-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/101.10.10.1/32.

That is governed by link-security-control on the macsec-entity, which controls the link security policy for handling data packets when the MACsec connection is not available. It accepts must-secure or should-secure and defaults to must-secure, so by default the link is required to be secured. Set it with set macsec-entity-<name> [link-security-control <value>], or supply it at add time. Other attributes on the entity are supporting-facility, enabled (true, false; default true), alarm-report-control (allowed, inhibited; default inhibited), label, replay-protection (enable, disable) and replay-protection-window (range 0..4294967295, default 0). Example: add macsec-entity-6-3-3 supporting-facility ethernet-6-3-3.

Use the macsec-mka object: set macsec-mka-<name> [connectivity-association-key <value>] [connectivity-association-key-name <value>] [mka-policy <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [psk-lifetime <value>] [psk-expiration-warning <value>] [psk-lifetime-enable <value>]. connectivity-association-key is the pre-shared Connectivity Association Key and connectivity-association-key-name its name, both strings of length 0..64. The key server is identified by the is-key-server attribute, true or false with default false, which indicates whether the local end is the key server; read it with show macsec-mka-<name> [is-key-server]. Example: set macsec-mka-6-3-3 connectivity-association-key 1122334411223344556677889900112233445566778899001122334455667788 connectivity-association-key-name aa.

On the mka-policy object, which is the MACsec Key Agreement policy referenced by the macsec entity related to the ethernet facility: add mka-policy-<name> [key-server-priority <value>] [macsec-cipher-suite <value>] [confidentiality-offset <value>] [sak-rekey-interval <value>], with matching set, show and delete forms. macsec-cipher-suite selects the cipher suites for Secure Association Key (SAK) derivation. sak-rekey-interval is the SAK rekey interval in seconds, range 0|30..65535, default 30s. key-server-priority is the priority used by the MKA protocol to select the key server. confidentiality-offset specifies the number of octets in an Ethernet frame sent in unencrypted plain text. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the re-auth command, which performs a re-authentication operation of IKEv2 security associations. Syntax: re-auth [ikev2-peer=]<value>, where ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA), given as a string. Access mode is Operational mode. Examples: re-auth ikev2-peer=ikev2-NE202, and re-auth ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX2. The scheduled equivalent is the re-auth-frequency attribute on ikev2-peer, range 3600..604800 seconds, default 43200.

The re-key command performs on-demand re-keying against one of three targets: re-key [ipsec-security-association=]<value> | [ikev2-peer=]<value> | [secure-entity=]<value>. ipsec-security-association points to an IPsec SPD entry object (Child SA), ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA), and secure-entity points to a secure entity object (Child SA), that is a data path encryption secure entity. All three are strings with no default. Access mode is Operational mode. Examples: re-key secure-entity=NE202-1-4-L1-1, and re-key ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX.

Set the starting port to all. remote-ports is keyed by its start and stop values: add remote-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>, with only add, show and delete available. start accepts all, opaque, or a port number. stop is a port-number defaulting to 0; if the stopping port is not set the system assumes 0, and 0 is only accepted if the starting port is set to all or opaque, which is why the all form can be given without a stop value. Examples: add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all, and add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/49/49.

Use add remote-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>. prefix is the list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, or broadcast for IPv4 only) and forms part of the instance path, so the command supports add, show and delete only, with no set; change a subnet by deleting it and adding the replacement. Instance, peer and traffic selector names are strings of length 1..64 with pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*), and the SPD entry name is a string of length 1..32. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add remote-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/102.20.20.2/32.

Use `show sc-rx-<name>/<index>` and read the `state` attribute. The Receiving Secure Channel is a show-only object; the full form is `show sc-rx-<name>/<index> [sci-rx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]`. `state` is returned by the MKA stack and has two values: `in-use`, meaning Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use, and `not-in-use`, meaning no Secure Association under this channel is in use. `name` is a String of length 0..64, `index` is the Receiving Secure Channel Index (uint8), and `sci-rx` is the Receiving Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

`sc-tx` reports the Transmitting Secure Channel attributes and is read-only: the only syntax defined is `show sc-tx-<name>/<index> [sci-tx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]`. There is no add, set or delete form, so it cannot be configured; the values come from the MKA stack. `name` is a String of length 0..64, `index` is the Transmitting Secure Channel Index (uint8), `sci-tx` is the Transmitting Secure Channel Identifier as a hex-string of length 16, and `state` is either `in-use` (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use) or `not-in-use` (no Secure Associations under this channel are in use). Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A secure-application is an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. Set which certificate it presents with `set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <value>` (string, length 0..128); several may be listed comma-separated, for example `set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY`. The certificate actually applied is reported by `in-use`, a leafref to active-certificate-id. To demand a certificate from clients, set `verify-client-cert` to `required`: the client certificate is then requested and validated, which is what TLS Mutual Authentication needs. The default is `disabled`, meaning no client certificate is requested. Changes to verify-client-cert take effect only for new TLS connections. `show secure-application-<id>` also returns `type` (server or client) and `status` (enabled or disabled); `show secure-applications` lists them all.

Not by default. The behaviour is set by `re-key-fail-policy` on the secure-entity, available on both `add secure-entity-<name>` and `set secure-entity-<name>`. Its values are `kill-traffic` and `continue-traffic`, and the default is `continue-traffic`, so an unsuccessful re-key of the IKE security association leaves traffic running. If you choose `kill-traffic`, `traffic-kill-offset` sets how long the system waits before killing all encrypted data security associations tied to that IKE SA; range 0..86400 seconds, default 0. The re-key period itself is `re-key-frequency`, 3600..86400 seconds with a default of 28800. Example: `add secure-entity-NE202-1-4-L1-1 supporting-facility optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 remote-secure-entity '1-4-L1-1' re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic traffic-kill-offset 300`.

No. `secure-entity-sa-proposal` is show-only: the sole syntax is `show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> [encryption-algorithm] [encryption-key-length] [integrity-algorithm] [dh-group]`, with no add, set or delete form. Each algorithm attribute has exactly one permitted value, which is also its default: `encryption-algorithm` is aes-gcm-16, `encryption-key-length` is key-length-256, `integrity-algorithm` is none, and `dh-group` is ecp-521. The integrity algorithm and DH group are the values advertised to the far-end secure entity peer. The proposal `number` likewise has the single value 1, default 1, and `name` is the proposal name for the secure entity SA. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Through the `security-policy-database` object, which is keyed by `<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name>` and carries the `associated-secure-entity` attribute. Create the binding with `add security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity <value>]`; `set` changes it, `show` displays it, `delete` removes the entry. `ikev2-local-instance` is the name (ID) of the local IKE protocol daemon instance, `ikev2-peer` is a reference to the IKE peer object (the IKE SA), and `associated-secure-entity` is the list of all SPD entries associated with that far-end peer for which IKE negotiates security associations (keys). Example on 1830 GX G40: `add security-policy-database-ikev2-local-instance-1-6/ikev2-NE202-1-4 associated-secure-entity secure-entity-1-6-L1-1`.

Yes. Configure a CRL Distribution Point: `add cdp-<name> url <value> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>]`. Each CDP supports download and auto-refreshing of one specified CRL. `url` is the HTTP URL of the CRL, format `http://<host>[:<port>]/<path to crl file>` where host is an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and the file conventionally has a .crl extension, for example http://crl.example.org/pki/myCA.crl. `enabled` (true, false; default false) turns on automatic download and periodic refresh; enabling immediately triggers a CRL auto-download, and when disabled no refreshes occur but existing CRLs are unaffected. `refresh-interval` takes the special enum `use-next-update` (next refresh from the CRL next-update field) or a duration such as `2w`, `5d 12h`, `1h 7m 30s`. `show cdp-<name>` reports next-update-time, last-update-time and last-update-result. Requires System Administrator privilege.

Use `cert-gen`, an Operational mode command: `cert-gen [-f] [certificate-name=]<value> [[days=]<value>] [[org-name=]<value>] [[common-name=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [SAN=]<value>] [auto-install <true|false>]`. `days` is the number of days the certificate is valid and defaults to 365. `certificate-name` is a string of length 1..128, `org-name` and `common-name` are strings 1..64, and `subject` is the full certificate subject name, 1..1024; when generating a self-signed certificate you must specify either `subject` or `common-name`. `auto-install` defaults to true and auto-assigns the certificate to any secure-application without an active certificate. `-f` forces the command without confirmation. Example: `cert-gen -f certificate-name=self-signed-cert1 days=10 org-name=testorg common-name=testcert auto-install=true`.

Via `cert-to-name`, a prioritized set of rules that map an X.509 client certificate to a specific user identity: `add cert-to-name-<id> map-type <value> field <value> mapped-user-name <value> criteria <value> [priority <value>] [issuer <value>] [enabled <value>] [label <value>]`. `map-type` is `extract` (derive the identity from a certificate field) or `map` (use an explicit username). With `extract`, `field` selects the attribute: common-name, san-any, san-dns-name, san-ip-address, san-rfc822-name, san-upn or san-uri. With `map`, `mapped-user-name` names the local or remote user. `criteria` defines the attributes and conditions required for the rule to be invoked, `priority` ranges 1 to 255, and `issuer` (value `any`) filters to certificates from a specific issuer in the trust chain. `enabled` defaults to True. Example: `add cert-to-name-rule_name map-type extract field san-dns-name`.

Remove it with `clear [-f] certificate [type=]<value> [id=]<value>` in Operational mode. `type` is `trusted`, `local` or `peer`; `id` is a string of length 0..128 and must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type, and <tab> lists the certificate-ids that can be cleared. Examples: `clear certificate local certX` and `clear certificate type=trusted id=certY`; without -f the CLI prompts 'Are you sure? [y/n]'. To list what is installed, run `show certificates`, which displays all managed local/trusted/peer X509v3 certificates imported by the download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles; `show certificate-revocation` shows certificate revocations. The type field also accepts bulk purge options: purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused.

Use `clear [-f] crl [[clear-target=]<value>] [crl-name=]<value>`. The `clear-target` values are `single-crl` (the default, removing only the CRL named in <crl-name>, which is then mandatory and must match a currently installed CRL), `purge-invalid-crls` (purge all invalid CRLs), `purge-cached-crls` (purge all CRLs automatically cached from a configured CDP or a certificate CDP extension) and `purge-all-crls`. To drop stale entries only, run `clear crl purge-invalid-crls`; valid CRLs are left in place. Use <tab> to obtain the list of CRL names that can be cleared. Before purging, `show crls` and `show crl-<name>` report `status` (valid, expired, future), `type` (cached or manually), `next-update`, `last-used-time`, `associated-cdp` and `downloaded-from-uri`. Clear is Operational mode; show also works in Candidate Configuration mode.

`csr-gen` leaves the node with a local-certificate in the `pending-import` state, plus the CSR output in PKCS#10 PEM format. That CSR is taken to an external Certificate Authority to produce a full certificate, which is then downloaded into the system to produce a complete local-certificate; until that happens `show local-certificate-<id> status` reports pending-import. Syntax (Operational mode): `csr-gen [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>] ...`. Defaults: key-algorithm eccp256; signature-hash-algorithm sha256 for rsa2048/rsa3072/eccp256, sha384 for eccp384, sha512 for rsa4096/eccp521; metadata-template generic; key-usage digitalSignature,keyAgreement; extended-key-usage serverAuth,clientAuth. The subject CN RDN is mandatory.

Use `display-cert [certificate=]<value> [display-type=]<value>`. The `display-type` values are `all-certificate-hierarchy` (the default when the parameter is omitted), `certificate-hierarchy` and `certificate-details`. So for the trust chain rather than the certificate's own fields, pass `display-type=certificate-hierarchy`; `certificate-details` gives just that one certificate's details. `certificate` is the certificate to display and tab-completion offers the installed names, for example local-certificate-pace_client, local-certificate-server_cert, trusted-certificate-ca_root, so `display-cert trusted-certificate-ca_root`. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related: `show local-certificate-<id> trust-chain` lists the trusted certificates constituting that certificate's trust chain.

Use Enrollment over Secure Transport. The node's EST client talks to a dedicated EST server over HTTPS and replaces the manual CSR process. Syntax: `est [target-command=]<value> [[est-ca=]<value>] [certificate-name=]<value> ...`, where `target-command` is `cacerts`, `enroll` or `re-enroll`. `est-ca` defaults to 1. Supply either `key-algorithm` (eccp256, eccp384, eccp251, rsa2048, rsa3072, rsa4096) or `key-from-certificate`; `signature-hash-algorithm` is sha512, sha384 or sha256, default sha256; `metadata-template` is from-existing-certificate, from-openssl-cnf, generic, generic-tls-server, generic-tls-client or generic-ikev2-identity, default generic. `http-user` and `http-password` authenticate when no valid mTLS certificate exists. Example: `est enroll certificate-name=myNewCertificateA subject='/CN=NewCertA' http-user=<username> http-password=<password>`.

Yes, with `set est-ca-<name> auto-re-enrollment <value>`. It sets how far ahead of expiration re-enrollment is performed for all leaf certificates issued by that EST CA: either a number of days before expiration (1 to 365) or a percentage of the 'not after date' minus 'not before date' interval, rounded up, accepted from 10% to 90% in 10% increments. The default is disabled, so automatic re-enrollment is off until configured. If auto re-enrollment fails for any reason, the RE-ENROLL-FAIL alarm is raised for the affected certificate and re-enrollment is retried once per day until it succeeds or the certificate becomes invalid, for example through expiration. The CA is pinned by `explicit-ca-root`, the trusted root certificate for the EST CA, and `root-fingerprint`, a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash verifying the Root CA identity for a secure initial connection. Example: `set est-ca-1 auto-re-enrollment 40`.

`server-port` defaults to 443. Configure with `add est-server-<name>/<server-name> server-address <value> [server-port <value>] [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] [path-segment <value>]`, for example `add est-server-1/my-est-server server-address 10.23.55.123 server-port 8443`. Yes, more than one can be defined: each entry is keyed by <name>/<server-name>, and `priority` defines the server's precedence with a value range of 1 to 10. If priority is omitted it defaults to the current lowest precedence (highest existing number) plus one; if a priority of 10 already exists, the value must be configured manually. `enabled` is True or False, default True. `path-segment` is an optional label added to the EST base url, string length 0..64. `set` and `delete` use the same key; access is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use `import-certificate` in Operational mode: `import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]`. Give the certificate type (local-certificate, trusted-certificate or peer-certificate), an optional certificate-name under which it will be known in the system, the PEM string holding the certificate(s) and any private keys, and a passphrase to decode encrypted input certificates (applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles). The `-i` flag imports any intermediate certificates present in a PEM bundle, or for a single certificate, any intermediates specified through the AIA extension; root certificates must be installed individually. Without a certificate-name, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix. Example: `import-certificate peer-certificate certificate-name=peer-cert1 <string in PEM format>`. `import-certificate -h` shows help.

Run `show ISK-<name>` (or `show ISKs`) and read `is-key-in-use`, which indicates whether the key is in use in this FRU; values true or false, default false. Two related flags help: `is-key-verified` (true, false; default false) shows whether the key is verified in this FRU, and `being-deleted` is set to true once the system receives an ISK delete command, meaning deletion is already under way. The show also returns CPU, key-name (String 0..64), key-serial-number, issuer-name (name of the CSA, Code Signing Appliance, String 0..20), key-length in bits, key-payload, KRK-name (the Image Root Key that signed this ISK), signature-hash-scheme, signature-algorithm, signature-payload and signature-gen-time. To remove one, `clear [-f] isk key-name=<value>`, where -f forces without confirmation. Show works in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode; clear is Operational Mode only.

Use `show KRKs` for the list of Image Root Keys, and `show KRK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload]` for one key, for example `show KRK-1-5-0-KRK_E1`. The attributes are `CPU`, the identifier for member CPUs on cards which starts at 0 (uint8), `key-name` (String 0..64), `key-serial-number` (String), `issuer-name`, the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), String 0..20, `key-length` in bits (uint16) and `key-payload` in hex format (String 0..1100). These are show-only commands; there is no add, set or delete. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The KRK that signed a given Image Signing Key is reported as the `KRK-name` attribute of `show ISK-<name>`.

`show key-replacement-package`, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Full form: `show key-replacement-package [KRP-name] [KRP-version] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time] [install-status]`. `install-status` indicates whether this KRP has been installed in the system and takes not-installed, installing, installed or failed. `KRP-version` is the package version, `issuer-name` is the CSA (Code Signing Appliance) name, string 0..20, and `KRK-name` is the Image root key that signed this ISK. `signature-hash-scheme` is SHA2 256, SHA2 384 or SHA2 512; `signature-algorithm` is ECDSA, RSA or none; `signature-payload` is a hex string 0..1024; `signature-gen-time` is a date-time YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. The command is show-only.

Yes: `set local-certificate-<id> revocation-mode force-revoked`. The `revocation-mode` attribute controls how the revocation status of the certificate is determined and accepts `auto` (the default), `force-revoked` and `force-unrevoked`. It is one of only three settable attributes on local-certificate, the others being `alarm-report-control` (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and `label` (String 0..256); every other attribute is show-only. Check the result with `show local-certificate-<id> [revocation-mode] [status] [used-by]`, where `status` reports valid, revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted or future, and `used-by` lists the secure-applications, ikev2-peers and other consumers of the certificate. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. peer-certificate carries the same revocation-mode attribute with the same values and default.

Add one with `add ocsp-server-<name> url <value> priority <value> [enabled <value>]`, for example `add ocsp-server-1 url http://1.2.3.4:8101 priority 3 enabled true`. `priority` is a uint8 in the range 1..10 and sorts the OCSP responders in order of precedence: lower numbered responders are consulted before higher numbered ones, so priority 1 is tried first. `url` is the HTTP URL of the responder, format `http://<host>[:<port>]` where host is an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name; if the port is omitted the default HTTP port 80 is used (string length 0..1024). `enabled` (true, false; default false) controls whether this server is consulted for revocation status. Change precedence later with `set ocsp-server-<name> [priority <value>] [enabled <value>]`, remove with `delete ocsp-server-<name>`, and view url, enabled, priority and `last-query` with `show ocsp-server-<name>`.

A peer-certificate is the X509v3 end-entity certificate that represents a trusted 'remote peer' certificate for the L1 encryption secure application. `white-listed` is a show-only true/false flag with default false: if true, the peer-certificate does not have an associated trust-chain and was explicitly white-listed at import time; otherwise it has an associated trust-chain, which is the leafref list of trusted-certificate ids reported in `trust-chain`. Read it with `show peer-certificate[-id] [white-listed] [trust-chain] [status] ...`. Only three attributes are settable: `alarm-report-control` (inhibited, allowed; default allowed), `label` (String 0..256) and `revocation-mode` (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked; default auto). `status` values include valid, revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted, future and unsupported.

SSH listens on port 8022 by default; `port` is a number in the range 1..65535 and is changed with `set ssh port <value>`. It is not on by default: `enabled`, which enables direct access to the shell via ssh, is true or false with a default of `false`, so you must run `set ssh enabled true`. The ssh object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Two banner attributes also exist: `pre-login-message`, a String 0..1440 displayed before user login with no default, and `post-login-message`, a String 0..1440 displayed after login whose default is the built-in warning that the system is restricted to authorized users for business purposes, unauthorized access is a violation of the law, and the service may be monitored. Use `show ssh [enabled] [port] [pre-login-message] [post-login-message]`. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Add a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication with `add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>]`. `user-name` is the user owning the authorized key, a String 0..32, and can be a local or remote user; `key-id` is a unique identifier for the entry, String 1..64. `public-key` is the SSHv2 (OpenSSH Portable) public key component encoded in PEM format, `<key type><SPACE>...base64 encoded OpenSSH public key...<SPACE><comment>`, String 0..2048. `show ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label]` reports the algorithm, one of ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096. `set` changes only the label; `delete ssh-authorized-key-admin/1` removes an entry after a confirmation prompt. Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show ssh-host-key`. These are the global SSHv2 host keys used by both server-side and client-side SSHv2 applications. There must be one host key per supported algorithm, so yes, more than one exists. The system auto-generates a host-key in the default DB, and additional host-keys can be added or overwritten via the ssh-keygen RPC. The public-key-algorithm values are ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096 and ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 support starts at R9.0). Each entry also shows public-key (PEM string, 0..2048 chars), label (0..256 chars), fingerprint-algorithm (md5 or sha256) and fingerprint (0..95 chars). Query one algorithm directly, e.g. `show ssh-host-key-ecdsa-sha2-nistp521`. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

`ssh-keygen [-b=<key-length>] [-l=<key-label>] [-t=<type>]` generates a new private/public key pair and the existing keys in the system are replaced with the newly generated pair. It runs in Operational mode only. `-t` selects rsa, ecdsa or ed25519; the default type is rsa. `-b` sets the strength: RSA 2048/3072/4096, ECDSA 256/384/521, ED25519 256 only. With secure mode (security-policies/secure-mode) enabled, RSA supports only 4096 and ECDSA only 384 or 521 (default 384); with secure mode disabled, RSA supports 2048/3072/4096 (default 2048) and ECDSA 256/384/521 (default 256). ED25519 is 256 regardless of secure mode. `-l` sets the key label; if omitted the label is the value of ne-id. Retrieve the resulting public key with `show ssh-host-key`.

Create an SSHv2 known-hosts entry: `add ssh-known-host-<id> address <value> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value> [label <value>]`. The id is a unique name, String 0..64 characters. address is the hostname, IPv4 or IPv6 address of the allowed/known peer host, optionally with a %-separated zone index (IPv4 dotted-quad; IPv6 per RFC 5952, zone per RFC 4007). public-key-algorithm is one of ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096, ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 from R9.0). public-key is the OpenSSH host public key in PEM form, String 0..2048 characters. label is a user-defined String 0..256. Afterwards use `set ssh-known-host-<id> [label]`, `show ssh-known-host-<id>` and `delete ssh-known-host-<id>`. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

The `trusted-certificate` object holds the X509v3 CA (Root and Intermediate) certificates trusted by the system. Use `show trusted-certificate[-id]` to display version (v3), serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, modification-time, status, public-key-length (rsa2048/rsa3072/rsa4096/ecdsa256/ecdsa384/ecdsa521), public-key-type (rsa, ecdsa), signature-key-type (rsa, ecdsa, rsassa-pss), signature-hash-algorithm (sha256, sha384, sha512, sha1), certificate-bytes, key-usage, extended-key-usage, revocation-mode, alarm-report-control and label. Writable attributes via `set trusted-certificate[-id]` are alarm-report-control (allowed default, or inhibited), label (0..256 chars) and revocation-mode (auto default, force-revoked, force-unrevoked). Removal is done with `clear certificate`. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Issue `terminate cable-id` in Operational mode; it stops all running CableID verification tests. Because verification runs on a port-pair basis, the test can only stop after the port-pair currently under test completes and before the next port-pair starts: the in-flight port-pair always runs to completion, so the maximum delay to terminate is one port-pair verification time. Confirm it stopped with `show cable-id cable-id-status`: termination is complete once cable-id-state changes to idle (from running-incl-switching or running-no-switching). `show cable-id` lists the cable-id entities; show is allowed in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, while terminate is Operational mode only.

The CableID signal can only be sourced or terminated by the CAD10A and RD20TM cards; the signal is transparently passed in the OPSM. A CableID path starts at the end A port and terminates at the end Z port, where the signal is sourced/terminated, specifically at a CAD10A DWDM port or an RD20TM ADE port. `show cable-id-path-<name>` reports card-type-a and card-type-z, each valued RD20TM or CAD10A, plus port-a and port-z as port AIDs. The card type is derived from the provisioned fiber-connection at the port-A/port-Z attribute: when a fiber-connection is created, the CableID function checks whether it lands on a port of a CableID-capable sled and, if so, records the card type in the CableID path topology. In R8.0.1 the supported sleds are CAD10A and RD20TM.

Yes. `show cable-id-status [cable-id-state] [test-progress]` is the container holding the process status and progress of a CableID-based fiber connection verification, and you may issue `show cable-id cable-id-status` at any time to query progress. cable-id-state is idle (verification not running), running-incl-switching (running for both active and protected paths) or running-no-switching (running only for the active path); default idle. test-progress is a string (0..255 chars, default 'None') reading "N out of M completed", where M is the total number of port-pairs to be tested and N the number already completed, or "Not applicable" when cable-id-state is disabled. Example output: cable-id-state idle, test-progress '1 out of 1 completed.' Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Each carrier can discover up to one node. It is possible for multiple collocated carriers to discover the same node multiple times, each time connected to a different remote carrier. Use `show carrier-neighbor-<local-carrier> [last-update] [age] [local-carrier-id] [ne-id] [ne-name] [ne-type] [remote-carrier-id] [ipv4-loopback-address] [ipv6-loopback-address]` to see the local carrier instance that discovered the neighbor node. local-carrier is a string 0..16; ne-id and ne-name are strings 0..256; ne-type is 0..64; remote-carrier-id is the AID of the remote carrier connected to the local carrier (0..64) and implies a specific remote port id. last-update is a date-time in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ format. The loopback addresses may be empty if not configured. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]`. degree-number is a uint16 in range 1..20 and must be greater than zero and not greater than max-degrees. index is a uint32 in range 1..2 but is always 1 in the 1830 GX, since dwdm-line ports are bi-directional. port-name is an instance-identifier giving the dwdm-line port of the RD or ILAx card; as a consequence the OMS of the corresponding dwdm-port is created. `show connection-ports*` lists them all, for example connection-ports-1/1 -> port-1-3-dwdm-line1, connection-ports-5/1 -> port-4-1-dwdm-line1. `show connection-ports-5/1` shows a single entry. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show custom-tlv-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<oui>/<subtype> [value]`, which lists the Organizational Specific TLV (Type-Length-Value) parameter information. lldp-port is the local port associated with the LLDP agent, string length 0..64. direction is ingress or egress. oui is the Organization Unique Identifier of the TLV, the hexadecimal representation of the 24 bit identifier, string length 1..6. subtype is the sub-type identifier of the TLV in the scope of the OUI, string length 1..507. The value attribute carries the TLV contents. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. The external-fiber-connection is set autonomously by TNMS; although it is possible to configure it manually, it is not recommended to do so. It represents the physical link between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations. If you do add one: `add external-fiber-connection-<name> src-port-name <value> dst-port-name <value> [label] [scope] [src-node-id] [src-card-name] [dst-node-id] [dst-card-name] [fiber-connection-type]`. scope is general-purpose (default) or cable-id; intra-NE connections between RD20TM ADE ports, or between CAD10A DWDM and RD20TM ADE ports, must use cable-id or CableID verification skips them. After upgrade the scope defaults to general-purpose, so existing entries must be deleted and re-added. fiber-connection-type is one-way or two-way (default two-way). Before R8.0 the port external-connectivity also had to be set to yes.

A fiber-connection is the physical link representation of a connection between two distinct ports (or two distinct sub-ports) in the same NE, used in an OADM/ILA topology: `add fiber-connection-<name> [label] [src-port] [dst-port] [fiber-connection-type]`, where src-port and dst-port are instance identifiers, name is 0..64 characters, label 0..256, and fiber-connection-type is one-way or two-way (default two-way). An external-fiber-connection is the physical link representation of a connection between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations; it is keyed on src-port-name/dst-port-name strings plus src-node-id/dst-node-id and card names, adds a scope attribute (general-purpose or cable-id), and is set autonomously by TNMS rather than configured by hand. Both are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode with no pre- or post-conditions.

Yes. icdp is the Nokia Carrier Discovery Protocol, and its only attribute, global-switch, is a flag to enable icdp with values true or false and a default of true. Manage it with `set icdp global-switch <true|false>` and `show icdp [global-switch]`, for example `set icdp global-switch true`. The icdp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Discovered neighbors are then viewed with `show carrier-neighbor-<local-carrier>`.

INCI is the Inter-NE Communication Interface, an API-based communication infrastructure for control plane communication across different network elements, for example between a transponder such as CHM6 on 1830 GX G40 and a line system such as FLEXILS. It uses gRPC server/client as the core mechanism: when the INCI service is enabled the gRPC server starts and binds to the local IP address, and when an INCI neighbor instance is configured gRPC client sessions are established. It is not running by default: the inci-enabled switch takes true or false with a default of false. Enable it with `set inci inci-enabled true` and check with `show inci [inci-enabled]`. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Compare the configured and discovered names on the inci-neighbor object. configured-node-name is the user-provisioned name of the remote NE (string 0..128) and is used to compare against the discovered-node-name, which is the name of the remote NE as sent by the remote NE (string 0..128). `show inci-neighbor-<neighbor-id> [neighbor-address] [neighbor-port] [connection-status] [configured-node-name] [discovered-node-name] [discovered-node-id] [alarm-report-control] [oper-state]` also gives discovered-node-id, the node ID of the remote node as received from it (string 0..12), connection-status, and oper-state (enabled or disabled). neighbor-id is the node-ID AID of the provisioned neighbor and neighbor-address is the IP address of the remote NE. alarm-report-control is allowed or inhibited, default inhibited. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Two attributes on interface-neighbor control this. discovery-cycle-time is the periodicity at which SNDP discover messages are sent, range 30..300 seconds, default 30. discovery-timeout is the time after which discovery is considered failed; when this timeout occurs the neighbor-adjacency-state transitions to blackout. Its range is 300..1800 seconds, default 300. Set them with `set interface-neighbor-<local-interface> [discovery-cycle-time <value>] [discovery-timeout <value>] [discovery-enabled <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]`. discovery-enabled is true or false, default true, and switches discovery on the local interface. neighbor-adjacency-state reads blackout, discovery, holding or unknown (default unknown). Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. `show links` displays the links container within the topology, and these links are dynamically filled in by the system, allowing the NCT topology to be derived and displayed. The command takes no parameters. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The related `show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port>` gives the underlying NCT port-to-port connectivity in a multi-chassis NE, and those links are likewise dynamically filled in by the system.

The global lldp object carries a single attribute, hold-on-timer: the time to keep neighbor information in case the neighbor does not have an explicit Time-To-Live (TTL) TLV. It is a number of seconds with a default of 900. Use `show lldp [hold-on-timer]` to view it and `set lldp [hold-on-timer <value>]` to change it, for example `set lldp hold-on-timer 60`. The lldp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Per-neighbor, the lldp-neighbor ttl attribute gives the seconds until the remote system information expires, and if the remote system does not provide a ttl value that parameter is set to the global hold-on-timer. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

`show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port> [chassis-id-subtype] [chassis-id] [port-id-subtype] [port-id] [port-description] [system-name] [system-description] [supported-capabilities] [enabled-capabilities]` shows the LLDP local system information sent on an lldp-port. On the 1830 GX: chassis-id-subtype is chassis-component and chassis-id is the chassis serial number; port-id-subtype is local and port-id is the port AID; port-description is the port name; system-name is the NE name; and system-description is the string 'Nokia Corporation.Converged OS, Version <release id> _ build <software label>'. All these strings are 0..255 characters. supported-capabilities and enabled-capabilities take router and bridge. `show lldp-local-info` covers all LLDP ports; example: `show lldp-local-info-comm-eth-1-11-ETH4`. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No, the egress direction is not supported. For `show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/<direction>` the direction parameter, the direction in which the neighbor was detected, takes only ingress, for example `show -r lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-1-3/ingress` or `show -r lldp-neighbor-comm-eth-1-11-ETH4/ingress`. The same restriction applies to lldp-port-statistics, whose direction is also ingress only. The neighbor data is kept indefinitely, until the port is decommissioned or the data is manually cleared by the user. Attributes include last-update, age (seconds since discovery), chassis-id-subtype and chassis-id, port-id-subtype and port-id, port-description, system-name, system-description, supported-capabilities, enabled-capabilities and ttl. Note custom-tlv does accept both ingress and egress for its direction key.

No. All counter values in a particular lldp-port-statistics entry are maintained on a continuing basis and are not deleted upon expiration of the TTL timing counters associated with the LLDP neighbor information. All statistical counters for a port do become frozen whenever lldp-admin-status is disabled for that port. `show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/<direction>` reports last-change-time (default: when the lldp neighbor is formed), last-clear-time (default 0000-01-01T00:00:00Z), total-ageout (count of times a neighbor's information is deleted from the lldp-neighbor list due to TTL expiry), total-discarded-frames, error-frames, total-frames-in, total-frames-out, total-discarded-tlvs and total-unrecognized-tlvs, all defaulting to 0. Direction is ingress only; egress is not supported.

Use `show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port> [src-chassis] [dst-chassis] [src-chassis-state] [dst-chassis-state]`, which shows NCT connectivity between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE; the links are dynamically filled in by the system so the NCT topology can be derived. src-chassis-state and dst-chassis-state take node controller, provisioned or unprovisioned. src-chassis/dst-chassis is the chassis AID for a commissioned chassis, or the chassis serial number for an unprovisioned one. Similarly src-port/dst-port is the port AID for a commissioned chassis, or '<chassis-serial-number>-<slot>-NCT-<id>' for an unprovisioned one; all four are strings 0..64. Example row: nct-connection-1-1-NCT-1/254-1-NCT-2 with src-chassis 1, dst-chassis 254, states node-controller and provisioned. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

The sndp command controls the SNDP feature through a single attribute, sndp-enabled, which is a switch with values true or false and a default of true. Use `set sndp [sndp-enabled <value>]` to change it and `show sndp [sndp-enabled]` to view it, for example `show sndp sndp-enabled`. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. SNDP discover messages are the ones sent at the interval given by the interface-neighbor discovery-cycle-time attribute (30..300 seconds, default 30), so per-interface behaviour is tuned on interface-neighbor while sndp is the global on/off switch.

`add submarine-link-<name> src-node-id <value> src-port-name <value> dst-node-id <value> dst-port-name <value> degree-target-tx-power <value> [...]`. The mandatory attributes are src-node-id and dst-node-id (the NE names, strings 0..256), src-port-name and dst-port-name (the OTS dwdm-line port of the degree at each endpoint, strings 0..128), and degree-target-tx-power, the launch power at the ROADM into the primary fiber. fiber-length is the fiber length in km of the associated fiber pair ID, decimal64 in range 0..25000 km, default 0, and excludes branch segment length. Other attributes: label, src/dst-card-name, fiber-connection-type (two-way default, and it is two-way only for submarine links), link-name, fiber-pair-id, segment-list (0..512), bu-segment-index (uint16, default 0), rx/tx-fiber-type, gsnr in dB, degree-expected-rx-power, commissioning-snr-margin, launch-condition (flat-tx or pfib, default pfib) and allocated-spectrum-list (max 32 start/end frequency pairs).

`show supporting-fiber-connection-<name> [fiber-connection-list]` shows the list of fiber connections that support a path. name is the entity name, a String of length 0..64, and fiber-connection-list is an instance-identifier giving the supported fiber connection path. It is the container referenced by CableID: on `show -r cable-id-path-<name>` the supporting-fiber-connection container with its fiber-connection-list is displayed when the -r flag is used, for example supporting-fiber-connection-1-6-ade6-1-8-ade6 with fiber-connection-list supporting-fiber-connection-R1. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `clear [-f] topology [target=]<value>` in Operational Mode (the paired `show topology` also runs in Candidate Configuration Mode). The target is an instance-identifier and may be an lldp-neighbor instance discovered via LLDP, a carrier-neighbor instance discovered via ICMP, or an lldp-port-statistics instance holding the details of an LLDP-enabled port. Tip: type 'clear topology <tab>' to list the valid topology objects. The -f flag forces the command without the confirmation prompt. Example: `clear topology lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-4-T1-1`. For viewing, `show topology` accepts inci, links, lldp, icdp and sndp.

Run `verify [-f] [type-select=]<value> [[target-select=]<value>] [allow-switching]` in Operational Mode. type-select currently supports only fiber-connection. target-select is the port instance-identifier of the CableID-capable card; if omitted, verification is done on all paths, and a port in multiple CableID paths has all of them checked. allow-switching is boolean, default false: false verifies active paths only with no system-initiated switching (safe in service), true lets CableID initiate switching on the OPSM so active and inactive paths are both verified. Pre-condition: equipment-policies cable-id-control must be enabled. The command prompts for confirmation (-f skips it), is non-blocking, and raises the CID-verification-in-progress alarm against the NE until all queued requests complete. Example: `verify fiber-connection port-1-6-ade3 allow-switching=true`.

The `bert` command runs in Operational Mode with operations start, stop, get and delete. Start example: `bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=ingress test-duration=10`. test-id is alphanumeric and optional on start (the system generates a unique one), but it is mandatory for `bert stop test-id=TestX`. 100GE/400GE use scrambled-idles; ODU4 uses PRBS31 or PRBS31NONINV; CarrierCTP monitoring uses fec-frames. Directions are ingress or egress (100GE/400GE/CarrierCTP monitor ingress only). test-duration is 0 or 10 secs up to 1000 hrs, default 0 meaning indefinite. Multiple simultaneous BERTs may run on a facility. Read records with `bert get`, remove them with `bert delete test-id=TestX` or by resource.

You cannot create one: the cid-ptp facility is created by the system when a card supporting the CableID function is created, for example RD20TM or CAD10A. It represents the CableID SFP and its connection to the card via the CID port. Only set and show are offered (Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode), and managed-by reads system, so it is not user deletable either. admin-state is not editable, the only supported value is unlock, and CableID operation is not affected by the cid-ptp admin-state. label (String 0..256) is the settable attribute. The 'used' attribute is true when CableID functionality is supported, default false. Example: `show cid-ptp-1-4-spcid` or `show cid-ptp-1-6-spu`.

The Digital Coherent 400ZR eth-zr facility is auto-instantiated when the ZR TOM is provisioned; interface-type reads 400ZR (Media-interface 400ZR-CFEC-DP-16QAM) at 400.000 Gbit/s. fec-type is settable with default ofec, values not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC, G709, i4 (EFEC-I4), i7 (EFEC-I7), sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7 (7% HDFEC Staircase) and ufec7. Degrade thresholds are in average BER over range 0.000000001..0.1: fdd-threshold default 0.0195, fdd-clear-threshold 0.01062, fed-threshold 0.0206, fed-clear-threshold 0.01125. fdd-monitoring and fed-monitoring are both disabled by default. link-degrade-indication shows none, local-degraded, remote-degraded or local-and-remote-degraded. Example: `set eth-zr-1-6-T8 fed-threshold 0.011870000`.

Set it with `set ethernet-<name> max-packet-length <value>`. max-packet-length is the maximum transfer unit for the ethernet facility in octets, default 1518. The range is 1280..18000 octets on the 1830 GX G30 and 1518..18000 octets on the 1830 GX G40. Two restrictions apply: the parameter is configurable on card level only and applies to all interfaces in that card, and it is used only for determining the undersized/oversized packet count in 100GbE PMs. The command runs in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode, and the value is readable with `show ethernet-<name> max-packet-length`.

`show facilities` lists the facilities configured on the node. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The output is a flat list of facility instance names under the facilities container, for example super-channel-group-1-4-L1, super-channel-1-4-L1-1, optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1, optical-channel-1-4-L1-1, trib-ptp-1-4-T11, comm-channel-1-4-L1-1, otu-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni, otu-1-4-T11, ethernet-1-4-T2, odu-1-4-L1-1-ODUCni and odu-1-4-L2-1-ODUflexi-1. Use the individual facility commands (ethernet, otu, odu, trib-ptp and so on) to see the attributes of any listed instance.

The `fc` facility (set/show, Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode) carries two Fibre Channel specific attributes: tts, which enables or disables Transmitter Training Signal support for a 32GFC client (enabled/disabled, default disabled), and laser-toggling-for-tts, which enables or disables laser toggling when tts is enabled/disabled for a 32GFC client (enabled/disabled, default enabled). fc-type is read-only and reports FC1G, FC2G, FC4G, FC8G, FC16G or FC32G. The rest of the facility is the usual client set: label, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control, tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode (GMP default, plus BMP, openZR+, FlexE-4x100G, GFP-F, GFP-F-extOPU2, AMP, iGMP, none), loopback (none/facility/terminal), loopback-mode, and test-signal-type/direction/monitoring.

foic-type is a read-only attribute of the `flexo` facility. FOICx.k means k parallel lanes carrying a FlexO-x interface where x is the rate in units of 100G (G.709.3 FlexO-LR and G.709.1 FlexO-SR). Supported values are foic1.2, foic1.4, foic2.4, foic2.8, foic3.6, foic4.8 and foic4.16, with foic4.8 the default. resource-mode is settable and selects the resource configuration: ADM for add-drop, XC for add-drop with regen; the default is ADM. Example: `set flexo-1-5-L1-1 resource-mode 'XC'`. Also on the facility: fec-type (show only, default ofec), iid to identify a member and its order within a group, and the read-back accepted-group-id and accepted-iid.

`add flexo-group-<name> carriers <value> rate <value> modulation-format <value> group-id <value>` requires four mandatory attributes besides the name: carriers (the list of carriers bound to the facility, string 1..32), rate (carried signal basic rate class in Gbit/s), modulation-format (not-applicable, DP-QPSK, DP-16QAM, DP-8QAM or BPSK) and group-id, the interface group instance the FlexO-x interface belongs to, an integer in range 1..1048575 that must be unique in the NE. Optional on add are label, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (default allowed) and fec-type (default ofec, also cfec, noFEC, G709, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7, ufec7, not-applicable). The command runs in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

`set high-speed-monitoring [enabled <value>] [port <value>]` configures the node's high speed monitoring function, and `show high-speed-monitoring [enabled] [port]` reads it back. There are only two attributes: enabled, the user configurable switch that turns high speed monitoring on or off, with values true or false and default false; and port, the user configurable port for the function, a uint16 in range [1..max] with default 57500. The command is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The `interlaken` facility represents the SPN2 Interlaken interface, supported by the trib-ptp facilities of the card ports (for example supporting-port 8,9 giving supporting-facilities trib-ptp-66-1-8 and trib-ptp-66-1-9). Its capacity attribute is read-only and fixed at 500 Gbit/s. Only four attributes are settable with `set interlaken-<name>`: label (String 0..256), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed) and loopback (none, facility for a test towards the facility side, or terminal for a test towards the terminal side; default none). managed-by is system, so the facility is not user deletable. Example: `set interlaken-66-1-8 label interlaken_66_1`.
