On line-ptp, auto-in-service is governed by two attributes settable with add or set. auto-in-service-enabled is the auto-in-service switch for the facility, true or false, default false. valid-signal-time is the configurable time that represents detection of a valid signal used by the auto-in-service mechanism, a number in the range 1..7200 minutes with a default of 480 minutes. The read-only remaining-valid-signal-time (also 1..7200 minutes) shows the actual time left before the facility is automatically enabled by the mechanism. Example output: auto-in-service-enabled false, valid-signal-time 480 minutes, remaining-valid-signal-time 0 minutes. Both configurable attributes are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

They are different commands. `show network-xconnect` is a display-only command with no parameters, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode, that lists the services of the multiple user cross connections commissioned in this NE. `nw-xconnect` is the configuration command for an individual user channel cross-connection: `add nw-xconnect-<name> endpoint1 <value> endpoint2 <value> [xcon-type <value>] [rate <value>]`, plus `set nw-xconnect-<name> [rate <value>]`, `show nw-xconnect-<name>` and `delete nw-xconnect-<name>`. So use network-xconnect to see the list, nw-xconnect to create, edit, inspect or remove one instance.

Management-channel bridging is done with `add nw-xconnect-<name> endpoint1 <value> endpoint2 <value> [xcon-type <value>] [rate <value>]`. The xcon-type values are L1-ETH-TO-GCC0, L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0, L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC, with L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0 the default; a direct GCC0-to-OSC type is not among them. For a GCC0 pair use `add nw-xconnect-test xcon-type L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0 endpoint1 comm-channel-ch1 endpoint2 comm-channel-ch2`; for an OSC pair `add nw-xconnect-OSCuserch1 xcon-type L1-OSC-TO-OSC endpoint1 comm-channel-2-5-dwdm-line1-OSCX5 endpoint2 comm-channel-2-5-dwdm-line2-OSCX5`; ETH-based types take a comm-eth (set to mode L1) as endpoint1. Both endpoints are mandatory at creation. rate is 1..20 Mbps, default 13 for L1-ETH-TO-GCC0 and 20 for L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC.

No. The high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH is created; when a CHM6 has an OTU configured on it, use the `show odu` command to determine whether the ODU exists. The class attribute is set by the system according to order of creation: high-order marks the top-most ODUCn/ODUk entity created by the system, low-order (the default) marks children supported by a high-order ODU, and mapped marks a mapped OTN or non-OTN client signal. What you create yourself are the low order ODUs, ODU4i (100G) or ODUflexi (400G), which XCONs are mapped into, using `add odu-<name> odu-type <value> [parent-odu <value>] [time-slots <value>] ...`. Pre-condition: the super-channel must be added before Low Order ODUs can be added.

Yes. The odu-diagnostics entity is keyed by direction, `add|set|show|delete odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction>`, where direction is ingress or egress, and each direction has its own values. Per direction you can set tti-style (ITU-T-G709, which splits the TTI into SAPI, DAPI and OPER bytes, or proprietary, a single 64 byte string; default ITU-T-G709), tx-tti and expected-tti (hex string with 0x prefix 1..130 characters, or printable ASCII 1..64), and the ITU-style tx-sapi/tx-dapi (1..15) and tx-operator (1..32) with their expected-* counterparts, all defaulting to empty. tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting (default disabled) selects the TIM criteria. Example: `set odu-diagnostics-Lodu4i/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI-DAPI-OPER`.

Yes, FEC is enabled by default on an OTU. fec-mode, the configured Forward Error Correction mode on the OTUk/OTUCn client, takes enabled or disabled and defaults to enabled, and fec-generation-mode, the FEC generation mode towards the far-end receiver, also takes enabled or disabled and defaults to enabled. fec-type defaults to ofec; the permitted values are not-applicable, cfec, ofec, G709, noFEC, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7 and ufec7. All three are available on add, set and show, in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode, for example `add otu-1-5-L1-1-OTU4-1 parent flexo-group-1-5-L1-1 time-slots 1`.

Use the tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting attribute of otu-diagnostics, which is per direction: `set otu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting <value>` with direction ingress or egress. It states whether the TTI-Mismatch (TIM) alarm is reported or masked and, when reported, the criteria used. Values are disabled (the default), full-64-bytes, SAPI, DAPI, OPER, SAPI-DAPI, SAPI-OPER, DAPI-OPER and SAPI-DAPI-OPER, so choose SAPI to alarm only on a mismatched source trace rather than the whole 64-byte string. Example: `set otu-diagnostics-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI`. Set the expected value with expected-sapi (hex with 0x prefix 1..32, or printable ASCII 1..15). tim-act-enabled (default disabled) separately controls inserting a maintenance signal on TIM.

The stm facility terminates STM-16 and STM-64. stm-type, the type of SDH signal (STM-N), is a show-only attribute whose values are STM-16 and STM-64; the facility name follows Synchronous Transport Module N, for example N=16 or 64, per ITU-T G.691. Configurable attributes with `set stm-<name>` are label, admin-state (Lock, Unlock, Maintenance; default Unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode, tti-style (ITU-T-G709 default, or proprietary), tim-monitor (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tx-tti and expected-tti, loopback and loopback-mode (none, facility, terminal; default none), and test-signal-type/direction/monitoring. Example: `set stm-1-5-T9.2 tx-mapping-mode BMP`.

The trib-ptp attribute tributary-disable-action decides what the network element does towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed, either shutting off the laser or inserting a replacement signal. Values are laser-shut-off (the default), none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais and send-nos (1830 GX G30 only). tributary-disable-holdoff-timer delays the client shutdown or replacement signal at egress, uint16 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0 meaning holdoff disabled; it applies only when the TDA action is laser-turnoff. Related switches: near-end-tda (default disabled), tda-degrade-mode for BERSD-ODU triggering ALS (default disabled), and forward-defect-trigger (default true). Example: `set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off`.

Create one with `add xcon-<name> source <value> destination <value> [payload-type <value>] [direction <value>] [label <value>] [circuit-id-suffix <value>]` in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode, for example `add xcon-1 source ethernet-1-4-T1 destination odu-1-4-T1-1-ODUni-1`. source and destination are instance IDs; direction only supports two-way, which is the default; circuit-id-suffix is 0..48 characters. protection-type is a show-only attribute reporting y-cable, snc-n, snc-i or unprotected, with unprotected the default. Other read-only fields are payload-type (100GBE, 400GBE, OTU4, 100G, ODU2, ODU2e, empty), payload-treatment (transport, switching, transport-without-fec, regen, regen-switching), network-mapping, and type (add, drop, add-drop, express). managed-by defaults to user and only user-created XCONs can be user deleted.

An L2-bridge is identified by bridge-name, a String of length 0..64 used in the entity name: `set L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name <value>] [description <value>]` and `show L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name] [description]`. Only two attributes are configurable: chassis-name, a leafref to the chassis associated with this L2 bridge, and description, a String of length 0..255 describing the bridge and its intended purpose. There are no add or delete forms in this section, only set and show, and both run in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use `clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>`. The clear app subcommand clears third party apps (installed apps), and app-name identifies the third party app to remove. The command is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. As with every clear subcommand, the operation requires user confirmation; the -f flag forces the command without the confirmation prompt, otherwise a confirmation prompt is displayed. clear app sits alongside the other clear subcommands such as clear alarm, clear certificate, clear file, clear log, clear pm, clear system and clear topology.

Use `appctl [app-name=]<value> [command=]<value> [[target=]<value>] [[parameters=]<value>[,<value>]*]`, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. app-name is a leafref to an existing third-party-app entry under system sw-management. command takes restart to restart the third party application, netls to show the list of subnet networks used by the containers, or exec to execute a third party application operation given in parameters. target says whether the command is executed for the entire system or for a chassis/card AID; it is a string or the keyword system, and defaults to system. parameters is an optional string list, max 50 elements, applicable when command is restart or exec.

Yes. Use the call-home command: `call-home [dial-out-server-name=]<string>`, for example `call-home collector-x`. It executes a manual connection trigger to a configured dial-out-server and forces a connection attempt. If the dial-out-server is currently in the 'connecting' state, the command forces an immediate attempt and will not wait for some time before retrying. The dial-out-server-name parameter is the pre-configured name of the dial-out server (string, no default). Access Mode is Operational Mode. Pre-condition: the dial-out server must be configured for this command to execute properly. `call-home -h` displays help.

Use `show current-subscription-<subscription-name> [related-session-id] [related-dial-out-server] [session-type] [session-protocol] [encoding] [transfer-mode] [updates-only] [user-access]` (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). encoding specifies the data encoding scheme for data sent to and from the target device and may be json, bytes, proto, ascii or json-ietf, defaulting to json-ietf. transfer-mode may be stream (values streamed by the target, the default), once (values sent once-off) or poll (values sent in response to a poll request). session-protocol is gnmi (default gnmi), and session-type is gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel or gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc. updates-only is true/false, default false.

No. The enabled attribute of a data-model defaults to false, so YANG data models are not all loaded; enabled allows you to load/unload the model, and a loaded data model means it can be used via the management interfaces. Turn one on with `set data-model-<name> enabled true`. Inspect with `show data-model-<name> [description] [enabled]`, or `show data-model` to view all available YANG data models for loading/unloading. name is a string of length 0..256 and is used in both set and show; description is a string of length 0..256 and is show-only. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The dial-out-server retry-policy can be progressive-back-off (the default), retry-then-stop, or retry-forever. The retry attribute (integer 0..5, default 3) is only applicable when retry-policy is retry-then-stop. timeout is the time before the next retry, integer 1..255 seconds, default 10, and is not applicable for progressive-back-off, which has a dynamic timeout. port is integer 1..65535 with default 4334, the default for the netconf protocol over ssh; protocol is netconf (default) or restconf, and transport is ssh. auto-connect defaults to true; if false the server can still be connected manually via the call-home RPC. Set these with `add`/`set dial-out-server-<name>`.

Yes, gNMI/gRPC is enabled by default: the grpc object's enabled attribute is true false with default true, and the port that listens for gNMI access via gRPC defaults to 50051. Configure with `set grpc [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity <value>]` and inspect with `show grpc [enabled] [port] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity]`. gnmi-get-encoding-granularity controls the granularity of data in gNMI Get responses when encoded with JSON: per-path puts all path data on one Update message, per-object divides the path data into multiple Update messages, one per YANG container/list entry; the default is per-object. The grpc object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted.

NETCONF listens for access via ssh on port 830 by default (port-number, uint16, range 1..65535). hello-timeout specifies the number of seconds a session may exist before the hello PDU is received/transmitted; the session is dropped if no hello PDU is received/transmitted before that number of seconds elapses. It is a uint16 in the range 1..3600 seconds with a default of 2. Configure with `set netconf [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [annotate-cli-name <value>] [static-info-in-notifs <value>] [hello-timeout <value>]`. enabled defaults to true and it is not possible to disable NETCONF from within a NETCONF session. annotate-cli-name defaults to false.

Plain HTTP is available but off by default: http-enabled is true/false with default false, and RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode. http-port defaults to 8080 (range 1..65535). https-enabled defaults to true with https-port 8181, and the overall enabled switch defaults to true. Session length is governed by cookie-timeout, the timeout of a cookie based RESTCONF session, a number in the range 1..300 minutes with a default of 5; the cookie expiration date is reset every time there is activity on the session. Example: `set restconf cookie-timeout 10`. api-root (string 0..64) is show-only.

Use `show snmp [enabled] [port] [snmp-engine-id] [engine-boot-count]`, or just `show snmp` to view the SNMP instance. snmp-engine-id is a show-only string of length 0..256 giving the SNMP EngineID of the NE; it follows the EngineID format 3 defined in RFC3411, and the MAC address in the Engine ID is the first MAC address of the MAC addresses Pool of the NE. engine-boot-count is a show-only uint16 with default 0 that counts how many times the engine has restarted. The settable attributes are enabled (true/false, default true) and port, the port where the NE listens for SNMP requests (range 1..65535, default 161). Access Mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. The snmp-community attribute community-string-access, the SNMP access right of the community string, has read-only as its only permitted value and read-only as its default, so read-write communities cannot be created. Create a community with `add snmp-community-<name> community-string <value> [enabled <value>] [community-string-access <value>]`, for example `add snmp-community-mycommunity community-string public community-string-access read-only enabled true`. name is a string of length 0..64 and is distinct from the community string itself; community-string is a string of length 1..32; enabled is false/true with default true. Note the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object.

Add a trap listener with `add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>]`. snmp-version is v2c or v3 and defaults to v2c. trap-community-string is the community string used for SNMP traps, a string of 0..32 characters defaulting to infinera. target-port is a UDP port number in the range 0..65535, default 162, and target-transport is udp (only value, default udp). enabled defaults to true, target-name is a string of 0..32 characters, and snmpv3-user only applies when snmp-version is v3.

A new SNMPv3 user gets user-sec-level no-auth-no-priv by default; the permitted values are auth-no-priv, auth-priv and no-auth-no-priv. The privacy protocol priv-protocol may be DES, AES128, AES192 or AES256, with AES128 as the default. auth-protocol has SHA as its only value and default. Create with `add snmpv3-user-<snmpv3-user-name> auth-passphrase <value> priv-passphrase <value> [user-sec-level <value>] [auth-protocol <value>] [priv-protocol <value>]`; both passphrases are mandatory strings of length 8..64 and the user name is a string of length 1..32. Example: `add snmpv3-user-bob user-sec-level auth-priv auth-protocol SHA auth-passphrase public123 priv-protocol AES128 priv-passphrase private123`.

The subscription-path attribute subscription-path-mode governs how subscription updates are sent: target-defined (the default), on-change, or sample. sample-interval is the time in milliseconds between the device's sample of a telemetry data source, default 0 (set to 0 when optional); for a target-defined stream subscription, if sample-interval is not set the system automatically adjusts it from 0 to 10 seconds. heartbeat-interval is the maximum interval in milliseconds between updates, default 0; for a target-defined stream subscription, if sample-interval is not set and heartbeat-interval is lower than 10 seconds, the system adjusts it to 20 seconds. suppress-redundant (true/false, default true) suppresses redundant updates. View with `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>`.

Use `show subscriptions`. It shows a list of subscriptions, takes no parameters, and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the detailed list representation of the telemetry subscriptions configured in the system, use `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` with attributes such as related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type, session-protocol, encoding, transfer-mode, updates-only and user-access. For the paths within a subscription use `show subscription-path` or `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>`. Telemetry itself is viewed with `show telemetry`.

Telemetry is configured through the telemetry object: `show telemetry` and `set telemetry id <string>`, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The command is used to configure persistent and dynamic telemetry, and the object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. The single parameter is id, described as persistent and dynamic telemetry, a string of length 0..4096 with no default. The guide does not define the persistent versus dynamic distinction beyond that; the related views are `show subscriptions` for the subscription list, `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` for configured telemetry subscriptions, and `show subscription-path` for the paths.

Use `show third-party-app-<app-name> [version] [vendor] [product] [label] [state] [information] [enable]`, or `show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> [version] [state] [information]`. The state attribute reports the third party app state with values running, stopped or failed, and its default is stopped. The separate enable attribute is the third-party-app enabled state, true or false with default false, so an app is not enabled by default: if enabled the app is started and is also enabled upon system restart; if disabled the app is stopped. Set these with `set third-party-app-<app-name> [state <value>] [enable <value>] ...`. Access Mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Type `add <tab>` to visualize all entity types that are creatable at that time, and `add -h` for help. The add command reference also lists the creatable entities (among them aaa-server, access-rule, ace, acl, card, chassis, dial-out-server, dns-server, file-server, interface, log-server, ntp-server, odu, ospf-instance, snmp-community, snmp-target, snmpv3-user, task, template, tom, user, user-group, xcon), each with a page reference to its own command section where the mandatory and optional attributes are given. Some entities have mandatory attributes that must be provided on creation; if a mandatory attribute is not provided in the command itself, the CLI will automatically ask for it. Entities managed by the system cannot be created with add. Syntax: `add [-v|-m|-f] <entity id> [(<attribute> <value>) ...]`.

Yes. In all cases the clear command requires a user confirmation, and a confirmation prompt is displayed if the -f flag is not provided; -f forces the command without confirmation. Syntax is `clear [-f] <subcommand> ...`, with -h for help, and the Access Mode is Operational Mode. The subcommands are alarm, app, certificate, crl, database, dns, file, isk, log, ospf, pm, recover-mode, statistics, system and topology. Note that `clear system factory-reset` with the shutdown option is not supported on the L0 cards.

Yes, with the cli object attribute show-alarm-columns, which sets the columns to display in the output of the 'show alarm' CLI command. Permitted values are a list of columns separated by commas, default-columns to show the pre-defined columns, or default-columns,<additional-details> to add the <additional-details> column to the pre-defined columns. The default is default-columns. This configuration has a global effect and takes effect on all CLI sessions. Examples: `set cli show-alarm-columns col1,col2,col3` and `set cli show-alarm-columns default-columns,corrective-action`. Other cli attributes are enabled (default true), port for CLI access via ssh (1..65535, default 22), default-interactive-mode (default true), and the show-only script-dir.

Use `set cli-session-config-<session-id> [cli-lines <value>] [cli-columns <value>]`. cli-lines is the configurable number of rows used for display before pausing the output, a number in the range 10..1000 with default 40; after pausing, pressing [SPACEBAR] resumes the display. cli-columns is the number of columns used for display, range 80..4000, default 80. Example: `set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-lines 30`. The same object also carries interactive-mode (true/false, default true, set per CLI session and not persistent) and display-timestamp (true/false, default false). View with `show cli-session-config-<session-id>`.

Yes. The connect command establishes an ssh session directly from the CLI: `connect [target-address=]<value> [user-name=]<value> [[port=]<value>]`. target-address is a mandatory attribute and may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or hostname (if DNS is configured); it requires connectivity. user-name is a string of 0..64 characters. port is optional; port 22 is used by default but another can be provided if needed, which is useful to access the shell port. Access Mode is Operational Mode. Example: `connect 10.41.24.55 admin port=8022`, which then prompts for the target user's password.

Yes, the convert command: `convert [target-representation=]<value> [command=]<value>`. target-representation may be netconf-xml (an entire NETCONF xml payload), netconf-python (Python code performing the NETCONF request), restconf-json (HTTP method, URI, headers and body with JSON payloads), restconf-xml, restconf-python, plaintext-to-encrypted, snmp-oids (OIDs for the objects in a show command), or netsnmp-cmd (a shell command performing the SNMP request). The command string should be enclosed in quotes; multiple CLI commands separated by ';' are merged into one payload when possible. Generated Python works with Python 2 or 3 and needs ncclient for NETCONF or requests for RESTCONF; host, IP and user-name are auto filled and only the password must be entered. Example: `convert restconf-python 'ping 1.23.151.23'`.

No. The default command assigns default values to the targeted entities, but some configuration attributes will not be reset to default, including mandatory parameters and attributes only settable at creation. If attributes are specified only those are set to their default value; otherwise all possible configuration attributes are defaulted. Syntax: `default [-f] [entity-id=][,]* [[attribute=][,]*]`, where -f forces the command without confirmation and -h displays help. Multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*), for example `default alarm-severity-entry-FAN/*` or `default alarm-severity-entry-*`; specific attributes are given as a list, for example `default tom-1-4-T16 label,phy-mode`. The default command is not supported in 1830 GX G30 Releases 5.0 and 5.1.

Use the best effort delete flag: `delete -b <object>`, introduced in R9.0. Standard behaviour is that `delete <object>` fails if the object does not exist; with -b the check for object existence is bypassed without returning a failure, so no error is displayed if the object is missing. It has the same functionality as a NETCONF 'remove' operation. Note that -b may still produce other errors, such as precondition failures. For scripts you will normally combine it with -f, which forces the command without confirmation (delete otherwise displays a confirmation prompt, and each instance must be confirmed individually when multiple are selected). -v validates the command only, replying 'OK' if valid.

The exit command logs you out of the current CLI mode: it terminates the current CLI session if you are in operational mode, or leaves configuration mode if you are in candidate mode. A confirmation prompt is displayed unless the -f flag is provided, which forces the command without confirmation; -h displays help. Syntax is `exit [-h|-f]`. The keyboard shortcut Ctrl+D has the same effect as `exit -f`, that is, it exits immediately with no confirmation. Access Mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use the expect command, which ensures that an attribute matches an expected value: `expect [-r] [<instance>=]<value> [<expected-value>=]<value> [<attribute>=]<value>`, for example `expect ne ne-name GX-NE-123`. If the value matches, no output is seen; if it does not, an ERROR message is shown. It is intended for scripts and automation to guarantee specific assumptions and may be invoked multiple times to validate multiple attributes; if the script runs in 'stop-on-error' mode, a failed expect stops the script immediately. The -r flag enables regex mode, making the expected-value a regular expression instead of a literal string, for example `expect -r software-load-active swload-version R5.*`. Wildcards to select multiple object instances or attributes are not supported.

Yes. The `export` command defines variables for use in CLI; reference them as ${variable} in any CLI command. Syntax: `export [-h]` and `export [<variable>=[<value>]]`. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The variable name can be any alphanumeric string; the value can be any supported character, including spaces. Variables are locally defined per session, so they are removed after the session is closed, i.e. they do not survive logout. This is particularly useful in CLI scripts. `export SLOT_NUMBER=2` declares one, `export SLOT_NUMBER=` deletes it, and `export` with no arguments lists all existing variables (for example export MYSESSIONID="10.100.152.29:56154" and export MYUSERNAME="admin").

`shell` launches a Linux bash shell on the node itself, running as the currently logged-in user with that user's command access; certain commands can be run with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo' (permitted binaries include /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and a set of /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts). `gshell` launches a bash shell inside a Guest Container instead, with syntax `gshell [-h] [<cmd>]`, and has a pre-condition: the dial-out server must be configured for the command to execute properly. Both are Operational mode, both allow a single command to be passed inline (`shell ifconfig`, `gshell ls -l`), and both return to the CLI prompt on 'exit'.

No. `kill-session <session-id>` closes any established session regardless of type (CLI, NETCONF, etc.), but the <session-id> must match an existing session-id in the form '<ip-address>:<port>' and cannot match the id of the current session. To end your own session use the normal `exit` command instead. Access mode is Operational mode. Use `show session` first to list current sessions and get the id. Example: `kill-session 10.24.11.25:56212`.

Use the `message` command, which sends a message to other CLI sessions: `message [message-content=]<value> [[target=]<value>]`. Access mode is Operational mode. message-content is a string of 1-4096 characters. target defaults to 'all', so a bare `message "System will reboot in 5 minutes"` broadcasts to every CLI session. Other target values are local (only serial console or CRAFT sessions), remote (only remote sessions such as SSH), a specific session-id, or a username (all CLI sessions of that user). Example targeted form: `message "System reboot in 5 minutes" 0.0.0.0:36`. The command can also be executed from NETCONF and RESTCONF, but the message is only ever delivered to CLI sessions.

The `property` commands set or show a type-specific property that the system auto-instantiates but the user can configure. Syntax: `show property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value] [description]` and `set property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value <value>]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Two properties are supported: fast-client-recovery, which indicates whether fast client signal recovery is enabled or disabled in case of client signal failures, with values disabled or enabled and default disabled; and max-packet-length, the maximum packet length supported by the CHM6 / CHM6L DCO, with a range of 1518 to 18000 and default 1518. Example: `set property-1-5/fast-client-recovery value enabled`.

Use `run`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Pre-condition: the task or script to be called must already be defined. Syntax: `run task [[task-name=]<value>]` and `run script [-q] [-y] [-e=<value>] [-r] [[script-name=]<value>] [[arguments=]<value>]`. task-name is a leafref to /ioa-ne:ne/ioa-ne:system/ioa-ne:scheduled-tasks/ioa-ne:task/ioa-ne:name; script-name is a relative path within the script directory, with optional arguments. Flags: -q runs the script quietly (only command output, not the commands themselves), -r executes the script as a declarative config script that replaces system configuration with the script content, and -e sets the error option: continue (default), stop, or rollback. Examples: `run task collect-diag`, `run script config.cli -e=stop -q`.

Both add, set, show and delete user-configurable scheduled commands in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode, and both use the same core attributes: enabled (true/false, default true), command (string), command-type (CLI command), frequency in w/d/h/m/s, start-time, end-time, persistent (true/false, default true) plus read-back task-status, next-run, previous-run, previous-result and previous-output. `task` is the richer form: `add task-<name> command <value> ...` also takes label, alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed) and number-of-runs (1..65535 or no-limit), and reports task-status as scheduled, disabled, finished or ongoing with previous-result success/fail. `scheduled-task` is addressed as scheduled-task-<name>, listed with `show scheduled-tasks`, and an empty frequency means a single-occurrence task.

Only if you are an SA user. `show session` lists currently established management layer sessions; only SA users can access the list of all sessions, and remaining users can only see their own session. Syntax: `show session-<session-id> [session-user] [session-type] [session-protocol] [created-time] [local-ip-address] [dial-out-server-name]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. session-id is the IP address and transport port of the session, or 'NA' if initiated from the serial port. session-type can be cli, snmp, netconf, restconf, webgui or gnmi; session-protocol can be telnet, telnet-raw, serial, ssh, ssh-raw, https or http. RESTCONF sessions appear in CLI when Cookie Based Authentication is used; the default keep-alive is 5 minutes, changeable with the restconf cookie-timeout attribute.

Yes. `set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...]` accepts wildcards (*) to set an attribute on multiple instances at once: as replacement of the whole instance key (card-*), of a single instance key (port-1-4-*, port-1-*-3), of all following keys to the right (odu-1-4,5,6,7-*), for auto-completing instance keys (user-admin*, ethernet-*), and for auto-completing attribute names (admin* for admin-state). Ranges use [] (card-1-[1..4]) and lists too (interface-[DCN,CRAFT]). Filters in the form <attribute>=<value> restrict the set to matching entities, e.g. `set port port-type=line admin-state lock`. All pairs must belong to the same managed entity; if no entity id is given the currently scoped entity is used. The command asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances; -f forces without confirmation and -v only validates.

User access to the `shell` command can be limited to users in the NA, NE and TT user-groups. The command launches a Linux bash shell from within the CLI in Operational mode, syntax `shell [-h] [shell command]`. The shell is launched as the currently logged-in user and allows only the commands accessible to that user; exiting the shell (for example with 'exit') returns to the CLI prompt. Certain commands can be run with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo', limited to a fixed list including /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and scripts under /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin such as download.sh, config_ip.sh and docker.sh. A single command can be passed inline, e.g. `shell 'sudo netstat -alnp | grep sshd'`.

Yes. If a user executes a `show` command that generates more than 50000 objects, an error message is displayed to indicate that the output is too large. Narrow the request instead: give a specific <entity-id> rather than an <entity-type>, use filters (<attribute>=<value>), name individual attributes, or limit recursion with -r=<n> (full recursion if n is omitted). Other flags that reduce output are -c (container instances only), -a (attributes only), -x (configuration/read-write attributes only) and -o (state/read-only attributes only); -l gives long display, -t tabular format and -d shows default values. Piping to `| more` pages long output. Since R9.0 show output is sorted numerically.

Yes, with `simulate`, in Operational mode: `simulate [trigger=]<value> ([holder-AID=]<value> [type=]<value> [[subtype=]<value>] | [alarmed-entity=]<value> [alarm-type=]<value> [[alarm-direction=]<value>] [[alarm-location=]<value>])`. Triggers are raise-alarm, clear-alarm, plug-in-fru and plug-out-fru; note that plug-out-fru is not supported. Equipment simulation needs the holder-AID matching the card slot or TOM port (string 1..64) and, for plug-in, the card type, with subtype optional. For alarms, alarmed-entity and alarm-type are given; if either is omitted when clearing, all simulated alarms are cleared. alarm-direction and alarm-location default to auto, selected automatically by the system. The command works in a simulator and on a real system, but simulation cannot interfere with real hardware, for example you cannot simulate plug-out of hardware physically present. Example: `simulate plug-in-fru 1-5`.

Yes. The `sleep` command specifies a delay for a specified amount of time, and the sleep time may be an arbitrary floating point number. Syntax: `sleep <time in seconds>` (plus `sleep -h` for help). Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The single parameter is the duration of delay in seconds. `sleep 1` waits one second and `sleep 0.1` waits 100 milliseconds.

Add a task with no frequency: leaving frequency unset makes it a single-occurrence task that runs once at start-time. Syntax: `add task-<name> command <value> [enabled <value>] [label <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [command-type <value>] [frequency <value>] [number-of-runs <value>] [start-time <value>] [end-time <value>] [persistent <value>]`. name is up to 64 characters, command is 1..1024 characters, command-type defaults to cli, enabled defaults to true, persistent defaults to true so the task survives a system restart, alarm-report-control defaults to allowed, and end-time defaults to never. Documented example: `add task-db_backup_once command "upload database file-server=xfr1" start-time 2021-04-23T05:05:00+00:00 alarm-report-control allowed label "DB Backup once"`. The file server xfr1 must be configured before this command is used. task-status shows finished once a single-occurrence task has executed.

`terminate` stops a running operation, in Operational mode. Forms: `terminate location-led <entity>` (a chassis or a card; no effect if no location led test is active there), `terminate otdr [entity=]<value>` for an ongoing OTDR measurement on a port, `terminate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<value>` for a manually triggered OTDR-based Raman fiber check on an OTS-R entity, `terminate loopback [entity=]<value>[,<value>]*` for WSS loopback on NMC entities (all channels under the loopback in a degree must be terminated, and channels cannot be added or removed while a loopback is active), and `terminate cable-id` for a CableID verification test. Aborting OTDR restores otdr ne function attributes and reverts ots-r-auto-otdr auto-otdr-state, re-raising PUMPS-DISABLED-OTDR-TEST-FAILED if it was fail. CableID verification stops only after the current port-pair completes (maximum delay one port-pair verification time); confirm with `show cable-id cable-id-status` that cable-id-state is idle.

`update` does not assign an arbitrary value the way `set` does; it triggers a predefined update action on an object attribute according to the provided <type>. Syntax: `update [type=]<value> [[entity-id=]<value>[,<value>]*]`, Operational mode only, and multiple instances can be selected with a wildcard (*). The four types are span-loss-alarm-threshold (re-evaluates the OTS attribute span-loss-alarm-threshold), filter-insertion-date-now (updates the chassis dust filter insertion date to the current date), set-under-commissioning (sets the entity to under commissioning state, applicable to NE entities in SLTE systems) and clear-under-commissioning (sets the entity to Ready for Service state, likewise for SLTE NEs). Examples: `update span-loss-alarm-threshold ots-1-1-dwdm-line` and `update filter-insertion-date-now chassis`.

Use the auxiliary commands `tic` and `toc`. `tic` starts a timer for the typed command and `toc` displays the elapsed time since the timer was started and the command was executed by the system. Both are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. For a single command, chain them on one line separated by semicolons: `tic;show log;toc`. The same pattern works for a list of commands in a script, for example `tic ;show log ;traceroute 10.128.1.1 ;toc`, which times the whole sequence.

Yes. Use `help -s <keyword> [<keyword> ...]`, which searches the provided keyword(s) in all commands' help text and displays the matches in order of relevance. Partial keywords can be given with a wild card, for example `help -s inventory` or `help -s data*`. Related help forms: `help <command/container/attribute>` shows how that item can be used (`help show`); '?' on its own lists all available commands; `<command> ?` lists the addressable parameters for a command (`show ?`); `<command> -?` lists its options (`show -?`); `<command> -h` gives the complete help (`show -h`); `<command> <container> ?` shows the sub-containers and attribute list of a container; and `<command> <attribute> ?` lists the attributes of a container.

Yes to both: aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions. The `alias` command defines a friendlier alphanumeric string for one or more commands, containers, attributes or values, in Operational mode. Syntax: `alias [-h]` and `alias [<name>=<value>]`. With no arguments it prints the current list of aliases in the form 'name=value'. Multi-word values must be quoted, and aliases can reference other aliases; an alias <name> can be used without resolving it by quoting it. Examples: `alias s=show` and `alias sa='show alarm'`. Remove aliases with `unalias`.

Run `unalias -a`, which removes all defined aliases. The `unalias` command removes previously defined aliases in Operational mode; syntax is `unalias -h`, `unalias -a`, or `unalias [<name> ...]`, so you can also drop specific ones, e.g. `unalias foo` or `unalias bar baz qux`. Removing an alias has impact on all sessions and users, because aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions. The command is always successful unless a supplied <name> is not a defined alias. Use `alias` with no arguments to list what is currently defined before clearing.

`tree` displays the managed entity hierarchy in a depth-indented tree-like format, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Syntax: `tree [-h]` and `tree [-a|-o|-d=depth] ([<entity id> ...])`. Use -d=depth to cap the maximum display depth, i.e. the number of levels shown; if it is not specified all levels are displayed by default, for example `tree -d=2`. Use -a to display the target entity along with all its ancestors only, for example `tree -a interface-DCN` or `tree -a port usb`. -o displays the YANG tree of the provided top node. The base of the tree is the current working entity or the provided entity id, only managed entities and their instances are shown (no attribute names or values), and output uses the UTF-8 character set. Page long output with `tree | more`.

`edit <entity-id> [<entity-id> ...]` navigates to any entity in the managed entity hierarchy; the entity IDs can be absolute (from the system root) or relative to the current entity in the path banner, and editing a nonexistent instance fails. Examples: `edit card-1-1`, `edit port-1-5-T1`, or relative `edit chassis-1 slot-2`. `up` moves the current path up exactly one level, to the parent of the currently selected entity, and takes no parameters. `top` jumps straight back to the top of the hierarchy, the [ne] root. All three are available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, take only the -h flag, and their effect is visible on the CLI path banner, e.g. [ chassis-1 ] after `edit chassis-1` and [ ne ] after `top`.

Run `history`, which displays the current session's command history as a numbered list, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode (the only flag is -h). Repeat any entry with '!<n>', where n is the number in the history list, and repeat the immediately previous command with '!!'. To find a particular entry in a long history, filter it with a piped command, for example `history | include 'show'`.

Nothing happens. At the hierarchy top level the `up` command has no impact. `up` brings the current path up by one path level, changing the currently selected managed entity to its parent, and its effect is visible on the CLI banner; once the banner shows the root [ ne ] there is no parent to move to. The command supports no parameters other than -h and is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands are `edit`, which navigates to any entity in the hierarchy, and `top`, which returns directly to the hierarchy root.

Functionally they are the same command: both `| grep <filter>` and `| include <filter>` display only lines matching the filter, the guide states each is the same as the other, both accept multi-word filters when quoted, both support regex, both do a case-insensitive comparison (`show | grep abc` equals `show | grep ABC`), and both can be chained with other piped commands. The difference is that grep has several additional filtering options: -a=<n> shows n lines of context after each match, -b=<n> shows n lines of context before each match, and -n displays line numbers in the result. So the syntax is `<command> | grep [<option>] <filter>` versus `<command> | include <filter>`. Related filters are exclude (drops matching lines), begin and until.

Yes. Pipe the output through the `display` piped command with the `commands` mode: `<command> | display <mode>`. The `commands` mode displays the configuration as CLI 'set' and 'add' commands, and is specifically intended for creating CLI scripts from the current configuration. To capture the whole node, use the recursive show: `show -r | display commands`. Other supported modes for the show command are list (the default display mode, one value per line), table, csv, keys-table, single-table, only-values (useful for script building), xml, json, xpath, and interactive (JSON in the 'jless' viewer; press 'q' or CTRL-C to leave, ':help' for help). `display -h` shows help.

Yes. Combine the `begin` and `until` piped commands. `<command> | begin <words>` displays the output of the previous command starting from a specified word, and the output begins with the line that matches the word. `<command> | until <words>` displays the output ending at a specified word, and the output ends with the line that matches the word. The guide states explicitly that begin can be used together with the until piped command to retrieve a sub-set of an output, and vice versa. For both, <words> is the line to begin with or end with, and it may contain spaces if enclosed in quotes. Examples: `show | begin ne-location` and `show | until ne-location`. Each also accepts -h for help.

Yes, use the `more` piped command, and position matters: multiple piped commands can be used sequentially, but `more` needs to be the last one in the command line. Syntax is `<command> | more [-h]`, where <command> is any display command such as tree or show. The page size matches exactly the size of the CLI session window, so it follows the terminal size, except on the serial port where the terminal size is fixed. When the page limit is reached the display pauses; press any key to resume, or [CTRL]+[C] to terminate the display and return to the prompt. <enter> shows the next line, while any other key (including <space> or <tab>) shows the next page. Example: `tree | include led | more`.

It does not fail. With the `sort` piped command, if an unrecognized attribute name is used it is simply ignored. Syntax is `<show command> | sort [-i] [<attribute>*]`, plus `| sort [-h]` for help. <attribute> is any attribute name that exists in the context of the output, and a list of attributes can be provided as parameters to sort by. To flip the order, use -i, which inverts the order in the output and can be used on its own or together with an attribute list. Sort without parameters displays the output sorted by object instance, the same as the default display. Examples: `show card | sort`, `show port | sort port-type`, `show user | sort -i user-group last-login-date`, and `show odu | sort -i`.

Capitalisation does not matter, and yes, patterns are supported. The `exclude` piped command filters out the lines that contain the given word or string: `<command> | exclude <filter>`, with `exclude -h` for help. The <filter> does a case insensitive comparison, so `show | exclude abc` and `show | exclude ABC` are equivalent. The filter supports regex (regular expressions), and it may be multiple words separated by spaces if enclosed by quotes, e.g. `show | exclude 'ne oper'`. Multiple piped commands can be used in a single command. Examples: `show | exclude ne` and `show led | exclude status`. The inverse commands are `include` and `grep`, which filter the output that includes the filtering text.

Use the `highlight` piped command, which visually marks up a word or set of words in the output of the previous command: `<command> | highlight <word> [<word>]`, with `highlight -h` for help. More than one word can be provided. The quoting is what distinguishes the two cases: words given without quotes are searched for separately, while words enclosed within quotes are searched for as a sentence, so a whole phrase must be quoted. <word> is any word to highlight and may contain spaces if enclosed by quotes. Examples: `show odu | highlight odu4` for one word, `show odu | highlight odu4 oduflex` for two separate words, and `show odu | highlight 'idle lower-layer-down' odu4` to highlight the sequence of words 'idle lower-layer-down' plus the word 'odu4'.

Yes, use the `linenum` piped command, which adds line numbers to the output of the previous command. Syntax is `<command> | linenum`, with `<command> | linenum -h` for help. It takes no other parameters; <command> is any display command such as tree or show. Example: `show | linenum` displays an output with enumerated lines. If you are already filtering with `grep`, that command has its own -n option, which displays line numbers in the result, alongside -a=<n> (lines of context after the match) and -b=<n> (lines of context before the match).
